title: One 2027 NFL Draft Prospect From Each Team in AP Preseason Top 25 for the Falcons
summary: This is a celebration that both NFL and college football are back, and there is no better indicator than finding one 2027 NFL Draft prospect from the AP Preseason Top 25 and manifesting them into the red and black next season. This is a long exercise, so we’re not going to waste any time; let’s […]
full_text: ATLANTA, GA - JANUARY 09: Oregon quarterback Dante Moore (5) warms up prior to the start of the Indiana Hoosiers versus Oregon Ducks College Football Playoff Semifinal at the Chick-fil-A Peach Bowl on January 9th, 2026, at Mercedes-Benz Stadium in Atlanta, GA. (Photo by Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images This is a celebration that both NFL and college football are back, and there is no better indicator than finding one 2027 NFL Draft prospect from the AP Preseason Top 25 and manifesting them into the red and black next season. This is a long exercise, so we’re not going to waste any time; let’s get into it: Ohio State – DT John Walker Height: 6’4” Weight: 324 John Walker (6’4 324) Ohio State ✅ 79.0 run defense grade in 2025 ✅ Knock-back power in his hands ✅ 9.4% missed tackle rate ✅ Holding the point of attack ✅ Bull rush power pic.twitter.com/0K9bO7yups — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) July 19, 2026 It’s the first school, and I’ve already gone off the beaten path, but hear me out. If we’re in the running for Jeremiah Smith, Atlanta likely needs a quarterback more than a wide receiver. Julian Sayin and Austin Siereveld, who is probably best inside, are not one-to-one fits for their needs. So, let’s look to a potential day-two pick in defensive tackle/nose tackle John Walker. Powerful hands and is a fantastic asset at holding the point of attack against the run, a skill the Falcons desperately need on early downs. There are only so many exotic looks Jeff Ulbrich can throw at an offense; at some point, it’s going to have to be my best against your best in the run game, and Walker can be a good start in shoring that up for Atlanta. Oregon – QB Dante Moore Height: 6’3” Weight: 206 2025 Dante Moore. https://t.co/zWrTRd1rkH pic.twitter.com/snmqeftRES — Football Performances (@NFLPerformances) August 4, 2026 New York Jets fans are still kicking at the fact that Moore returned to Oregon this year instead of becoming the second quarterback off the board last draft cycle. Moore has a beautiful, easily catchable ball that falls into your hands as a receiver. The hope for 2027 is that he is more consistent and handles pressure better than last season. If he does, and the Falcons’ quarterback position does end up horribly, Moore would be a perfect fit for Kevin Stefanski and Tommy Rees’ plans in Atlanta. Georgia – CB Ellis Robinson IV Height: 6’0” Weight: 180 Ellis Robinson IV is a top 10 talent. Still needs some polish, but he’s ahead of schedule for a 1-year starter with 550 career snaps pic.twitter.com/ORtYmkrakl — James Foster (@NoFlagsFilm) May 2, 2026 All the sites where you find his information are saying that he’s 6’0”, 180 pounds, but Ellis Robinson IV plays a lot bigger than that. A physical corner with some long arms, Robinson has the potential to be the second-best corner in this draft, behind the next player on this list. Robinson is only a one-year starter, but his ability to get his hands on the football and fight through the receiver to make a play while the ball is in the air is special. He’s also quite the willing run defender. Someone is going to really enjoy having Robinson on the boundary of their defense. With Hughes getting up there in age and Terrell not far behind, it may be time to look for new blood on the outside. Notre Dame – CB Leonard Moore Height: 6’2” Weight: 197 Leonard Moore vs. USC is my favorite game for a prospect I've watched. It perfectly encapsulates Moore's lockdown nature as he follows Makai Lemon on practically every play. Truly an insane performance. pic.twitter.com/st73XQQ6QJ — Drew Collings (@DrewMCollings) August 15, 2026 A true lockdown corner. Leonard Moore will follow your number-one receiver to the ends of the earth, if he has to. Moore is an insanely talented cornerback whose large frame and elite athleticism make him a problem against the shiftier receivers, like Makai Lemon, and the bigger, more physical receivers. Him and safety Tae Johnson in the same secondary is honestly unfair, but it will be a ton of fun to watch. Texas – OT Trevor Goosby Height: 6’7” Weight: 325 Trevor Goosby pic.twitter.com/QZROmOvpfk — Owen Denny (@OwenDennyNFL) May 15, 2026 Jake Matthews has to ride off into the sunset at some point. To make it easier on him, the Falcons should take a good, hard look at a guy like Trevor Goosby. He won’t be there for the first few weeks of this season due to a non-contact knee injury, but by the end of September, you’ll be able to see why Goosby is rated as some people’s OT1 in this class. A massive human being with fleet feet and heavy hands, Goosby has the potential to be a game-changer as an offensive tackle. He does have warts in his game; he just turned 21 in May, but he’s going to be a solid tackle prospect that has fantastic upside in next year’s draft. Indiana – DT Tyrique Tucker Height: 6’0” Weight: 298 When you can generate pressure up the middle, it makes life easier for everyone else on the defense. That’s exactly what Indiana DT Tyrique Tucker ( @TuckerTyrique ) brings to the Hoosiers. One of several impactful JMU transfers, Tucker has 24 tackles, 7.5 TFLs, and 4.5 sacks this… pic.twitter.com/G7vD44r2de — Bryan (@RealBGauvin23) October 30, 2025 On day two, you’re looking for guys that can contribute early and often for your defense, and a guy like Tyrique Tucker can do that. A bit smaller than the average NFL defensive tackle, but Tucker’s production far outweighs his size. 12 tackles for loss and 6 sacks in 2025, on the way to a national championship, are definitely a great way to get your name out there. Miami – DT Ahmad Moten Height: 6’3” Weight: 311 Ahmad Moten Sr. | IDL | #Miami | 6-3, 311 Excited to watch this player this season. Disruptive interior defender that plays with explosive power and violent hands. High effort, upfield penetrator that can cause constant chaos. pic.twitter.com/WvBEkzu5Ym — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) July 16, 2026 Throughout Miami’s run to the national championship game, the talk was all about the two edges who went in the first round of last year’s draft: Rueben Bain and Ahkeem Mesidor. But my eyes couldn’t leave the middle of the defense as Ahmad Moten looked unblockable throughout the run. He has to learn to play the run better, but if he does, he could be this year’s DT1. Texas A&M – EDGE Anto Saka Height: 6’4” Weight: 255 Anto Saka (6’4 255) Texas A&M ✅ Explosiveness off the snap ✅ Freakish athleticism ✅ 28.9% win rate on true pass sets ✅ 12 career sacks in a heavy rotation ✅ Converting speed-to-power pic.twitter.com/TQXKd6HP08 — Bengals & Brews (@BengalsBrews) May 16, 2026 The losses of both Jalon Walker and James Pearce, Jr. showed just how important it is to have depth in your EDGE rotation. Saka is making the jump from Northwestern to Texas A&M this season to help Mike Elko fortify yet another intimidating defense. It will be interesting to see how Elko uses Saka’s explosiveness and where he ultimately falls in this year’s draft. Ole Miss – DT Will Echoles Height: 6’3” Weight: 315 Will Echoles | IDL | Ole Miss | 6-3, 309 Well rounded, disruptive DT. Active hands, explosive power, and finishing ability. Just turned 20 years old this week. pic.twitter.com/c2AVb9uNgj — Jordan Reid (@Jordan_Reid) August 8, 2026 Will Echoles and Walter Nolen being on the same defensive line feels like a crime against humanity. But with Nolen gone, Echoles gets a chance to be the guy on that Ole Miss line and I doubt he’ll disappoint. Echoles is already potentially this class’ best run defender, but can he continue to take that step to become a true three-down threat and be a consistent problem in the pass rush department, as well? David Stone is my personal DT1 in next year’s class, as he has a…

title: Ravens K Tyler Loop leaves only blemish on dominant win vs. Commanders
summary: The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Washington Commanders on Friday night, leaving M&T Bank Stadium with a 41-3 win and an undefeated debut preseason for head coach Jesse Minter. Minter, who was an assistant coach during the Ravens’ historic preseason win streak between 2016 and 2023, downplayed the result and redirected focus to his players. “You […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens place kicker Tyler Loop (33) reacts after making a field goal during the second half against the Washington Commanders at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Tommy Gilligan-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens throttled the Washington Commanders on Friday night, leaving M&T Bank Stadium with a 41-3 win and an undefeated debut preseason for head coach Jesse Minter. Minter, who was an assistant coach during the Ravens’ historic preseason win streak between 2016 and 2023, downplayed the result and redirected focus to his players. “You really want to play to your identity, and you want to create a play style of how you play in all three phases,” Minter said in his postgame press conference. “What are your standards? What are you accepting as playing for the Ravens?” Tonight, that standard was dominance on both sides of the ball for all 60 minutes. Minter’s defense held the Commanders to just 177 yards on 52 plays (a paltry 3.4 yards per play) and 1-for-14 on third and fourth down. Declan Doyle’s offense, led primarily by undrafted rookie quarterback Joe Fagnano, racked up 456 yards on 69 plays (6.6 YPP) and scored on four of their five trips to the red zone. The only blemish came on special teams. Kicker Tyler Loop, who ended the 2025 season with a franchise-altering miss vs. the Steelers, missed two of his four field goal attempts, fueling anxiety about the 2025 sixth-round pick heading into his second NFL season. Minter downplayed concerns about Loop after the game, noting that he “had a good camp overall,” but admitted that “it comes down to making the kicks in the pressure situations in the game. Loop, to his credit, took questions in the locker room as he did after that fateful miss in January. He insisted that his confidence “has only gone up” this preseason, but acknowledged the frustration of missing his kicks in-game. “My job is to go make kicks,” Loop said. “That is the expectation every time I go on the field. The 10 guys that are with me and the other guys on the sideline, they expect me to make the kick. That is my job, and I have to do that. When it does not happen, it is frustrating. When it does happen, it is fun. That is just the nature of the job.” Minter sidestepped a question about bringing in kicker competition before Week 1, and if this offseason has been any indication, the Ravens are planning to stick with Loop. This weekend’s roster cuts could give general manager Eric DeCosta an opportunity to add some kicking competition via the practice squad. Before that, though, he will have to set his own 53-man squad, a process that became indeterminately more difficult on Friday night. Fagnano’s impressive preseason could draw interest on waivers. So, too, could fellow undrafted rookie Ethan Burke, who has impressed off the edge throughout the summer. He and Adisa Isaac appear to be neck-and-neck for the Ravens’ fifth outside linebacker roster spot. And then there’s Baltimore’s defensive line room, which arguably has eight players who are worthy of a roster spot. “You want the guys to make the decisions really tough for us,” Minter said. “They have all done that.” Sorting through Friday night’s film will only be one part of the equation. Minter, DeCosta, and their staffs will go through every aspect of the Ravens’ upcoming season – including injuries, contracts, cap space, special teams roles, and more – to set their 53-man roster by Sunday evening at 6 p.m. ET. But even those players who do not make the team will still leave Baltimore knowing that, for at least one night, they truly played like Ravens. “The thing I am really most proud of is that all the guys out there play the way we want to play,” Minter concluded.“ And does that mean they are all going to be able to make the team? No. But, they have bought into how we want to play, and that has showed up in the games, so I’m just most happy about that.”
author: Nikhil Mehta

title: Ravens Roundtable: reactions to Baltimore’s 41-3 win over the Commanders
summary: The Baltimore Ravens left nothing on the field on Friday night, dominating the Washington Commanders start to finish and leaving with a 41-3 victory to close out an undefeated preseason. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s reactions to the win: This was about as dominant of a performance that you will ever see. Baltimore’s defense was absolutely […]
full_text: Aug 28, 2026; Baltimore, Maryland, USA; Baltimore Ravens head coach Jesse Minter prior to the game against the Washington Commanders at M&T Bank Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mitch Stringer-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The Baltimore Ravens left nothing on the field on Friday night, dominating the Washington Commanders start to finish and leaving with a 41-3 victory to close out an undefeated preseason. Here are Baltimore Beatdown’s reactions to the win: This was about as dominant of a performance that you will ever see. Baltimore’s defense was absolutely suffocating for the third game in a row this preseason. With so many quality players on defense, the Ravens are going to have to make several difficult decisions to get the roster down to 53 players. It was encouraging to see the rushing attack come alive on offense after struggling to get going in the first two games. Joe Fagnano had another excellent outing, making a strong case for Baltimore to carry three quarterbacks on the 53-man roster. The lone negative from this game is of course the performance of Tyler Loop. Loop entered this game on shaky ground and may have forced the Ravens to go to the street to find another kicker after two more misses tonight. – Dustin Cox If there’s one thing that I take away from this game, it’s part of a larger whole: this defensive staff looks like they’re going to do great things. This game wasn’t even close, and much of that was owed to the defense being disruptive early and often. You saw PBUs in big spots, several plays where the ball-carrier was blown up in the backfield, and Ethan Burke with another impressive play as he forced a fumble. Even with the grain of salt that Washington’s O-line is in terrible shape, having this defense allow only a single touchdown across the entire preseason with their second and third team defenses out there is a testament to how organized Coaches Minter and Weaver have this bunch. If that side of the ball is as organized as it looks and the offense can keep LJ upright, this team is going to be a squad to be reckoned with. – Kevin McNelis It was a dominant preseason debut for Jesse Minter’s Ravens, finishing 3-0 and only allowing one score in each of their three games. It’s hard to tell what roster questions were answered. Both Adam Randall and Rasheen Ali played well enough to justify carrying three or four backs. There’s no clear winner on the center starter. Even with Jenkins and Washington sitting out this game, they could still get traded with Peebles, Okoye, Benny and Olajiga all making plays to make the roster. Fagnano certainly made his case for keeping three quarterbacks but can the Ravens truly do that with how massive the roster crunch is this year? All three of Burke, Rucker, and Isaac made plays. In fact, with how many questions weren’t answered, we had another question added: will Tyler Loop make this roster? Loop only went 2/4 and his struggles from distance continued after going 1/5 last year from 50+. The Ravens should really consider signing a free agent. – Zach Canter
author: Zach Canter

title: Ravens-Commanders stock report: Joe Fagnano shines, Tyler Loop struggles
summary: The Baltimore Ravens thoroughly trounced the Washington Commanders on Friday night, taking home their straight preseason victory by a score of 41-3. Here is Baltimore Beatdown’s instant stock report with final roster cuts less than 48 hours away: Stock Up QB Joe Fagnano The undrafted rookie quarterback continues to make a case for the Ravens […]
full_text: BALTIMORE, MARYLAND - AUGUST 28: Joe Fagnano #12 of the Baltimore Ravens celebrates with teammates after scoring a touchdown in the first quarter during a preseason game against the Washington Commanders at M&T Bank Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Baltimore, Maryland. (Photo by Greg Fiume/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens thoroughly trounced the Washington Commanders on Friday night, taking home their straight preseason victory by a score of 41-3. Here is Baltimore Beatdown’s instant stock report with final roster cuts less than 48 hours away: Stock Up QB Joe Fagnano The undrafted rookie quarterback continues to make a case for the Ravens to carry three quarterbacks on the 53-man roster. Fagnano’s poise in the pocket and ability to go through progressions has been truly impressive this preseason, especially when you consider his lack of reps for much of training camp. Fagnano finishes his first preseason having completed 56 of his 75 passes for 509 yards, three touchdowns, and one interception, plus a QB sneak for a score tonight . That’s good for a 74.7% completion rate, 6.7 yards per attempt, and a 100 passer rating. Now we wait to see if his play forces Baltimore to stray from their usual roster approach. – Dustin Cox WR Chris Moore The veteran made a strong case for a practice squad spot with Baltimore at the least with three receptions on the opening drive, including an impressive touchdown catch. Moore has always been good on special teams and is a fine wide receiver in a pinch, making him an ideal candidate for the practice squad. – Dustin Cox RB Jonathan Ward While Ward doesn’t have a shot of making the 53-man roster, his impressive game against the Commanders could help him potentially land a spot on the practice squad. The veteran back displayed nice burst on several runs throughout the night, including a touchdown. – Dustin Cox RB Adam Randall If the Raven’s wanted to feel confident only carrying three running backs and cutting Rasheen Ali, Randall certainly made his case. Randall finished the day doing it all, averaging 5.0 yards a carry on five attempts while also adding 45 yards on three catches, including a 24 yard screen play where he stiff armed somebody and bounced their head off the grass like a ball. We’ll have to wait and see how the running back room shakes out but whether its three or four backs, Randall has earned himself a small role. – Zach Canter Stock Down K Tyler Loop The Ravens officially have a kicker problem. Misses from 58 and 51 yards against the Commanders may mark the end of Loop’s time in Baltimore. It would be hard for Baltimore to justify going into the season with Loop as the kicker after his preseason showing. NFL kickers need confidence, and Loop’s may be too far gone at this point. – Dustin Cox OL Corey Bullock Bullock has steadily slipped down the Ravens’ OL depth chart all summer, partially due to the time he missed while recovering from surgery. He went from competing from the starting center job to the roster bubble, and after an uneven night against the Commanders, he might be on the outside looking in. Bullock struggled on a pair of screens while playing guard in the first half, missing his assignment on one play and getting the other called back with an unnecessary roughness penalty. In the second half at center, he spiked a snap, resulting in a lost play. At this point, he might not even be a priority practice squad signing. – Nikhil Mehta RB Rasheen Ali Ali’s longest play of the day got called back by Bullock’s penalty, but otherwise, he was relatively ineffective on the ground and did not pick up much YAC as a pass-catcher. Throw in a bad drop and strong nights from the rest of the Ravens’ backfield – especially Adam Randall and Jonathan Ward – and Ali may have made the Ravens’ roster math a little easier tonight. – Nikhil Mehta UPDATE: Jesse Minter revealed that Ali left halfway through the game with a baby on the way. Never mind football – he’s the biggest winner on the team tonight. Stock through the roof for a new dad?

title: Ravens roundtable: what to watch in preseason finale vs. Commanders
summary: The Baltimore Ravens’ 2026 preseason will come to an end tonight against the Washington Commanders. Most of the roster is set, but Baltimore Beatdown’s staff will still have their eyes on a few key position groups during the game. Here’s what to watch: Even with many starting roles finalized, there’s still a ton to watch […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MN - AUGUST 22: Baltimore Ravens center Corey Bullock (67) and guard Jovaughn Gwyn (54) walk onto the field before the NFL preseason game between the Baltimore Ravens and the Minnesota Vikings on August 22nd, 2026, at U.S. Bank in Minneapolis, MN. (Photo by Bailey Hillesheim/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens’ 2026 preseason will come to an end tonight against the Washington Commanders. Most of the roster is set, but Baltimore Beatdown’s staff will still have their eyes on a few key position groups during the game. Here’s what to watch: Even with many starting roles finalized, there’s still a ton to watch out for. The big one is who gets the only starting job up for grabs, the center role, between Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethic Pocic. Beyond that, its depth. Do the Ravens keep three or four running backs with Adam Randall and Rasheen Ali? Who wins the fifth edge role between Adisa Isaac, Kaimon Rucker, and Ethan Burke? Can a cornerback force them to keep more than six on the roster? On the defensive line, you’ve got John Jenkins, Broderick Washington, Aeneas Peebles, Rayshaun Benny, and CJ Okoye fighting for probably three spots. And lastly, who gets the ninth spot in the offensive line group? Andrew Vorhees, Gerald Lichtenhan, Corey Bullock, and Diego Pounds are the ones fighting there. I don’t expect Carson Vinson to lose his spot to Pounds as the backup swing tackle. – Zach Canter There are a few position battles worth watching in this game, most notably at center. I am curious to see if Pocic will get the start over Gwyn tonight and whether or not he can show enough to win the starting role. Running back is another position to watch, as both Adam Randall and Rasheen Ali fight to prove they belong on the 53-man roster. No competition is more crowded perhaps than the defensive line, where players such as Aeneas Peebles, Rayshaun Benny, and CJ Okoye will duke it out for the one or two open spots at the position. I am also interested to see if Joe Fagnano can force the Ravens to keep three quarterbacks with another strong preseason game. – Dustin Cox My eyes will be on the defensive line rotation tonight. The battle between Aeneas Peebles and Broderick Washington has been well documented and to me, Peebles would be the pick for a final roster spot because of his upside as a pass rusher. Washington brings more solidity to the run game but Baltimore already has plenty of capable run stuffers along the defensive line. Obviously, the center competition by default has been cut down to Ethan Pocic and Jovaughn Gwyn. Personally, I think Gwyn will be the starter week one and we’ll gradually see Pocic overtake that role as he continues to get healthy. However, the starters that are rolled out tonight should be an indication of how those final roster spots and rotations are going to be handled. – Stephen Bopst
author: Stephen Bopst

title: Top storylines for the Ravens’ preseason finale vs. the Commanders
summary: The Baltimore Ravens are just one game away from real football. Tonight at 6 p.m. ET, they will take on the Washington Commanders in their preseason finale with 53-man roster cuts due just 48 hours later. Here are the team’s biggest remaining questions heading into today’s game: Will a starting center emerge? A season-ending injury […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: Ethan Pocic #77 of the Baltimore Ravens holds the ball against the Minnesota Vikings during the third quarter of the preseason game at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Baltimore Ravens are just one game away from real football. Tonight at 6 p.m. ET, they will take on the Washington Commanders in their preseason finale with 53-man roster cuts due just 48 hours later. Here are the team’s biggest remaining questions heading into today’s game: Will a starting center emerge? A season-ending injury to Danny Pinter turned the Ravens’ starting center competition into a two-man race between Jovaughn Gwyn and Ethan Pocic . The former has been praised for his athleticism, while the latter brings experience and leadership that could be valuable in a new offensive scheme. The battle is neck-and-neck. The division of reps tonight will be a key marker, as Pocic’s ramp-up from last season’s Achilles tear has limited his time with his potential fellow starters. If Gwyn still gets all of the first-team snaps, he likely has the job sewn up. But the Ravens could mix Pocic in with the first team, indicating the competition is still undecided, or even start him outright, suggesting he has surged ahead. Can an undrafted rookie make the 53-man roster? The Ravens historically retain at least one undrafted rookie on their 53-man roster. Last year, they kept three. But with two of those players returning and plenty of depth across the squad, there may not be room this time around. Outside linebacker Ethan Burke , offensive tackle Diego Pounds , and quarterback Joe Fagnano have all made strong cases, but will the Ravens move on from Adisa Isaac, Carson Vinson, or another player to accommodate them? All three of those players have already stood out in the preseason, so it might take an undeniable performance tonight vs. the Commanders to secure a roster spot. How will the Ravens pick from their defensive line depth? The Ravens have two moral locks at defensive tackle: Travis Jones and Calais Campbell. Broderick Washington could be a trade candidate but is otherwise guaranteed a place. Nnamdi Madubuike is somewhat of an X-factor, as his gradual ramp-up from last year’s neck injury could land him on injured reserve to start the regular season. Then there’s the depth. 2025 sixth-round pick Aeneas Peebles has flashed in the preseason and likely earned his place. One of John Jenkins and C.J. Okoye will take a roster spot as the backup nose tackle. The other will still have a case, as does seventh-round pick Rayshaun Benny. And then there’s David Olajiga, Aaron Graves, and Dion Wilson, who have all popped at different times this summer. Baltimore typically carries five defensive linemen, but depending on Madubuike’s status, there might be a case for six. That could lead the team to carry 26 defenders rather than their usual 25-25-3 offense-defense-special teams split, something Jesse Minter hinted was a possibility this week. I would argue Minter said nothing of the sort and in fact opened the door to keeping an extra player on one side of the ball! Should be defense, imo. This could also be trade bait – telling other teams that the player they may want to sign won’t be available. https://t.co/VZTsCS7MT5 pic.twitter.com/bWZ3ype3Ss — Nikhil Mehta (@nikknowsball) August 26, 2026

(Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Welcome back to Loose Feathers, a regular round-up of the latest news and analysis about the Baltimore Ravens. In today’s edition, we cover best- and worst-case scenario’s for Ja’Kobi Lane’s rookie campaign, a 2026 season preview from The Athletic Football Show , and a key injury update for the Ravens’ Week 1 opponent. Let’s dive in! Best/worst-case scenarios for Ja’Kobi Lane’s rookie year NFL offensive rookies: Best and worst case for 17 players in 2026 – Lance Zierlin (NFL.com) Best-case scenario: Baltimore’s new coaching staff showcases Lane from the jump and he rewards them by continuing his mastery in the red zone. He makes highlight-reel catches and finishes among the team leaders in touchdown grabs. Worst-case scenario: Lamar Jackson focuses his targets on Zay Flowers, Mark Andrews and others, leaving Lane to wait until the 2027 season for his chance to shine. Projected stats: 40 catches for 470 yards, 3 TDs. Excitement around rookie wide receiver Ja’Kobi Lane has no doubt been the Ravens’ biggest storyline of the summer. But non-first-round wideouts have rarely seen a substantial target share as rookies for a variety of factors. Luckily for Lane, he is primed to overcome them all. John Harbaugh’s rookie tax: Under the last coaching staff, rookies who were not drafted to be immediate starters often had to earn their playing time on special teams before seeing much offensive or defensive involvement. But Lane has been held out of special teams work at training camp along with Zay Flowers and Rashod Bateman. He was even dressed in street clothes after a cameo in last weekend’s preseason game in Minnesota. There’s a new sheriff in town, and he and his deputies are looking for Lane to prove himself doing what he does best: catching passes. Lamar Jackson’s trust: Jackson’s chemistry with his receivers has been a key factor in their success. The two-time MVP has been working to develop his connection with Lane in camp, frequently testing the rookie with tough-but-catchable passes to figure out where he likes the ball best. They will need to fine-tune things in live action, especially over the middle, but the early results are promising. Lane has delivered with several highlight grabs, and Jackson has responded with more targets. Target competition: Zay Flowers just got paid like a WR1; now, expect the Ravens to feed him the ball like one. Mark Andrews and Rashod Bateman are also primed for bounce-back seasons, and Baltimore has a host of young pass-catchers jockeying for targets. This is firmly (and literally) in Lane’s hands. Talent wins out in the NFL; if he can take advantage of his early opportunities, the ball will continue to come. In short, there’s every reason to think he can eclipse Zierlein’s projection. How will the Ravens’ defense evolve under Jesse Minter? ‘The Athletic Football Show’ previews the 2026 Baltimore Ravens – Robert Mays (The Athletic) I’m interested in not only the overall quality of this, but also how they play. Do they feel like they can play a little bit more man coverage because they have Wiggins and Marlon Humphrey on the outside? Do they get a little bit matchier? The Chargers played two-and-a-half times the amount of quarters that the Ravens played last year. When the Ravens were at their best with this core of pieces two years ago when Mike Macdonald was there, it was these ideas. Even if the system and the language were the same with Zach Orr, stylistically, they had really drifted away from a lot of the stuff that they were doing with Macdonald when this was the best defense in the NFL. And so I think we’ll see them move back in that general direction. And I think with this collection of players and just what we’ve seen from Minter over the last couple of years, it’s a group that’s pretty easy to get excited about. Ravens’ Week 1 opponents get key injury update Colts CB Charvarius Ward Sr. returns to practice, expects to be ready for Week 1 vs. Baltimore Ravens – J.J. Stankevitz (Colts.com) Colts cornerback Charvarius Ward Sr. participated in individual drills during practice Tuesday and worked his way into a handful of full-team reps Wednesday, which stand as important developments after the veteran was sidelined for the last two weeks with a back injury… …In the immediate future, though, Ward’s availability for Sept. 13’s season opener against the Baltimore Ravens could be key. Cornerback Cam Taylor-Britt, who’s had an impressive preseason and has 38 career passes defensed, is suspended for Week 1; the Colts on Wednesday waived cornerback Mekhi Blackmon, who started 11 games during the 2025 season.

title: Buffalo Bills 2026 scouting report: tackle Dion Dawkins
summary: The Buffalo Bills have been remarkably stable along the offensive line over the last few seasons. Between right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, who has taken nearly every snap on offense throughout his career, center Connor McGovern, who has played through myriad injuries and still been remarkably effective, and right tackle Spencer Brown, who overcame an early-career […]
full_text: ROCHESTER, NEW YORK - JULY 29: Dion Dawkins #73 of the Buffalo Bills signs autographs for fans on the way to the field during training camp at St. John Fisher University on July 29, 2026 in Rochester, New York. (Photo by Joe Hrycych/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills have been remarkably stable along the offensive line over the last few seasons. Between right guard O’Cyrus Torrence, who has taken nearly every snap on offense throughout his career, center Connor McGovern, who has played through myriad injuries and still been remarkably effective, and right tackle Spencer Brown, who overcame an early-career bout with the injury bug to settle in as an elite protector, the Bills have multiple incredible linemen up front. That’s obviously missing one very important, very consistent, and very good player. The left tackle is not only the most tenured player on Buffalo’s offense, but he trails only Reid Ferguson as the player who has been on the team for the longest amount of time. Now entering his tenth season, the man tasked with protecting quarterback Josh Allen’s blind side is playing at a lower weight, something he hopes will maximize his enormous talent. You already Schnow who the subject of today’s edition of “91 players in 91 days” is. _____________________________________________________________________________ Name: Dion Dawkins Number: 73 Position: T Height/Weight: 6’5” 320 lbs. Age: 32 (33 on 4/26/2027) Experience/Draft: 10; selected by Buffalo in the second round (No. 63 overall) of the 2017 NFL Draft College: Temple Acquired: Second-round draft choice Financial situation (per Spotrac): Dawkins enters the second year of a three-year, $60.06 million extension that he signed in March of 2024. For the 2026 season, his cap hit is $24,837,833. That cap number trails only Josh Allen on Buffalo’s roster. If the Bills were to release Dawkins, they would carry a dead cap hit of $22,446,833 this year. 2025 Recap: Dawkins once again entered the year as Buffalo’s starting left tackle, and he made his fifth straight Pro Bowl after another strong season. Dawkins suffered a concussion during Buffalo’s 23-19 loss at the Houston Texans, and while he was cleared to return to the game, he dealt with symptoms the following day. Those symptoms caused him to miss Buffalo’s game at the Pittsburgh Steelers the following week. Dawkins was cleared to return the week after against the Cleveland Browns, though, and he only sat out one more game: Buffalo’s regular-season finale where they rested multiple starters. Continuing a troubling trend, Dawkins was flagged for double-digit penalties for the second straight season. False starts have been an issue, as he’s been called for 16 of them over the last two years alone. For context, he had been called for 14 false starts in his first seven seasons combined. Pro Football Focus ranked him as the No. 26 tackle overall out of 89 qualifiers, grading him at a 74.1 for the season. He was ranked much higher in pass blocking (81.8; No. 7 overall) than he did run blocking (66; No. 44 overall). Positional outlook: Dawkins is one of five players listed at tackle. Spencer Brown and Chase Lundt are listed exclusively at tackle, like Dawkins is, while Jude Bowry and Tylan Grable are listed at tackle/guard. 2026 Offseason: Dawkins is healthy and he has participated in training camp practices. He said he is down around 45 pounds from last season, and while his listed weight was 320 lbs. as it’s always been, I don’t think he currently weighs 275 lbs. That tells me that he was playing above his listed weight last season, and frankly, that tracks given how he looked physically last season. 2026 Season outlook: Entering his tenth season, it’s a positive sign that Dawkins has taken steps to improve his overall health, quickness, and agility this offseason. Training camp is loaded with players who say they are in the best shape of their lives, but Dawkins does look better than he did last year. He said that he wanted to be lighter and more agile than he was last year, and that commitment to his pjhysical conditioning should go a long way towards helping him be the best version of himself this year. Dawkins is a vital part of what the Bills do. He’s a vocal leader on and off the field, and he’s one of their most consistent players on Sundays. He is going to start every game when he’s healthy, and he has done a good job remaining available throughout his career. The 2026 season holds very few questions as to Dawkins’ role. However, given his age and the realities of the business of football, it’s fair to wonder whether the 2026 season will be his last in Buffalo. The Bills could choose to hand the left tackle spot to someone like Bowry, who has impressed in camp, and save nearly $12 million on the salary cap by moving on from Dawkins next season. Now, if Dion is still playing at a high level, this isn’t something I think I would do. His importance to the team reaches far beyond the playing field. However, Buffalo is going to be tight to the cap again next year, and they have committed big resources to three younger offensive linemen in Spencer Brown, O’Cyrus Torrence, and Connor McGovern. The Bills could have redone Dawkins’ contract this offseason, but rather than lower his 2026 cap hit and kick salary down the road, they chose to keep his number high this year. That could indicate that they don’t know what they want to do with Dawkins moving forward. This whole line of thinking could also be much ado about nothing. Whatever the future holds, the present iteration of the Buffalo Bills needs No. 73 to be the best version of himself. Dawkins seems to be up to the challenge.

title: Buffalo Bills 53-man roster projection: At conclusion of preseason, before roster cuts
summary: The Buffalo Bills mounted a glorious comeback to beat the Pittsburgh Steelers 28-27 on Thursday night to cap a 3-0 preseason. Now Brandon Beane, Joe Brady, and Co. have to trim the roster from 91 players to 53 by Sunday at 6pm EST. Therefore it’s time for my final roster projection of the summer. Quarterback […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - OCTOBER 26: Sedrick Van Pran-Granger #62 of the Buffalo Bills looks on prior to his game against the Carolina Panthers at Bank of America Stadium on October 26, 2025 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by Matt Kelley/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Buffalo Bills mounted a glorious comeback to beat the Pittsburgh Steelers 28-27 on Thursday night to cap a 3-0 preseason. Now Brandon Beane, Joe Brady, and Co. have to trim the roster from 91 players to 53 by Sunday at 6pm EST. Therefore it’s time for my final roster projection of the summer. Quarterback (2) Josh Allen Kyle Allen Allen won the QB2 battle — a competition that did have some legs in training camp — with another surgical performance in the second preseason game. He’s not the best backup in the NFL but appears comfortable in Joe Brady’s system. Running Back (4) * James Cook Ray Davis Frank Gore Jr. Ben VanSumeren Tipping the scales back to Gore Jr. after he demonstrated how he can make something out of nothing on multiple occasions against the Steelers and had another stellar blitz pickup on a Shane Buechele long completion for the second-straight week. This is no slight on Ian Wheeler. He was dynamic in the preseason. Gore Jr. has earned this spot on the roster that he’ll at least hold until Ty Johnson returns from what I’m predicting will be a IR designation to begin the season. Wide Receiver (6) D.J. Moore Khalil Shakir Josh Palmer Keon Coleman Skyler Bell Trent Sherfield No changes here — I wanted to include Mecole Hardman here as the primary punt returner. But he muffed a punt last season and had three drops in the preseason. I’m guessing Ray Davis will be the primary kick and punt returner this season. Yes, his initial muff was ugly. Tight End (3) Dalton Kincaid Dawson Knox Jackson Hawes Despite strong pushes by Keleki Latu and even Shane Zylstra, the Bills opt to keep their normal three tight ends on the roster. Do not sleep on Latu or even Zylstra getting practice-squad elevations this season. They’ve proven their worth this summer. Offensive Line (9) * Dion Dawkins Alec Anderson Connor McGovern O’Cyrus Torrence Spencer Brown Austin Corbett Lloyd Cushenberry Tylan Grable Sedrick Van Pran-Granger For now, I have nine Bills blockers making the roster but there are caveats galore here. Given that Jude Bowry was seen in a walking boot at practice this week, it’s sensible for this raw, high-upside rookie to start the season on IR, making room for another player on the 53-man roster. That player is Van Pran-Granger who, despite losing the backup center job to Cushenberry, pieced together a strong summer. Then there’s this reasonably distinct possibility — the Bills trim the roster to 52 players to prep to add a veteran blocker released by another team after they trade Van Pran-Granger to the Commanders (or another interior offensive line needy club). Defensive Line (6) * Ed Oliver Deone Walker T.J. Sanders Landon Jackson Greg Gaines Zane Durant No changes here, although Durant leaving the Steelers game late with what looked to be a non-serious injury, is worth monitoring. Inside Linebacker (4) Terrel Bernard Kaleb Elarms-Orr Dorian Williams Joe Andreessen Yes, I just advocated a place for Jenkins on the 53-man roster earlier this morning … but Andreessen is more of a proven commodity as a depth linebacker and special teams ace. He is ahead of Jenkins’ developmental track by a year, having first made the team in 2024. In this case, the Bills cling to hope Jenkins isn’t snagged by another club after Buffalo moves him to the practice squad. Rush Linebacker (6) Greg Rousseau Bradley Chubb Michael Hoecht T.J. Parker Javon Solomon Mike Danna Based on WAWW, Danna would not make the roster. He played the majority of the fourth quarter in the final preseason. That’s typically a dead giveaway that a player isn’t going to be part of the original 53-man roster to start a regular season. HOWEVER, Danna provides Buffalo serious experience on the edge — along with some interior rushing flexibility — and I expect Leonhard would want an extra rush linebacker over another inside linebacker (see: Keonta Jenkins). Although special teams coordinator Jeff Rodgers probably would lean in the opposite direction. . Defensive Backs (10) Christian Benford Maxwell Hairston Dee Alford Davison Igbinosun Cole Bishop CJ Gardner-Johnson Jordan Hancock Jalon Kilgore Kani Walker Sam Franklin Jr. I’ve gone back and forth on Damar Hamlin — he was an afterthought this offseason but has parlayed a strong camp into a solid preseason, and I do think in a perfect world, the Bills would like to keep him as veteran experience at safety behind Cole Bishop and CJ Gardner-Johnson. For this projection, he’s left off the 53-man roster with Buffalo hoping he can be stored on the practice squad, although I do think it’s very possible Hamlin vs. Franklin Jr. is the final roster decision for Beane to make. Specialists (3) Reid Ferguson Tommy Doman Jr. Tyler Bass Hard to say if there’s been a clear winner in the punter battle — as both Mitch Wishnowsky and Doman only got cracks at it in the second preseason game. This one could go down to the wire. *Phidarian Mathis will begin serving his three-game suspension at the start of the regular season so he will not originally be on the 53-man roster Week 1. *Ty Johnson and Jude Bowry begin the season on IR in this projection

title: 4 Buffalo Bills who helped their cause vs. Steelers in preseason game No. 3
summary: The Buffalo Bills ended their 2026 preseason 3-0 with a dazzling comeback win over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night, and now have 53-man roster decisions to make ahead of Sunday evening. Which roster-bubble players made a final push to make the team with their performance in the preseason finale, you ask? My answers below. […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OH - AUGUST 22: Buffalo Bills defensive end Mike Danna (51) leaves the field following the National Football League preseason game between the Buffalo Bills and Cleveland Browns on August 22, 2026, at Huntington Bank Field in Cleveland, OH. (Photo by Frank Jansky/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images The Buffalo Bills ended their 2026 preseason 3-0 with a dazzling comeback win over the Pittsburgh Steelers on Thursday night, and now have 53-man roster decisions to make ahead of Sunday evening. Which roster-bubble players made a final push to make the team with their performance in the preseason finale, you ask? My answers below. EDGE Mike Danna I’m a staunch advocate of Bruce Nolan’s WAWW philosophy in the preseason, and Danna played a whopping 43 snaps, most of which came in the second half and well into the fourth quarter, so the writing may be on the wall regarding his future on the Bills. But it would’ve been nearly impossible for Danna to do more with his time on task late in this trio of Bills preseason games. Danna added three tackles, two more pressures, and another tackle for loss to his stellar preseason against the Steelers. I have no idea if the Bills will have room for Danna on the 53-man roster, and he feels like a potential poaching target on the practice squad. If I was the GM, I’d very much like to have a wily, versatile, thick defensive linemen with gobs of deep playoff experience in my back pocket, and that’s precisely what the 29 year old Danna is. LB Keonta Jenkins Am I the only one who visualizes Tremaine Edmunds when watching Jenkins in the Bills No. 49? In actuality, Edmunds was a first-round pick and stood at 6’5” and 250 pounds. Jenkins was undrafted out of Virginia Tech and is only 6’2” and probably in the 220-230 pound range now. But the long hair out of the back of his helmet and the way he effortlessly glides to the football is very Edmunds-esque. Jenkins had six tackles against the Steelers, one of a which was a thudding tackle for loss and tacked on a sack in his 24 snaps. Joe Andreessen did not play defense against Pittsburgh, which hints that he’s a lock to make the 53-man roster as the primary inside linebacker contingency plan. But Jenkins put quite the emphatic stamp on a summer in which he demonstrated that his arrow is pointed decidedly upward. RB Frank Gore Jr. Gore Jr., now three years into his professional career — it seems less than that, doesn’t it? — feels like a real pro’s pro at this stage, even though we’ve almost strictly seen him in training camp and the preseason. Making cornerbacks whiff in space on catches in the flat or screens, knifing his way through small crevices between the tackles, and morphing into a small cement wall in pass protection against an A-gap blitz, for the third-straight preseason, Gore demonstrated that he does everything well that teams ask of modern-day running backs albeit not against first-teamers. And he put multiple exclamation points on film against the Steelers to prove his well-roundedness. The two long gainers on short throws from Shane Buechele, a stick on a pass-pro rep that allowed Buechele to deliver a strike on a deep over, and gritty, just-take-what’s-there runs between the tackles. It was all there from Gore Jr. in this game. On 15 touches he totaled 72 yards from scrimmage and scored a touchdown. If Buffalo wants to take the precautionary route with Ty Johnson to begin the season — see: short-term IR — I believe Gore Jr. has done enough to earn an opportunity when the games count. OG Ar’Maj Reed-Adams Reed-Adams isn’t going to make the 53-man roster. But I can’t quit him. And that’s partly due to my affinity for him as a prospect. But he was an old-school workhorse MLB pitcher this preseason — the rookie guard logged another 67 snaps in the preseason finale against the Steelers. And once again, Reed-Adams did not allow a single pressure. It capped a debut preseason for Reed-Adams without surrendering a single quarterback pressure — he did have a holding call that negated one but otherwise was not flagged. The nearly 6’6” and 315-plus pounder has absolutely done enough to secure a spot on the practice squad, and I’m incredibly into his upside as, first, a deep-depth option, and eventually, a starter at either guard position on this team.

title: Panthers final 53 man roster prediction
summary: The preseason is done and over with for the Carolina Panthers. Now, teams have until 6:00pm Eastern on Sunday to trim their rosters from 90 players down to 53. We’ll make our best guess on what the final 53 is going to look like. On one hand, we already know the majority of the players […]
full_text: The preseason is done and over with for the Carolina Panthers. Now, teams have until 6:00pm Eastern on Sunday to trim their rosters from 90 players down to 53. We’ll make our best guess on what the final 53 is going to look like. On one hand, we already know the majority of the players since a lot of the roster has been pretty much set since the start of the offseason. On the other hand, on the bottom of the roster, there is a lot of movement left to happen, between practice squad assignments, injury designations, and waiver claims from other teams. Still, we’ll give it the old college try. Starters in bold and the order of players is a rough guess of the depth chart. Offense Quarterback (3) Bryce Young, Kenny Pickett, Haynes King I didn’t know what to do about King given that he hasn’t played since the Hall of Fame game, but it seems like Canales thinks he’ll be ready to play in Week 1 . That would imply that he would be on the roster. I think he’ll be comfortably behind the other two for standard quarterback play, but I wouldn’t be surprised if there are some packages for him to utilize his rushing ability. As for Young, everyone’s favorite conversation subject enters a make or break season as he tries to prove that he’s a legitimate starter in the NFL. Running back (3) Chuba Hubbard, Jonathon Brooks, Trevor Etienne/AJ Dillon (pending Etienne’s injury) The Panthers keep bringing competition in for Chuba Hubbard, and he keeps earning the starting spot. He’ll be the lead back to start the season, but Jonathon Brooks will push him for touches if he regains his college form. Etienne left Friday night’s game with an ankle injury, so his status is in flux. AJ Dillon may end up on the practice squad if Etienne’s injury is a mild one. Wide receiver (7) Tetairoa McMillan, Jalen Coker, Xavier Legette, Brycen Tremayne, Jimmy Horn Jr., John Metchie III, Ja’seem Reed Having Reed on here instead of David Moore might be more hope than prediction. Moore has been a reliable presence in the system for a couple of years and he brings value on special teams. Reed has shown a lot more as a receiver in camp and in the preseason, but Dan Morgan has said that special teams contributions weigh heavily in the decision making process at the bottom of the roster. I don’t know how Reed stacks up to Moore in that regard, but if it’s comparable, he can make the roster as the annual training camp wide receiver story. Metchie and Horn have been heavily featured in the preseason and have been appearing relatively early in the games, so it seems like they’re the highest among the second tier of wide receivers on the depth chart. Tremayne seems all but locked in as a good fill-in receiver and excellent special teams contributor. Tight End (3) Tommy Tremble, Mitchell Evans, Ja’Tavion Sanders The Panthers made a little bit of a splash signing Darren Waller, but his lack of appearances in the preseason make it seem like he’s not fully ready for game action. He can come up if and when the Panthers move on from Ja’Tavion Sanders, who seems like the odd man out at some point. There’s also James Mitchell hanging around, who’s one of those boring veterans that coaching staffs always love to have keeping things together. Feleipe Franks is also lurking as a special teams ace with some upside as an offensive player. Offensive Line (9) Rasheed Walker, Damien Lewis, Luke Fortner, Robert Hunt, Monroe Freeling , Brady Christensen, Sam Hecht, Chandler Zavala, Stone Forsythe The starting five is locked in while the Panthers wait for Ikem Ekwonu and Taylor Moton to return from their respective ailments. Fortner’s spot it by far the most tenuous, but I don’t think anyone is really pushing him to take the job right now. I know everyone would be excited to see Zavala back in the mix. Forsythe might be swapped out for Jake Curhan, but I’m not super well versed in how the backup tackle battle has been going in camp. Defense Defensive Line (5) Derrick Brown, Bobby Brown III, Cam Jackson, Lee Hunter, Jared Harrison-Hunte The last spot is up for grabs. Both Harrison-Hunte and Aaron Hall have made cases for themselves throughout camp and the preseason, and it seems like a coin flip as to who makes the roster. Whoever doesn’t make it is probably going straight to the practice squad if they clear waivers. Tershawn Wharton will also have some say in this group if and when he gets back from injury. Edge (5) Jaelan Phillips, Patrick Jones II, Princely Umanmielen, Trevis Gipson, Thomas Incoom Jaelan Phillips is the alpha in this group and Jones is the obvious number two after Nic Scourton went down for the season with a knee injury. Umanmielen has been looking good as a pass rusher in camp, while Gipson provides decent pop as depth and Incoom has a lot of special teams value. Cam Gill left a strong impression in the preseason finale with two fumble recoveries, but I don’t know if that’ll be enough to earn a spot on the final roster. Inside linebacker (5) Devin Lloyd, Trevin Wallace, Claudin Cherelus, Bam Martin-Scott, Jackson Kuwatch It’s sort of a make or break year for Wallace as a starter since he hasn’t quite developed at the rate the Panthers would be hoping for. He’ll get a huge upgrade starting alongside him in Devin Lloyd, and we’ll see if that helps him find his footing. The other three all bring value as special teams players, which is where we’ll see them for the vast majority of their snaps if the starters stay healthy. Cornerback (5) Jaycee Horn, Mike Jackson, Chau Smith-Wade, Will Lee, Akayleb Evans I wasn’t sure who to put in the final corner spot, but the fact that Evans was given the night off in the preseason finale would imply that he’s a safe bet to make the team unless there’s an injury we don’t know about. He’s got a role as a gunner on special teams and will probably only play corner in emergency situations. Chau Smith-Wade will play the nickel while Horn and Jackson reprise their roles as one of the best corner duos in the league. Safety (5) Tre’von Moehrig, Nick Scott , Lathan Ransom, Zakee Wheatley, Isaiah Simmons Five safeties is a lot of safeties, but Simmons is really more a special teams player than a true safety. Moehrig is firmly entrenched as a very good starter, while Scott is likely to be pushed for reps by the young guys Ransom and Wheatley. Specialists (3) Kicker: Ryan Fitzgerald Punter: Sam Martin Long snapper: JJ Jansen No surprises here. None of the three have even gotten competition in camp. The Panthers will be rolling with the same trio as last season.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 15 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: Football: Jacksonville Jaguars offensive lineman Richard Collier (76) in action vs Carolina Panthers Mike Rucker (93). Jacksonville, FL 12/9/2007 CREDIT: Steve Jacobson (Photo by Steve Jacobson /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images) Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #15. Mike Rucker Mike Rucker was an elite complementary defensive end. It might be a disservice to call him that, but that’s kind of what he was simply due to the sheer talent alongside him for much of his time in Carolina. The Panthers drafted Rucker in the second round of the 1999 NFL Draft. He played in a rotational role for his first two seasons and accumulated 5.5 sacks in that time. After the retirement of Reggie White, Rucker slid in to the starting defensive end spot opposite Jay Williams. He was the best pass rusher on the team that season, leading the group with nine sacks as the team struggled to a 1-15 record. That putrid season allowed the team to draft Julius Peppers, and he and Rucker formed one of the most formidable edge duos in the league with monsters on the interior like Kris Jenkins making the entire front four a nightmare for the rest of the league. Rucker hit double digit sacks in each of his first two seasons opposite Peppers. His sack production dipped in the subsequent seasons, but he was still a very effective player as an edge setter and all around solid defensive end. He tore his ACL near the end of the 2006 season. He was able to rehab in time to return for the 2007 season, and despite quickly regaining his pre-injury form, he decided to call it a career after that season at the age of 33. Rucker amassed 55.5 sacks in his time in Carolina, good for third in franchise history behind Peppers and Charles Johnson. He was also credited with two safeties, which is tied for the most in Panthers history. He never suited up for another team and has remained connected with the franchise and the city of Charlotte since his retirement; he called Panthers preseason games on local TV for a number of years. He’s a Carolina Panther through and through, For that, and for his time and effectiveness on the field as a Panther, he earns spot number 15 on the list of top 100 Panthers of all time.

All NFL teams are required to cut their 90-man preseason rosters down to 53 players by Sunday evening. Carolina Panthers gneral manager Dan Morgan and head coach Dave Canales (+3300 to win AP NFL Coach of the Year per FanDuel ) will have their work cut out for them. Not only do they have to release 37 players and build a 16-player practice squad, but they also have to keep an eye on their favorite roster bubble players from around the league to try to bring to Charlotte via the waiver wire. How does the waiver wire work? Teams have until 1 PM ET the day after roster cuts—that’s Monday, August 31st for those following along at home—to file a waiver claim. That’s just 19 hours after cuts are finalized. The NFL will then review claims and assign players to teams in order of their waiver wire priority. What is waiver wire priority? Waiver wire priority follows, for the first three weeks of the NFL season, the pre-trade NFL draft order. That order then adjusts to a record-based order, essentially the next year’s projected draft order. The Carolina Panthers are currently 19th in the waiver wire priority order. The full list is as follows: Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville Jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills San Francisco 49ers Houston Texans Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks

title: Panthers 16 Texans 13: Preseason ends on a high note
summary: First Quarter If you thought a game in the rain featuring no starters was going to be a slog to watch offensively, you were right. Though there were moments to enjoy from a defensive perspective. Trevis Gipson and Trevin Wallace each registered a sack to force a punt on the Texans’ first drive. The offense […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NORTH CAROLINA - AUGUST 28: Kyle Trask #14 of the Carolina Panthers looks to pass the ball during the first half of a preseason game against the Houston Texans at Bank of America Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Charlotte, North Carolina. (Photo by David Jensen/Getty Images) | Getty Images First Quarter If you thought a game in the rain featuring no starters was going to be a slog to watch offensively, you were right. Though there were moments to enjoy from a defensive perspective. Trevis Gipson and Trevin Wallace each registered a sack to force a punt on the Texans’ first drive. The offense didn’t do anything and punted right back, but the defense got the ball right back with an interception by Lathan Ransom that was aided by more good pressure up front. The Panthers at least got a couple of first downs on their next drive, but Kenny Pickett wasn’t able to find anyone on a 4th and 4 and the Panthers turned the ball over. DeVonta Smith broke up a couple of passes to get the ball back to the home team. Pickett found Ja’seem Reed over the middle for a 17 yard gain as the first quarter came to a close. Second Quarter A false start by John Metchie III put the Panthers behind the sticks, and they couldn’t catch up. A Sam Martin punt downed the Texans at the 10. The defense held up again and forced another punt. Kyle Trask checked in at quarterback and promptly through a very poor interception. That gave the Texans the ball in scoring range, so they were able to put a field goal on the board despite another stop by the defense. The Trask-led offense picked up one first down before punting once again, but the defense got the ball back a couple plays later after a botched exchange was picked up by Cam Gill. Just like with the Texans, the offense couldn’t punch it in and settled for a field goal. The Texans put together a decent drive in the two minute, but Brett Rypien overthrew a receiver and had his pass intercepted by Cam Miller. Trask strung together a couple of nice passes to get the Panthers into field goal range, where Ryan Fitzgerald knocked in his second kick of the night. Third Quarter The Panthers got the ball first and Ja’Seem Reed caught another 20 yard pass from Trask to get the offense moving. The drive stalled at midfield, and Sam Martin punted away. The Texans muffed the punt and recovered it inside their own five, but it was all moot as a flag for too many players on the field gave the Panthers a first down. Jimmy Horn Jr. had a nice run on a screen pass, but it was called back. Still, Trask was able to connect on a couple of passes to keep the drive alive into the red zone, though it wouldn’t make it to the end zone. Ryan Fitzgerald field goal number three put the Panthers up 9-3. The Texans responded with a field goal drive of their own. There weren’t any explosives, but they nickel and dimed their way to a field goal to make it 9-6. Fourth Quarter The fourth quarter with a couple of quick passes to move the Panthers out past midfield. Trask seemed to have found a rhythm and was delivering his passes on time and on target. He worked the team into the red zone, then Miles Davis picked up a hard two yards on a 4th and 2. On the next play, he battered his was through the defense for what was almost a 10 yard touchdown. A review took the touchdown off the board. It took a couple more tries, but Davis eventually got his touchdown. The Texans marched back down the field in response as they went into chase mode. They picked up a bunch of small gains and capped off the drive with a touchdown to Zay Jones. The Panthers couldn’t put together a drive to clinch the game and had to punt back to the Texans with a little over two minutes to play. It looked like the defense had done their job and gotten off the field with a fourth down interception, but the game was extended by a pass interference penalty. All that did was gave the Panthers a chance to rack up two more violent sacks from Elijah Garcia and Jeremiah Moon. The latter jarred the ball free, and Cam Gill pounced on it for his second fumble recovery of the game. Overview There’s not a whole lot to glean from a preseason game in which none of the starters played, but the defense showed out and a number of players put plays on film that are going to have the coaches talking. Rosters have to be finalized by Sunday, and then the regular season kicks off two weeks later.

title: 2026 Season Opener Countdown: 16 Days Remaining
summary: Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to […]
full_text: NEW ORLEANS, LA - JANUARY 07: Jonathan Stewart #28 of the Carolina Panthers runs the ball against the New Orleans Saints during the first half of the NFC Wild Card playoff game at the Mercedes-Benz Superdome on January 7, 2018 in New Orleans, Louisiana. (Photo by Layne Murdoch/Getty Images) | Getty Images Here at Cat Scratch Reader we have counted down the final 100 days leading up to the Carolina Panthers season opener by for at least the past ten years. We’ve always done this by highlighting the current player on the roster whose jersey number matches the day on the countdown. This year, we decided to change that up a bit by counting down our own list of the Top 100 Panthers of all time. This does not correspond to jersey number, does not need to be somebody who wore a jersey, and will in no way be controversial. #16. Jonathan Stewart If there’s one position group that’s always been a strength of the Carolina Panthers, it’s running back. That’s in large part due to the fact that the franchise has historically over-invested in the position, but at least they’ve gotten strong returns for those investments. A quintessential example of that is Jonathan Stewart, who comes in as the highest ranked running back on our list. The Panthers used a first round pick (13th overall) on Stewart despite having used a first round pick on current starter DeAngelo Williams just two years prior. While the allocation of resources was definitely not the most efficient, it did create one of if not the most memorable player duo in the team’s history. He and Williams combined to form Double Trouble. Stewart racked up 836 yards and 10 touchdowns as a rookie despite splitting time with Williams. In Stewart’s second season, Williams missed a couple games due to injury, and that allowed both to top 1,100 rushing yards for the season. It remains the only time that’s been done in the history of the NFL, and I’d venture to guess that record is pretty safe for the foreseeable future. Stewart would continue to split carries with Williams until the latter was let go by Dave Gettleman in one of many high-animosity moves. That finally gave Stewart the backfield mostly to himself for the first time in his career, and he responded with two seasons in which he would have been well on pace to top 1,000 yards had he not missed a couple games each season due to injury. The Panthers continued their trend of over-investing in the position by drafting McCaffrey in the first round of the 2017 draft after those two seasons from Stewart. Stewart served as the veteran battering ram while the shifty McCaffrey got up to speed with the NFL. Stewart was let go after the 2018 season due to his diminishing play and role along with some cap relief. He went on to sign for the Giants, but he only carried the ball six times before a foot injury ended his season and ultimately his career. Jonathan Stewart has maintained a central figure around the Panthers since his retirement. He’s often involved in promotional material from the team and is all over the place on social media and in local events talking about the team. While he didn’t have some of the peaks that DeAngelo Williams and Christian McCaffrey had, his longevity and tight bond with the organization earn him the highest ranking among running backs and the number 16 spot on the top 100 Panthers of all time.

title: Ben Johnson is ‘the most influential person that I’ve been around’
summary: Declan Doyle was the youngest offensive coordinator in the NFL last season under Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, and the Bears let him make the lateral move to the Baltimore Ravens so he’d get an opportunity to call plays. This year, he’s still the youngest play caller in the NFL (now 30), and he […]
full_text: CHICAGO, IL - AUGUST 03: Head Coach Ben Johnson of the Chicago Bears, Defensive Coordinator Dennis Allen of the Chicago Bears, and Offensive Coordinator Declan Doyle of the Chicago Bears observe warmups during Bears training camp at Soldier Field in Chicago, IL on Saturday, August 3rd, 2025 (Photo by Ben Hsu/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Declan Doyle was the youngest offensive coordinator in the NFL last season under Chicago Bears head coach Ben Johnson, and the Bears let him make the lateral move to the Baltimore Ravens so he’d get an opportunity to call plays. This year, he’s still the youngest play caller in the NFL (now 30), and he made an immediate impression on the Ravens. You’ve heard the players rave about Declan Doyle all offseason. Now see why for yourself. Check out Wired right now: https://t.co/FHwqKSF8Hm pic.twitter.com/iaUwOnJERC — Baltimore Ravens (@Ravens) July 23, 2026 Doyle’s coaching career started at Iowa in 2016, where he was an offensive student assistant until 2018, but in 2019 he was hired by head coach Sean Payton and the New Orleans Saints. When Payton retired following the 2021 season, Doyle stayed in New Orleans one more year, but when Payton unretired to take the Denver Broncos job in 2023, Doyle followed Payton to the Mile High City. This is Doyle’s 11th year coaching football, and he spent just one year in Chicago with Johnson, but it was an impactful time for him. “He is brilliant; he’s detailed. He made me view football in a completely different lens.” Doyle said of Johnson via Ryan Mink, the Editorial Director for the Ravens’ team site. “From the spacing of the field, the spacing of the passing game. He taught me more about football in a year than … he’s arguably the best coach I’ve ever been around. He’s probably the most influential person that I’ve been around. In addition to it, my relationship with him is like he was the older brother I never had. I felt like he was the closest thing to myself that I’ve ever been around in coaching in just how he approaches the game, how he felt about offense, his logic.” Now I gave you Doyle’s coaching history to highlight all his time spent with Payton, the 2006 NFL Coach of the Year, 2009 Super Bowl champion, owner of a 184–108 record (.630), and a likely future Hall of Famer, and yet he has all that praise for Ben Johnson based on their lone year together.
