title: Packers fans should be watching Pierre Strong in the preseason finale
summary: Pierre Strong was drafted by the New England Patriots in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL draft after an incredible final season at South Dakota State, when he carried the football 240 times for 1686 yards and 18 touchdowns. In his draft guide, The Beast, Dane Brugler had him as a likely fifth rounder […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 21: Que Robinson #51 of the Denver Broncos tackles Pierre Strong Jr. #22 of the Green Bay Packers during a preseason game at Empower Field At Mile High on August 21, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Tyler Schank/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images) | Getty Images Pierre Strong was drafted by the New England Patriots in the fourth round of the 2022 NFL draft after an incredible final season at South Dakota State, when he carried the football 240 times for 1686 yards and 18 touchdowns. In his draft guide, The Beast , Dane Brugler had him as a likely fifth rounder praising his vision and speed , though Brugler emphasized his lack of size and an issue with fumbling (partially due to small-ish hands). Strong was traded to the Browns after his first season, and his his workload slightly increased from 10 carries as a rookie to 63. During his Cleveland stint, Strong mostly served as a passing downs specialist while averaging a respectable 4.5 yards per carry and 8 yards per reception, and there’s definitely some big play ability and elite agility in his repertoire. This was on display in last week’s preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and Denver Broncos; while wearing green and gold, Strong averaged 4.6 yards per carry on eight carries and ripped off a 68-yard kickoff return. I actually like Strong better than Marshawn Lloyd as both represent the potential “lightning” to Josh Jacobs’ thunder, and while Lloyd is quite a bit larger, Strong is the better athlete, and despite his small size, he’s been more durable. The Josh Jacobs problem Matt LaFleur may be a very successful offensive football coach, but I still think he runs the ball too much. I don’t mind running the ball, and in 2024 when Josh Jacobs was ripping off 4.4 yards per carry and scoring 15 touchdowns, it was mostly fine. Unfortunately, since that time the Packers’ offensive line has declined as a run-blocking unit, and it’s possible that seven years of physical punishment has started to wear on Jacobs. And now, with Jacobs charged with assault and a pretty nasty video tape of the incident allegedly out there, there is an opportunity for the team to move on from Jacobs before he falls off a cliff (and also to get an alleged abuser off the team). Back in 2022 Josh Jacobs led the league in rushing yards with 1653 , and was also elite in exceeding his expected rushing total. The NFL’s NextGenStats page has a series of metrics which tracks how many more yards a back gains than expected based on the blocking on the play, the quality of the opponent, and several other factors. (This advanced metric was born out of the NFL’s Big Data Bowl contest in 2020 ) Jacobs gained 0.47 yards over expected per attempt that year, which ranked 11 th among qualifiers. That may not sound overly impressive, but maintaining that level of production of his robust total of 340 carries is impressive. Of the ten backs that ranked higher, only Cleveland’s Nick Chubb was even in the ballpark with 302 carries. Jacobs plummeted the following year due to injuries that caused him to miss four games, but he rebounded nicely in 2024 in his inaugural Packer season with 0.73 yards over expected per attempt, which tied him in tenth with teammate Emanuel Wilson . In 2025 Jacobs also suffered some injuries, and once again fell to -0.03 yards over expected . It’s possible that this is just a matter of health, and that after an offseason of rest and recovery he would be back to his old self again. But, running back is a young man’s game, Jacobs is expensive for a running back, and Jacobs turned 28 in February. He also uses a punishing running style and he has exceeded 200 carries in every season of his career (and 300 twice). He is not a great bet to age gracefully, and weird, bad offseasons don’t help. Committee Time While I’m not a huge fan of Marshawn Lloyd, a committee of Strong, Lloyd, and Chris Brooks would probably be fine. Brooks is an outstanding blocking back and a good enough receiver. He’s very useful and he’s capable of rattling off 5 yards a carry against light boxes while keeping your QB upright. I love Chris Brooks as a player, just not at 200 carries. In the unlikely event the Packers did move on from Jacobs, I could see the case for bringing in another power back, but even if they didn’t, they could probably get by with Lloyd/Strong/Brooks just fine, and with one additional hidden benefit. Matt LaFleur would be somewhat likely to run less without a proven workhorse, and so the number of passes the team throws would likely increase. Given that Jacobs isn’t what he once was anyway, this could actually provide a massive benefit to the team. Jacobs is one of Matt’s favorite toys, but it’s not working so well anymore. The remaining running backs have enough combined skills to make up for most of what Jacobs does at this point in his career. I don’t think they will move on, but if there really is a video out there , they’re playing with fire for no good reason. Use tonight’s game to check out the backups.
author: Paul Noonan

title: Packers Film Room, Preseason Week 2: Emptying the Notebook on the Offense
summary: During the season, I tend to dig into either specific plays or look at some of the bigger picture takeaways. Scheme and gameplan and blah blah blah. The preseason is different because those things don’t really matter. I’m more concerned with how individual players looked. So I watch a ton of players, taking notes and […]
full_text: DENVER, CO - AUGUST 21: Green Bay Packers tight end Drake Dabney (49) runs after a catch in the first quarter during a preseason game between the Green Bay Packers and the Denver Broncos at Empower Field at Mile High on August 21, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Dustin Bradford/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images During the season, I tend to dig into either specific plays or look at some of the bigger picture takeaways. Scheme and gameplan and blah blah blah. The preseason is different because those things don’t really matter. I’m more concerned with how individual players looked. So I watch a ton of players, taking notes and gathering clips, then look up and realize I don’t have time to write about them all. What a fool I’ve been! The week is almost over! This week I got a chance to write about Jordan Love and Trey Smack , but then it all went south on me. So, today, we’re just doing a bit of a data dump. I’ll write about some of the players I watched on offense, throw out some notes and clips and we’ll all move on with our days. Let’s go. Offense Isaiah Neyor (80) Week 1 saw Neyor as a possession receiver. A lot of stuff close to the line. He has speed (ran a 4.4 40 at the Combine), but we didn’t get a chance to see him open it up last week. He had a few snaps running deep this week. I’ll say that it didn’t look quite as explosive as Sturdivant, but his speed was on display more than we saw in week 1. He shows a solid ability to stack the corner when he gets over the top, as well. One issue I had in Week 1 was Neyor’s blocking. He showed both a willingness to block and an understanding of where to be, but every single block attempt involved him wrapping his arms around his target. We saw some better form in that regard this week. In the shorter area, he shows some really nice snap at the top of his routes to create separation. Week 1 saw him working primarily outside. This week saw him in the slot a bit more, and he looked good when put there. If he’s able to improve his blocking form, working as a blocker out of the slot could be a nice spot for him. We didn’t necessarily get a ton of flashes this week, but he continues to show a well-rounded skillset. J. Michael Sturdivant (87) Unlike Neyor, we pretty much only got go routes from Sturdivant in Week 1. His explosion/speed was on full display, but we didn’t see much more than that. This week we got a little more, with Sturdivant showing good, sharp breaks at the top of his shorter routes. This is something that could really serve him well with more room to work: threaten with his speed, then break off a route. In this next clip, you can see him attacking the outside shoulder of the defender before snapping back inside. Unfortunately, this is the play he was injured on, so there were limited snaps for Sturdivant this week. We did get to see a bit of blocking, and the process looked much better than we had previously seen. In Week 1, he was tentative and didn’t always seem to know where he was supposed to be as the play unfolded. This week he attacked the blocking much better. Drake Dabney (49) I thought Dabney looked much more comfortable this week. Locked down some of his blocking assignments, and was at the very least a general nuisance when he wasn’t locking up. He knew where to be and wasn’t shy about engaging. Has a little movement as a receiver as well. Not necessarily a field-stretching type of guy, but there might be a little more here than I had previously thought. McCallan Castles (47) Looked a lot like Dabney in terms of his approach, but didn’t work quite as well as a receiver. Of the two, I’d certainly prefer Dabney at this point, but Castles showed some nice things as a blocker. Jager Burton (52) I didn’t get a chance to highlight Burton on all of these clips. Apologies. If you’ve seen one clip of Burton this week, it’s this one. And it’s a good one. He’s working as left guard, going against Zach Allen. Burton has good drive off the line, controls the rep and ends up burying Allen. Tremendous rep. I’m also a sucker for a young guy who is always looking for work. As the rep goes on Burton doesn’t have anyone to block, so he puts a shoulder into #96. You can also see his strength as he drives as part of a double team. He keeps driving through the whistle, which is always something I like to see. Unfortunately, it’s not all sunshine and rainbows. We saw him win against Zach Allen earlier. Here, he very much does not do that. Allen gets into Burton’s body and easily sheds the block attempt to hit Lloyd. Down in the low red zone, he fires off and gets out over his skis quickly, allowing #98 to control the rep and easily shed the block. Burton has showed some really nice stuff that makes me believe he will be a good player, but it doesn’t seem like he’s ready just yet. There are too many reps of him getting overpowered or controlled through the entire rep. Other times it seems like he’s fine, but the defensive lineman is just holding him in place until he needs to shed. Burton also got beat multiple times by an inside swim move. His recovery move was to turn and lunge with his arms wide, which feels like offensive holding waiting to happen. Albums listened to: Pedro the Lion – It’s Hard to Find a Friend ; Dolly Parton – Ultimate Dolly Parton

title: Tyrod Taylor vs. Kyle McCord: The Case Against Each Packers QB
summary: A few days ago, I tried with all my might to make the case for why each of Tyrod Taylor and Kyle McCord are worthy of being the Green Bay Packers QB2. Dear reader, there was a reason that article was like 300 words long. With one preseason game left for the Packers, the team […]
full_text: ASHWAUBENON, WISCONSIN - JULY 31: Tyrod Taylor #6 of the Green Bay Packers throws a pass during the Green Bay Packers training camp at Ray Nitschke Field on July 31, 2026 in Ashwaubenon, Wisconsin. (Photo by Patrick McDermott/Getty Images) | Getty Images A few days ago, I tried with all my might to make the case for why each of Tyrod Taylor and Kyle McCord are worthy of being the Green Bay Packers QB2. Dear reader, there was a reason that article was like 300 words long. With one preseason game left for the Packers, the team will soon have to decide who they want stepping in if they find themselves without Jordan Love. Here’s what’s wrong with both of their candidates. The Case Against Tyrod Taylor A career journeyman, Taylor has spent time with 8 different teams since being drafted in 2011. The experience is there, but the ride has been bumpy. Taylor has started 63 career games, but has just one playoff start to show for it, way back in 2017 with the Buffalo Bills. AKA: When Tyrod is your long-term starter, your season is probably lost. To be fair—this can be said about most backup quarterbacks, and some starters! There’s a reason Taylor has lasted 15 years in the NFL. He’s been pretty serviceable, and has been somewhat of a dual threat with his legs over the years. The problem is, I’m worried he doesn’t have it in him anymore. Through two preseason games, the 37-year-old has completed 8 of 16 passes for 38 yards and 1 TD, and has rushed 3 times for 11 yards. Yes, this is preseason, and head coach Matt LaFleur isn’t pulling all of his regular season tricks out of the bag just yet, but I’m having a hard time envisioning a potential Taylor start going as well as what we saw with Malik Willis. The Case Against Kyle McCord And then we have…the baby! Kyle McCord has seen zero regular season action as an NFL player since being drafted in 2025 by the Philadelphia Eagles. So, we don’t exactly know what we’re working with, outside of what we’ve seen this preseason. Through two games, McCord has 24 completions on 35 attempts for 220 yards. He’s not considered much of a threat on his legs, which is a stark shift from one of the things that made Malik Willis so fun for Matt LaFleur in Green Bay. Now, I’m not here to judge a quarterback by his lack of explosiveness in the run game, but I can’t really judge Kyle McCord by much, can I? Therein lies the problem. The Verdict Personally, I think McCord gets cut, simply due to inexperience. There’s something there that should keep him on the practice squad, unless something uncouth happens during Friday’s game against the Arizona Cardinals. I think the Packers are looking for a guy who can lead a locker room if needed, and we’ve seen that Tyrod Taylor can at least do that. One thing is for sure: the Packers backup in 2026 is going to be either a guy who was drafted 180th overall 15 years ago, or a guy who was drafted 181st overall 1 year ago. Buckle up. The team’s final preseason game is at home against Mike LaFleur and the Arizona Cardinals on Friday at 7 PM local time.

title: Texans drop final preseason game to Panthers 16-13
summary: If you sat down to watch the third Texans’ preseason game and watched the entire thing, you get nothing but respect from me. Because this game was just difficult to watch. No starters played, as was expected because who wants to put starters at risk for a meaningless game, but there were things that we […]
full_text: CHARLOTTE, NC - AUGUST 28: Carolina Panthers linebacker Claudin Cherelus (53) tackles Houston Texans running back Deuce Vaughn (31) during a preseason NFL football game between the Houston Texans and the Carolina Panthers on August 28, 2026, at Bank of America Stadium in Charlotte, N.C.(Photo by John Byrum/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images If you sat down to watch the third Texans’ preseason game and watched the entire thing, you get nothing but respect from me. Because this game was just difficult to watch. No starters played, as was expected because who wants to put starters at risk for a meaningless game, but there were things that we could learn from the game. First of all, the offensive line cannot afford a single injury this season. Not a one. Because the depth behind the Texans line is upsetting. The backups, in the first drive of the game, surrendered two sacks of Davis Mills. That was the opening drive when our backups should have been up for the game getting completely pants’d by future grocery stockers. While it might not be enough to get him a spot on the roster, Sabastian Harsh had the game of his life, racking up three tackles, a sack, and a pass deflection on the day. He might make the practice squad based on that performance. Beyond that, it was a snooze for most of the game. Neither team scored a touchdown until late in the fourth quarter of the game. It was a bad, boring game that we had to get through to watch real football. And now we are clear for the regular season. The Houston Texans’ season starts Sunday September 6 at noon CDT against the Buffalo Bills. We’ll see you then!

title: Who’s on the Outside Looking In Before Houston’s Final Preseason Game
summary: The opportunities to impress this coaching staff have dwindled with one preseason game left before the 53-man roster cutdowns. Friday’s game against the Carolina Panthers represents the final opportunity for players to put compelling tape together and earn a spot on this roster. Given the number of injuries this training camp, there are more roster […]
full_text: The opportunities to impress this coaching staff have dwindled with one preseason game left before the 53-man roster cutdowns. Friday’s game against the Carolina Panthers represents the final opportunity for players to put compelling tape together and earn a spot on this roster. Given the number of injuries this training camp, there are more roster spots available than anticipated. Notably, the fourth defensive end, third and fourth running back, fifth and sixth receiver, and multiple linebacker spots are up for grabs. All it takes is one to two elite plays for a fringe player to compel Nick Caserio and DeMeco Ryans to keep them on the team. Below, you’ll find the eight players who are on the outside looking in of the roster who can secure their spot with a good performance. A few have climbed the depth chart thanks to injuries elsewhere, including Solomon Byrd, yet they still have to prove they’re a better fit than whoever becomes available once rosters are trimmed. Injured honorable mentions: Jawhar Jordan, RB Dominique Robinson, DE Collin Wright, CB Jake Hansen, LB Brevin Jordan, TE Solomon Byrd, DE The seas have parted for the former 2024 seventh-round draft pick. He’s been cut in successive offseasons, but finally has a chance to make the roster. Injuries to Dylan Horton and Dominique Robinson elevate him to he DE4 role. He’s looked stout against inside runs and play actions, but has struggled against outside zone where he loses contain. A big performance against the Panthers can seal a roster spot for him. British Brooks, FB/RB The veteran fullback has out with an injured wrist all training camp. The offense has fully adapted without his presence and TE Cade Stover has assumed the role. He must demonstrate him impact on the entire offense by proving the run game is incrementally better with him than without. Not a tall task given how poor the run game has looked, but he only gets one shot to do so. Texans running back British Brooks on Texans All Access told @jharrisfootball & @TexansVoice that he lost 17 lbs this offseason on top of weight lost at the end of last season: “I think coming off the rookie injury I played a lot heavier than what I was the year before & I was… pic.twitter.com/F0AdJ4T5ef — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) July 13, 2026 Brooks can also tote the rock. Fans have been dying to see the 17-pound weight loss’ affect on British Brooks’ mobility and power. Anther special teams ace who provides versatility to the offense. Jared Wayne, WR Wayne watched as Nick Caserio did his thing and added three wide receivers to the room. He was a rising star this offseason, making plays in training camp and rising up the depth chart. However, Caserio wouldn’t of added veterans Sterling Shepard and Zay Jones if he had the utmost confidence in Wayne. It’s unclear where Wayne ranks on the depth chart now and he needs to win on the field and through his knowledge of the offense. Alijah Huzzie, CB Huzzie is in contention for the final defensive back spot alongside injured Collin Wright and veteran Tremon Smith. Huzzie has been competing for reps throughout camp and has played significant snaps in the preseason. He is a smaller corner who plays primarily in the slot, but doesn’t have the safety versatility to completely match Pitre’s role. He has let up a handful of catches in games, but has overall played well. He was on the practice squad last year for the majority of the season and will try to avoid the same fate in 2026 with one final, solid outing today. Looks like Alijah Huzzie earning more reps. Nice win by Hutchinson. Good to see the Texans complete another fade route. pic.twitter.com/46vXJpXtP0 — Houston Stressans (@TexansCommenter) August 16, 2026 Jake Andrews, OC Andrews entered camp as the incumbent starter at center and will leave camp most likely without a roster spot. Evan Brown has leapfrogged him at center, and Brown can also play guard. Andrews lack of versatility limits his upside on an offensive line desperately in need of a solidinterior. It may already be too late for Andrews, but one final good showing could keep him on the roster as the 10th and final lineman. Naquan Jones, DT I wrote in the Rosterology that Jones has been given every possible opportunity to shine and has yet to impress. He played in four games last year, but may return as a practice squad. He has to beat out veteran and incumbent DT Mario Edwards Jr. and show that he’s the better, more durable option at DT. Aiden Fisher, LB The last rookie in the class has navigated this tumultuous linebacker room as well as possible. He’s the signal caller for the third string and made plays in special teams. Making the roster will be almost entirely predicated on his special teams play this game. Tremon Smith, CB After trading away safety Jaylen Reed, the five corner backs are slated to make the roster. That means two of Tremon Smith, Alijah Huzzie, and Collin Wright. Smith is the odds-on favorite and listed higher inthe roster. Smith has struggled with protection in the preseason, but he’s known best for his special teams. Smith has to hold off both Huzzie and wright by dominating this last preseason game on defense and special teams.
author: Kenneth Levy

title: One of the Colts’ hottest battles has nothing to do with the quarterbacks
summary: Spencer Shrader was becoming a bit of a hero for the Indianapolis Colts. It didn’t take long either. After a penalty gave the Colts new life against the Broncos, Shrader kicked the game winner as time expired. That moved the Colts to an unexpected 2-0 and let the good times roll. Those good times came […]
full_text: INDIANAPOLIS, INDIANA - AUGUST 22: Spencer Shrader #3 of the Indianapolis Colts kicks a field goal during a preseason game against the Atlanta Falcons at Lucas Oil Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Spencer Shrader was becoming a bit of a hero for the Indianapolis Colts. It didn’t take long either. After a penalty gave the Colts new life against the Broncos, Shrader kicked the game winner as time expired. That moved the Colts to an unexpected 2-0 and let the good times roll. Those good times came to a screeching halt, however, when a Las Vegas Raider ran into his knee and knocked him out for the rest of the year. Unfortunately, that’s how sports goes, and it has led to one of the more intriguing battles in camp. Michael Badgley was actually the second choice for the Colts, but his inability to hit extra points nearly cost the Colts wins and ultimately his job. Eyes turned to Blake Grupe. He didn’t disappoint. He was so good that he was actually perfect: 10-10 on field goals and nailing all 11 extra points. He even set the franchise record for longest made field goal. Grupe has carried that success into the offseason and appears to have the edge. So, how is there a battle? The Colts have a kicker, in-house, that was perfect last year and has been solid in camp. Practice is great, but when it comes to game-day kicks, Shrader has shone. His biggest knock was leg strength. That kick against Denver, yeah, it had to be re-kicked because his first attempt fell short. In two preseason games, though, Shrader has hit from 53 and 61 yards out, going a perfect 4-4. Meanwhile, Grupe has been the opposite of perfect, missing from beyond 60 and botching a 36-yarder. That can’t happen. Sports is all about doors. Doors shut. Doors open. When Spencer Shrader went down Week 5, it created an opportunity for Blake Grupe to eventually take over. Now that Grupe has struggled in game action, that same door Shrader opened is now allowing him back in. Grupe still appears to have the edge, but this is definitely a battle to watch as the preseason continues.

(Photo by Chris Carter/Getty Images) | Getty Images Anthony Richardson’s future with the Indianapolis Colts continues to feel uncertain. Could see multiple QBs on the move in the next few weeks. -Tua -Gabriel -McCarthy -Richardson All have had calls placed on them to varying degrees of interest. — Benjamin Allbright (@AllbrightNFL) August 27, 2026 Benjamin Allbright reported Wednesday that multiple quarterbacks could be on the move in the next few weeks, listing Tua Tagovailoa, Dillon Gabriel, J.J. McCarthy and Richardson as names who have had calls placed on them to “varying degrees of interest.” That does not mean Richardson is definitely being traded, and it does not even necessarily mean the Colts are actively shopping him. There is a big difference between teams calling about a player and a team being ready to move him. Still, Richardson’s inclusion is notable because of where things stand in Indianapolis. The Colts have already made their quarterback situation clear at the top. Daniel Jones is the starter, and Richardson is competing with rookie Riley Leonard for the backup job. Indianapolis has publicly backed Richardson throughout the offseason and training camp, and the team has said it plans to keep three quarterbacks. On the surface, that would suggest Richardson is not going anywhere. The problem is that the NFL can change quickly, especially at quarterback. Richardson remains one of the most interesting backup quarterbacks in the league because of his age, draft pedigree and physical tools. He was the No. 4 overall pick in the 2023 NFL Draft, and even after a frustrating start to his career, there will always be teams willing to talk themselves into the upside. Quarterbacks with his size, arm strength and athletic ability do not become available often, even when the production or play have not matched the traits. For the Colts, the decision would come down to value. Moving Richardson just to move him would make little sense, especially if the return is minimal. He still gives Indianapolis a high-upside backup behind Jones, and with Leonard also on the roster, the Colts have more quarterback depth than most teams. Trading Richardson would only be logical if another team made an offer strong enough to justify giving up on the remaining upside. For now, this is more smoke than fire. Calls being placed does not guarantee movement, and the Colts do not have to force anything. However, Richardson’s name appearing in quarterback trade chatter is another reminder of how quickly his situation has changed. Two years ago, he was supposed to be the future of the franchise. Now, teams are at least checking to see if Indianapolis would consider moving him.

summary: Sunday is cut day, which is always a tough one. Hundreds of players across the NFL suddenly find themselves looking for a new opportunity. For many, the next stop is the waiver wire. (Photo by James Gilbert/Getty Images) | Getty Images Sunday is cut day, which is always a tough one. Hundreds of players across the NFL suddenly find themselves looking for a new opportunity. For many, the next stop is the waiver wire. It gives teams the chance to claim players released by another club before they become free agents. Players with fewer than four credited seasons generally must go through the waiver process, while vested veterans with at least four credited seasons can typically become unrestricted free agents immediately when released. Once a player is placed on waivers, teams have a limited amount of time to submit a claim. If multiple teams want the same player, the team with the highest waiver priority gets him. Waiver priority is based on the NFL’s waiver order, which is determined by team records and draft position depending on the point in the season. Unlike fantasy football, teams do not automatically drop to the bottom of the list after making a successful claim. This means a team with a high waiver priority can potentially claim multiple players if it has the highest priority for each one. title: Waiver wire: Rules and where Chiefs are positioned in order
summary: On Sunday, all 32 NFL teams will cut their offseason rosters to 53 players, concluding the 2026 preseason. The following day, the waiver wire process will begin. Here’s what to know: When is the deadline for waiver claims? NFL teams must submit waiver claims for eligible players by 1 PM ET on Monday, August 31. That’s […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - JUNE 08: A detail view of the Kansas City Chiefs logo on a helmet on set during a production shoot at The University of Kansas Health System Training Complex on June 08, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by Aaron M. Sprecher/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Sunday, all 32 NFL teams will cut their offseason rosters to 53 players, concluding the 2026 preseason. The following day, the waiver wire process will begin. Here’s what to know: When is the deadline for waiver claims? NFL teams must submit waiver claims for eligible players by 1 PM ET on Monday, August 31 . That’s a little less than 24 hours after the official cutdown deadline on Sunday. After waivers process shortly after 12:00 p.m. Arrowhead time, the remaining players will become free agents and can be signed to practice squads or other rosters. Which players are eligible for waivers? When determining waiver eligibility, there are two types of players. Those with less than four “credited” seasons are subject to waivers and are subject to claims before becoming free agents. Those with four or more credited seasons are considered “vested veterans” and are not subject to waivers. Once released, they immediately become free agents and are eligible to sign with whomever they wish. A “credited” season is different from an “accrued” season. The latter is used to determine if players become Unrestricted Free Agents (UFAs), Restricted Free Agents (RFAs) or Exclusive Rights Free Agents (ERFAs). A credited season is as follows: a player must be on an active, inactive, IR, or PUP roster for three or more regular season games. A player who receives an injury settlement (or grievance) for the equivalent of three or more regular season games is also given a credited season. What’s the current waiver order? Here, we’ll track all the roster moves Kansas City is reported to have made. With each new report, we’re also updating our Chiefs roster page , so you can easily see how many players are left in each position group. We’re awaiting the 53-man roster that will attempt to bring the Chiefs back to the postseason. Currently, Kansas City has (-176) odds to make the playoffs, according to FanDuel Sportsbook . How roster changes are made When players with fewer than four accrued seasons are cut, they have been waived . (Players acquire an accrued season when they are on a team’s active roster, its Reserve/Injured list, or its Reserve/PUP list for at least six games in a given season). When players with at least four accrued seasons are cut, they have been released . They immediately become free agents. Waived players may be claimed by another team, which then assumes the balance of their contract. The team that had the most recent draft’s first pick has precedence over waiver claims from all other teams. The team with the most recent draft’s 32nd pick has precedence over waiver claims from no other teams — and so on. If a waived player isn’t claimed by noon on Monday, they become free agents. Players can also be waived with an injury designation — commonly referred to as waived/injured . If these players go unclaimed, they automatically revert to the team’s Reserve/Injured list. This has already happened with prior cuts of tackle Matt Waletzko and wide receiver Jeff Caldwell. That is one of three Reserve lists that do not count against the 53-man limit. The other two are the Reserve/PUP (physically-unable-to-perform) and Reserve/NFI (non-football-injury) lists. Players on the latter two lists at the final cutdown must miss at least four regular-season games before being activated to the roster, which occurs when they pass a physical. Defensive tackle Omarr Norman-Lott — who missed all of training camp recovering from a torn ACL from 2025 — is the only player eligible for the Reserve/PUP list. The salaries for players on a team’s Reserve/PUP and Reserve/Injured lists count against the salary cap. Outside of first- and second-round picks, most players without veteran status can see their base salary cut in half while on reserve lists at the discretion of the team. Salaries for players on Reserve/NFI are not paid (unless a contract provision specifies otherwise). Players placed on Reserve/Injured in the offseason (up through the final cutdown day) must miss the whole season. If a player is placed on Reserve/Injured after the final cutdown day, they may be designated for return after they have missed at least four games. But on final cutdown day, a team may declare up to two players being placed on its Reserve/Injured list as being eligible to be treated as if they are placed on Reserve/Injured after the final cutdown. Teams may make only eight designations for return during a given season — a limit that is extended to 10 if the team appears in the postseason. If a team labels a player as eligible for return at the final cutdown, it counts against this limit — even if the player is never actually designated for return. Players designated for return from Reserve/Injured are eligible to practice with the team for up to 21 days. At any time during that period, they may be activated to the roster. If they are not, they must remain on the Reserve list for the remainder of the season. Finally… players may be removed from the roster by being traded to another team. Just like with a waiver claim, the player’s new team assumes their existing contract, which counts against their cap. But any money that has already been paid to the traded (or waived) player (such as signing and workout bonuses) must be carried against the original team’s cap. title: 7 Winners from the Chiefs’ final Preseason Game
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs don’t win in the preseason — but sometimes, the team doesn’t lose either! The starting defense and most of the offense took the field Friday night to give us a glimpse of what the 2026 Chiefs could look like, and it was pretty good. The defense was difficult to run on, […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 28: Safety D'Anthony Bell #23 of the Seattle Seahawks stops running back Brashard Smith #24 of the Kansas City Chiefs short of the goal line on a fourth quarter run in NFL preseason game action at Arrowhead Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs don’t win in the preseason — but sometimes, the team doesn’t lose either! The starting defense and most of the offense took the field Friday night to give us a glimpse of what the 2026 Chiefs could look like, and it was pretty good. The defense was difficult to run on, and even got pressure with only four pass rushers at times. On offense, rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier played the entire game and looked the part of a young backup. Tight end Travis Kelce got some reps, including a catch and a little dance. But the big story should be the renewed focus on the running game: 37 carries split among a variety of runners with pretty consistent success. Here are a few Chiefs who stood out as Kansas City wrapped up the exhibition slate with a tie against the Seattle. Seahawks . Winners Defensive end R Mason Thomas: It doesn’t matter that it’s preseason, or who he was facing; Thomas just looks the part. He had a strip sack in this one along with some quick pressure on limited snaps. It’s not a stretch to say he’s already the most gifted edge rusher on the Chiefs’ defense, and the most promising speed rusher the team has drafted in recent years. He’ll keep getting better, but you can’t teach the explosion and the fight that he’s shown so far. Running back Brashard Smith: The Chiefs have really been working on their run game, and for the final preseason game, it was all about Brashard Smith. Each running back looked good, but Smith got the longest look, with the most carries and yards on either team. He’s improved, he’s gotten stronger, and he broke off a 57-yard kick return. Smith should be a roster lock, but he also looks like a guy they’ll want to get on the field with the ball in his hands. Defensive Tackle Peter Woods: He may have heard the criticism from the last two preseason games — or he may just have gotten healthier. Whatever happened, Peter Woods made his presence felt against the Seahawks. As a team, the Chiefs held their opponent to under 30 yards rushing by rallying to the ball and disrupting plays in the backfield. It was nice to see the rookie in the mix and looking good. Cornerback Mansoor Delane: He moves at a different speed than the average corner, especially for a rookie. Another perfect form tackle for a loss this week; Delane looks ready to dominate. Wide receiver Andrew Armstrong: He was the favorite target of Garrett Nussmeier this week, and for good reason. Armstrong continued to make his case for a roster spot with diving catches, sideline toe taps and physicality. The Chiefs’ offensive line: The run game looked solid, regardless of the ball carrier — over 4 yards per carry. But pass protection took a step forward as well; from the starters to the backups, Nussmeier made it through the game without taking a sack. Perhaps it was the return of right guard Trey Smith. Perhaps there was a bit more urgency for the incumbents given the trade for Josh Ezeudu. Either way, it felt like a step in the right direction for the big uglies. Defensive lineman Marcus Harris: He’s quietly put together a strong preseason and has a real chance to make an NFL roster this week. Marcus Harris helped close out this tie with three tackles in the closing minutes. His spot on the 53-man roster may depend on the health of some other guys, but Harris has done everything he can to make a strong impression. Losers I’m not sure it’s fair to call out many “losers” this week. Sure, there were too many penalties, Nussmeier threw an interception and kicker Harrison Butker missed from 58 yards away. We’ll find out on Sunday who did enough to earn a job, and who didn’t. Hopefully, most of these guys will get a chance to continue chasing their NFL dreams even if not in Kansas City.

title: Andy Reid gives slight update on Josh Simmons after Friday’s game
summary: On Friday, the Kansas City ChiIfs played to a 9-9 preseason tie with the Seatle Seahawks in their preseason finale. For many Chiefs fans, the biggest concern was on a player not actually playing in the game. Second-year tackle Josh Simmons has been absent from practice this week after being evaluated for back pain. On […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 15: Offensive tackle Josh Simmons #71 of the Kansas City Chiefs stands on the team sidelines during the fourth quarter of NFL game action against the Los Angeles Rams at Arrowhead Stadium on August 15, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images On Friday, the Kansas City ChiIfs played to a 9-9 preseason tie with the Seatle Seahawks in their preseason finale. For many Chiefs fans, the biggest concern was on a player not actually playing in the game. Second-year tackle Josh Simmons has been absent from practice this week after being evaluated for back pain. On Thursday, ESPN ’s Jeremy Fowler confirmed that Simmons was still undergoing testing while stressing that the issue could be prove minor. Speaking after the game, head coach Andy Reid expressed optimism to Pete Sweeney of the Kansas City Star that Simmons would practice soon and confirmed that the goal is to have Simmons playing pain free. “It’s going to take a little bit of time, here,” remarked the coach, “but he’s a hard worker when it comes to these types of things. It’s just a matter of eliminating some of the pain he has. And strength — making sure he has enough strength, there.” Rookie Kahlil Benson started at left tackle in Simmons’ place on Thursday. In three preseason games, Benson has played three different positions: both tackle spots and right guard. Reid is happy with what the rookie brings if called upon. “He’s made improvement every week,” Reid observed, “and I like the way he goes about his business. I think he stands a chance to be a good player as long as he keeps progressing. There’s still work to be done. He’s a willing worker, and I love that part. He doesn’t normally make the same mistake twice. I love that part. He is a big human being that is a good athlete, and I like that.” Reid had no updates on injuries from Friday’s game. Cornerback Melvin Smith Jr. went to the medical tent in the first half. The team later ruled Smith out with a rib injury. The Chiefs are expected issue their first official injury report for their Week 1 game against the Denver Broncos on Thursday, September 10.

title: 3 instant takeaways from Chiefs’ Preseason Week 3
summary: On Friday night, the Kansas City Chiefs battled the Seattle Seahawks to the end of an NFL Preseason Week 3 matchup; the game ended in a 9-9 tie. Here are five rapid-fire takeaways from the game: 1. The rookies on defense have turned up the team speed There’s no statistic for it, but the Chiefs’ defense has looked so […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MO - AUGUST 28: Mansoor Delane #5 of the Kansas City Chiefs flexes after making a tackle in the first quarter of an NFL preseason game between the Seattle Seahawks and Kansas City Chiefs on Aug 28, 2026 at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, MO. (Photo by Scott Winters/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images On Friday night, the Kansas City Chiefs battled the Seattle Seahawks to the end of an NFL Preseason Week 3 matchup; the game ended in a 9-9 tie. Here are five rapid-fire takeaways from the game: 1. The rookies on defense have turned up the team speed There’s no statistic for it, but the Chiefs’ defense has looked so much faster since rookie cornerback Mansoor Delane began playing with the starters in last week’s preseason game. He started Friday’s contest off with a tackle for loss. Five's on it 😮‍💨 @mansoordelane pic.twitter.com/eAuOD5Bear — Kansas City Chiefs (@Chiefs) August 29, 2026 Of course, the team needs willing, physical tacklers on the outside, but Delane’s speed to the point of contact was outstanding. It goes along with the play he made last week against the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, setting up his teammate for a tackle for loss on a quick screen. You love to see 'Thomas' turning the corner for a blindside sack in Arrowhead 🥹 pic.twitter.com/cpEyvSUUW2 — Arrowhead Pride (@ArrowheadPride) August 29, 2026 Up front, it’s clear rookie defensive end R Mason Thomas is going to be a difference maker for Kansas City’s pass rush in 2026. The speed with which he gets off the ball is paired with the flexibility to turn the corner and disrupt the quarterback in the back of his drop. The ease with which Thomas flies around the corner is truly different; the closest a defensive end has come to this skill set under defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo with the Chiefs was Frank Clark, and the Chiefs arguably got the latter half of Clark’s prime as a dominant pass rusher. 2. Brashard Smith and Andrew Armstrong will be hard to cut Since training camp began, it’s been clear the Chiefs see talent in running back Brashard Smith and wide receiver Andrew Armstrong. Each has been in the starting rotation throughout the preseason, but neither is guaranteed to make it through cutdown day. Both made statements on Friday night. Smith’s started in the return game, a facet of his skill set that could lead to a starting spot on the Chiefs. He is battling with wide receiver Nikko Remigio for the return job, and Smith showed the speed advantage he has in that competition during the preseason finale. He took one kickoff out of the end zone and gained 57 yards by winning to the edge of the coverage. Smith also had his best performance as a runner this preseason. He ran downhill with a purpose, using his quickness to cut back efficiently on his way to a team-leading 72 yards over 16 attempts. He was stuffed at the goal line over numerous short-yardage attempts, but that will never be Smith’s strength as a player. Wide receiver Andrew Armstrong led the team with five catches for 54 yards. The big-bodied receiver is a strong player among a receiving corps that doesn’t boast play strength. 3. Garrett Nussmeier, impressive, is still a rookie Rookie quarterback Garrett Nussmeier started this game and played the whole way through. He finished with 22 completions over 34 pass attempts, averaging 5.8 yards per pass (198 yards) and throwing one interception with a passer rating of 68. Trevon Diggs INT! Stream on @NFLPlus pic.twitter.com/9OGOus2fgu — NFL (@NFL) August 29, 2026 The interception was certainly a rookie moment: rolling left, Nussmeier lofted a pass leading wide receiver Xaiver Worthy to the sideline, or so he thought. Throwing off his back foot, the ball hung in the air and was short, making an easy interception for Seahawks cornerback Trevon Diggs. The play ended a nice drive that advanced to the Seattle 30-yard line. There were good stretches of rhythm from the Chiefs’ offense, especially with a commitment to the ground game. Rookie running back Emmett Johnson gained 39 yards over seven carries as the lead back in this contest. The offensive line fired off the ball and kept moving. Late in the game, Nussmeier made an impressive throw while on the move in the pocket for the second consecutive week to move the chains on 3rd & 12. Despite all that momentum, Nussmeier couldn’t lead the Chiefs to a touchdown, settling for field goals on three possessions that got inside the 10-yard line. There’s a lot to like about Nussmeier, but there is also reason to believe he needs more time to develop before overtaking veteran Justin Fields as the immediate backup to quarterback Patrick Mahomes.

title: Chiefs vs. Seahawks Final Score: Preseason finale ends in 9-9 tie
summary: The Kansas City Chiefs tied with the Seattle Seahawks in the preseason finale of the 2026 campaign with a 9-9 score. The countdown to Week 1 is on after an 0-2-1 record in exhibition games. Running back Brashard Smith led the team with 72 rushing yards over 16 attempts, including a team-long rush of 13 […]
full_text: KANSAS CITY, MISSOURI - AUGUST 28: Running back Emmett Johnson #10 of the Kansas City Chiefs runs during the first quarter of an NFL preseason game against the Seattle Seahawks at Arrowhead Stadium on August 28, 2026 in Kansas City, Missouri. (Photo by David Eulitt/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Kansas City Chiefs tied with the Seattle Seahawks in the preseason finale of the 2026 campaign with a 9-9 score. The countdown to Week 1 is on after an 0-2-1 record in exhibition games. Running back Brashard Smith led the team with 72 rushing yards over 16 attempts, including a team-long rush of 13 yards. Quarterback Garrett Nussmeier totaled 198 yards over 22 completions. Wide receiver Andrew Armstrong led all pass catchers with 54 yards over five receptions. Defensive tackle Marcus Harris held the game at a tie at the end with a few clutch tackles; he ended the game with a team-high six tackles. Defensive end R Mason Thomas had a strip sack, the only sack of the game for Kansas City. First Quarter The Chiefs opened the game with Garrett Nussmeier at quarterback and leaned heavily on Emmett Johnson to pick up an early first down. An 8-yard completion to Travis Kelce set up second-and-short, but a drop by Noah Gray followed by an incompletion brought out the punt team. Kansas City’s defense started strong, with Mansoor Delane coming up from his cornerback position for a 4-yard tackle for loss. Two more stops followed as the Chiefs forced a quick three-and-out. The Chiefs’ second possession started with a 12-yard run from Johnson followed by a 14-yard screen pass to the running back. After a short Emari Demercado run, Nussmeier connected with Tyquan Thornton for 11 yards. The drive ended on the next play when Nussmeier underthrew Xavier Worthy and was intercepted by Diggs. Seattle immediately took advantage with a 40-yard completion from Jalen Milroe to Montorie. Foster followed by a 24-yard completion to Elijah. Arroyo. The Chiefs’ defense tightened up from there, making three consecutive stops to force a field goal and limit the Seahawks to a 3-0 lead. Brashard Smith gave Kansas City excellent field position with a 57-yard kickoff return. Nussmeier opened the possession with a 20-yard completion to Armstrong before Johnson added 15 yards on three carries. A holding penalty eventually stalled the drive, forcing the Chiefs to settle for a field goal to tie the game 3-3. Second Quarter Seattle opened the second quarter with completions of 19 and 13 yards from Jalen Milroe before a holding penalty slowed the drive. On the following play, a backward pass resulted in a fumble that linebacker Cole Christiansen recovered at the Chiefs’ 36-yard line. Kansas City turned the takeaway into points. A 17-yard completion from Nussmeier to Jared Wiley highlighted the possession before the Chiefs settled for a field goal to take a 6-3 lead. The Seahawks picked up a quick first down on their next possession and benefited from a pass interference penalty, but R. Mason Thomas responded with a strip sack on first down that put Seattle behind the sticks. The Seahawks recovered the fumble but were eventually forced to punt. Starting from their own 5-yard line late in the half, the Chiefs moved the ball out to the 48 behind some nice plays from Nussmeier and Emari Demercado. An intentional grounding penalty resulted in a 10-second runoff, ending the first half with Kansas City leading 6-3. Third Quarter The Seahawks received the ball to start the second half, but the Chiefs’ defense quickly forced a three-and-out. Kansas City picked up two first downs on its opening possession behind a 12-yard run from Brashard Smith and a 12-yard reception by Cyrus Allen. The drive stalled from there, and Harrison Butker missed the field goal attempt wide right. Following the missed field goal, Jalen Milroe moved the Seahawks quickly down the field for a touchdown, throwing for 67 yards on the drive. Jason Myers missed the extra point, leaving Seattle with a 9-6 lead. The Chiefs picked up one first down on their next possession with another 12-yard run from Smith, but the drive stalled shortly afterward and Kansas City punted. Seattle’s next possession was short-lived, as the Chiefs forced three consecutive incompletions and another punt. Fourth Quarter The Seahawks opened the fourth quarter but failed to pick up a first down as the Chiefs’ defense quickly forced another punt. Kansas City was pushed behind the sticks by a first-down penalty and went three-and-out. Seattle’s offense continued to struggle, moving backward on its next possession before another three-and-out. The Chiefs picked up a first down on a nice completion to De Jesus, but an offensive pass interference penalty on the following play put the offense behind the sticks. Kansas City never recovered and was forced to punt. Seattle took over at its own 20-yard line with a little over three minutes remaining. A 30-yard completion to Henderson and several short runs moved the Seahawks into field goal range, but Jason Myers missed a 52-yard attempt as time expired, ending the game in a 9-9 tie. Special teams notes Kicker Harrison Butker connected on three of his four field-goal attempts, hitting from 19, 24 and 28 yards while missing from 58 yards. Jacob De Jesus averaged 9 yards on three punt returns, including a long of 20 yards, while Brashard Smith provided the biggest return of the night with a 50-yard kickoff return. Punter Matt Araiza averaged 44 yards on four punts, with a long of 53 yards.

Offense Best WR Quentin Johnston – 95.0 RB Greg DesRosiers Jr. – 92.4 TE Charlie Kolar – 86.5 WR Gary Jennings – 80.1 C Josh Kaltenberger – 75.9 DesRosiers ran rampant with 118 carries on 118 yards on nine carries while adding another reception foro eight yards. Undrafted rookie free agent Greg Desrosiers Jr. balled out tonight: Nine Carries 118 yards, 1 TD “At the end of the day, they’re going to have a big decision to make and my job was to make it hard for them.” – he said pic.twitter.com/7SZAdrikA8 — Kris Rhim (@krisrhim1) August 28, 2026 Jennings led the Chargers with three receptions against the Rams and finished with 44 yards. Worst OT Laekin Vakalahi – 27.0 OG/T Alex Harkey – 44.6 QB Trey Lance – 47.1 QB Justin Herbert – 49.8 TE Oronde Gadsden II – 51.1 Vakalahi allowed the strip sack on D.J. Uiagalelei and finished with a literal 0.0 grade in pass blocking. It should be a near-impossibility to receive that grade while actively trying to block people, but here we are. title: Rams running back Dean Connors is a gamer: Upon Further Review
summary: Dean Connors has given the Los Angeles Rams all they can handle when it comes to filling out their running backs room on NFL roster cutdown day this weekend. He’s not going to be RB1 or RB2 on this team with Kyren Williams and Blake Corum firmly entrenched in those spots, but his preseason performances […]
full_text: INGLEWOOD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 27: Dean Connors #33 of the Los Angeles Rams carries the ball during the first half in a preseason game between the Los Angeles Rams and the Los Angeles Chargers at SoFi Stadium on August 27, 2026 in Inglewood, California. (Photo by Harry How/Getty Images) | Getty Images Dean Connors has given the Los Angeles Rams all they can handle when it comes to filling out their running backs room on NFL roster cutdown day this weekend. He’s not going to be RB1 or RB2 on this team with Kyren Williams and Blake Corum firmly entrenched in those spots, but his preseason performances have certainly been an encouraging sign of what he could offer this team should he make the final 53-man roster. Will he? There’s no doubt it will be a tough ask for the undrafted rookie out of Houston. But in the following few clips, you can see why so many fans are clamoring for No. 33 to get a shot with the club this year. Connors led the Rams in rushing in their preseason finale against the Los Angeles Chargers , posting 69 yards on 18 carries in a 20-18 win. He’s a stocky back, standing 5-foot-11 and 205 pounds, but he runs with an impressive smoothness. In the following clip, watch how fluidly he breaks to the outside for a first-down gain. The Rams aren’t hiding the run here. Twin tight ends to the left of the formation (from the quarterback’s viewpoint) with C.J. Daniels motioning to an in-line insert as well. The play flows to the right, opening up a cutback lane left with space. One of those tight ends washes out the defensive end and Connors swiftly cuts and bounces to the outside without slowing his momentum. Then, he has the speed to beat a cornerback to the boundary and nets a 12-yard gain. A quick-twitch cut and a second gear to create an explosive. That sounds like a set of traits Sean McVay would love to get in the mix, given how aggressively the Rams seek out explosive plays. Vision and patience are something else about Connors that stands out. It can’t be emphasized enough how helpful it is to have an offensive line that is just wrecking shop in front of a ball carrier. The Chargers are getting blown off the ball here. But even with a line like that, there are countless examples of NFL running backs, both guys on the fringes and ones who make final rosters, who don’t have the patience to wait for the best possible running lane. Connors is willing to wait, though, and responds quickly once that hole opens. Instead of trying to play battering ram and ither running into his own man or trying to bounce outside too early, he stays in phase with his blockers and takes the easy gain straight ahead. He makes a quick cut right, then lets off the gas so he doesn’t outrun the blocking. It seems simple, but if you watch the league (or the players out of college entering it), it’s much easier said than done. Then there’s the toughness. Who doesn’t want that in a running back? The Rams have built this offense line with the idea that the interior players can use their massive size and strength to overwhelm defensive linemen and linebackers, clearing room for their backs. It led to one of the most efficient rushing attacks in the NFL history last year, statistically speaking. But when your running back can add an extra dash of toughness it only helps matters more. Credit goes to the offensive line here for creating plenty of space for Connors to work with, but once again he sees the correct alley immediately and, most importantly, he finishes the run. He sheds a linebacker and bounces off a pursuing defensive back to gain a couple extra yards, finishing with seven on the play. Again, this is not someone who is going to usurp Williams or Corum on the depth chart. And even if he doesn’t make the initial 53, he’s a no-doubt practice squad candidate and, given the modern elevation rules, it’s fair to assume he’d get some run at some point this season. But when you find an undrafted talent with good vision, quick decision making and plus fluidity, it’s hard to pass that up. For a team that loves to hunt big plays, Connors could be a useful weapon in 2026.

title: Four down territory: Rams turn focus to regular season
summary: The preseason is officially in the rearview mirror for the Los Angeles Rams, and now the attention shifts toward the games that actually count. After wrapping up their preseason slate, the Rams have plenty of reasons to feel encouraged, but there are also several major questions that must be answered before the regular-season opener. With […]
full_text: The preseason is officially in the rearview mirror for the Los Angeles Rams, and now the attention shifts toward the games that actually count. After wrapping up their preseason slate, the Rams have plenty of reasons to feel encouraged, but there are also several major questions that must be answered before the regular-season opener. With the roster deadline approaching and the first game less than two weeks away, here are four takeaways from the Rams’ final preseason game. First Down: Rams Put Together a “Historic” Offensive Performance The Rams’ offense provided plenty of reason for optimism throughout the preseason, but the most impressive aspect may have been what happened — or didn’t happen — up front. The Rams did not concede a single sack in any of their preseason games . No team since at least 1999 has gone through the entire preseason with no sacks or turnovers until the Rams this year. 📸 Kirby Lee, IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect https://t.co/mwQIpgH15u pic.twitter.com/NUTd6E7eBf — Rams Wire (@TheRamsWire) August 28, 2026 That’s an impressive accomplishment regardless of the competition, especially considering how many different combinations of offensive linemen typically receive playing time during the preseason. Protection is one of the biggest concerns for any offense entering a new season, and Los Angeles appears to have established a strong foundation with their starters but also their depth in this case. Keeping quarterbacks upright has been a consistent priority for Sean McVay, and the Rams’ ability to avoid giving up sacks throughout the preseason could be an early indication that the offensive line is ready for the regular season. Kudos to Ryan Wendell. Second Down: Tight Squeeze for Rams Draft Picks The Rams’ 2026 draft class has generated plenty of excitement, but the final roster could tell a different story for some of the team’s rookies. Wide receiver CJ Daniels and defensive tackle Tim Keenan III appear to be on the bubble as the Rams make their final roster decisions. That would be notable considering Los Angeles entered the draft with limited draft capital. If Daniels and Keenan don’t make the 53-man roster, two of the Rams’ five draft picks would fail to make the initial team. That doesn’t necessarily mean the draft class was unsuccessful. Players can develop on the practice squad and eventually work their way onto the active roster. Still, it would be an unusual outcome and shows just how difficult it is for rookies to immediately establish themselves in a competitive NFL roster. Third Down: Ty Simpson May Have Been the Right Pick There were plenty of analysts who believed the Rams reached when they selected quarterback Ty Simpson with the 13th overall pick. The preseason, however, has provided some evidence that Los Angeles may have identified a potential gem. Simpson has shown enough to make the Rams’ decision look increasingly defensible. His physical tools, poise and ability to operate within McVay’s system have stood out, particularly for a young quarterback making the transition to the NFL. It’s obviously far too early to declare Simpson a franchise quarterback based on preseason performances. But if he continues developing, the Rams could eventually look back at No. 13 of the 2026 draft as one of the more important picks of the McVay era. Fourth Down: Potential Suspensions Loom Perhaps the biggest uncertainty surrounding the Rams isn’t even related to the roster. With the regular-season opener now less than 14 days away, questions remain regarding potential suspensions for Alaric Jackson and Puka Nacua. The possibility of either player missing time continues to be a major talking point as Los Angeles prepares for the regular season. Jackson’s potential absence would impact the offensive line, while losing Nacua would create an even more significant challenge for an offense expecting him to be one of its primary weapons. The Rams can prepare for several possibilities, but until the NFL makes its decisions, there remains a cloud of uncertainty hanging over the roster. The preseason is over. Now, the Rams have to turn their attention toward making the final cuts, preparing for potential absences and getting ready for the games that matter most.

Teams working to get to their 53 may have to make some tough decisions; leaving other franchises potentially interested. The majority of players released will have to pass through waivers. The NFL waiver system determines which team has the first opportunity to claim a player who has been waived. If multiple teams submit claims for the same player, the organization positioned highest in the waiver priority receives the player. The Los Angeles Rams have an elite roster on paper right now and will likely release a handful of players that other teams have interest in. The Rams, themselves may have interest in cut candidates on other rosters but acquiring them may not be as easy. Waiver Rules For the initial waiver period following roster cutdowns, as well as the first three weeks of the regular season, waiver priority follows the league’s original draft order from that year. Trades involving draft picks and forfeited selections do not alter the waiver order. Players with fewer than four accrued NFL seasons generally must pass through waivers when released. An accrued season is credited when a player spends at least six games on a team’s active roster, PUP list, or injured reserve. Once a qualifying player is waived, other teams have an opportunity to submit a claim, with the waiver period typically lasting 24 hours. Players with four or more accrued seasons, often referred to as veterans, generally are not subject to the standard waiver process. 2026 Waiver Order 1. Las Vegas Raiders 2. New York Jets 3. title: Rams 53-man roster projection: Final pre-cuts edition
summary: In the final stages of building out their 2026 roster, the Los Angeles Rams took time out to knock off their roommates, the L.A. Chargers, 20-18 in the preseason finale. In perfect Hollywood fashion, the game and roster build was shrouded in mystery, a last-minute plot twist, and a touch of drama. Mystery still surrounds […]
full_text: Sean McVay is looking to score with the Rams 2026 opening roster (Photo by Sean M. Haffey/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the final stages of building out their 2026 roster, the Los Angeles Rams took time out to knock off their roommates, the L.A. Chargers, 20-18 in the preseason finale. In perfect Hollywood fashion, the game and roster build was shrouded in mystery, a last-minute plot twist, and a touch of drama. Mystery still surrounds the fate of Aaron Donald’s return. Just hours before the kickoff, the Rams turned the the table on roster projections by trading running back Jarquez Hunter , in the midst of a heated roster battle, for wide receiver Tutu Atwell, a roster lock. The controversy, amongst fans at least, is that Atwell had spent his first five years in L.A. with more potential than distinction and wasn’t offered a contract after the 2025 season. For the Rams newcomers, this roster was gong to be tough to make, there were just a few positions in play. General Manager Les Snead has filled the coffers with players that fit into Head coach Sean McVay’s exacting protocols. The Rams coaching staff has put together a mentally/physically tough squad that plays hard to the whistle. While the Charger game had a few watch-worthy individual performances, It appeared that the game had little effect on a roster reset. In fact, it was the few players that didn’t/hardly participate that told the story. Here’s my final roster reset, an opening 53 projection ( players in bold ), a 17-man practice squad (PS), and individual snap counts (in parentheses) from the Rams/Chargers game. Quarterback (3) Matthew Stafford, Ty Simpson (48), Stetson Bennett No changes, the only debate is the “official’ naming of QB#2. Simpson looked decisive and sharp on the short throws and it was cool to see Matthew Caldwell (26) get some play time. McVay doesn’t usually give his QB#4 camp arms that much action. TRENDING: Ty Simpson’s BEST PASSES from his first preseason in the NFL. 47/60 (78%), 382 passing yards, 3 TD’s, 0 INT’s, 19 FD’s, 109.9 passer rating 😳🎯 pic.twitter.com/lcUZveANt9 — Rookie Watch (@RookieWatxh) August 28, 2026 Running back (3) Kyren Williams, Blake Corum, Ronnie Rivers All of the roster battle debate went out the window before kickoff with the trade of Jarquez Hunter. The Rams do not usually give up on draft picks, unless their just not a fit. I’m going with Dean Conners (38) over Jordan Watwers (36) for a PS berth. Wide receiver (6) Puka Nacua, Davante Adams, Jordan Whittington, Konata Mumpfield, Xavier Smith, Tutu Atwell Welcome home, Tutu. “You can check out anytime you like, but you can never leave.” His addition almost assures that both CJ Daniels (34) and Brennan Presley (53) are the odd men out. Both are likely destined for the PS. I thought Presley was outstanding throughout the preseason slate, the best of the L.A. receivers. Tyler Scott (42) showed flashes over the preseason, but as is in his past, not near enough to justify a roster spot. Goodbye to Tru Edwards (38) and Alex Bachman (32). Tight end (5) Colby Parkinson, Terrance Ferguson, Tyler Higbee, Davis Allen, Max Klare (41) No surprises, most fans would agree that this was always going to be the lineup. Mark Redman (24) to the PS for sure and the Rams initial monetary investment in Dan Villari (20) gets him there as well. Rohan Jones (12) only received a handful mop-up offensive reps over three games. Offensive line (10) Alaric Jackson, Steve Avila, Coleman Shelton, Kevin Dotson, Warren McClendon, Beaux Limmer, David Quessenberry, Justin Dedich, Keagan Trost, Dylan McMahon Throwing in Dylan McMahon as the surprise 10th offensive lineman, he really played solidly in the first two games and got the night off in the finale. RG Austin Blaske, C Wyatt Bowles, LT AJ Arcuri, and RT Bryce Henderson all played every snap, 74. Bill Murray (30) was the fifth starter. In the first two drives, against most of the Chargers first teamer’s, they had their hands full, but over a body of work, all handled themselves quite well. Blake Hance stepped in for Murray. Tough battle for the PS. As much as I liked Wyatt Bowles effort and C/G versatility, the combination of AJ Arcuri, Austin Blaske and Bill Murray offers the Rams comprehensive versatility insurance. Special teams (3) Ethan Evans, Harrison Mevis, Joe Cardona No need to worry about the specialists, all three are solid. Again, double-teaming the gunner’s on punt returns, could really open things up. Upgrade onkick coverage? Well, fans will believe it when they see it. What a beaut from @ethanevans 🤩 📺 @CBSLosAngeles | 📲 https://t.co/R5m5kJYWYi pic.twitter.com/Oy7kp5nRIB — Los Angeles Rams (@RamsNFL) August 28, 2026 Defensive line (5) Kobie Turner, Braden Fiske, Poona Ford, Tyler Davis, Ty Hamilton The defensive interior, as a whole, has not played well in preseason. Bill Norton (30) has led the way, he’s tough to move, but doesn’t get much push. Tim Keenan (24) needs plenty of seasoning. Larrell Murchison (26) looks to be near the end. Although Payton Zdroik (27) and Jaxson Moi (27) both looked to have improved over three games, neither are ready to contend with higher grade competition. Edge (5) Myles Garrett, Byron Young, Josaiah Stewart, Desjuan Johnson, Wesley Bailey (2) The biggest recipient of the defensive line’s ho-hum play will be Bailey. I think the Rams will want to protect him, he strikes me as the only player at the bottom of the roster that would not clear waivers. Darryl Peterson (42) improved incrementally over his three outings and wins a PS role. Latecomers Tomon Fox (45) and Devean Deal (23) were always here as camp bodies. Darryl Peterson has been going crazy… someone to look at during final cuts 👀 possibly a practice squad player. pic.twitter.com/964EkMKBFQ — Rams Tapes 🇵🇷 (@RamsTapes) August 28, 2026 Off-ball linebacker (4) Nate Landman, Omar Speights, Shaun Dolac, Grant Stuard Another position where the end result was never in doubt. Nikhai Hill-Green (49) got in a lot of work over three games and while not outstanding, showed enough for a PS berth. Elias Neal (21) is cut from the same cloth, a good guy to have on the practice squad. Monty Rice (26) was added just for preseason games. Safety (5) Kamren Curl, Quentin Lake, Kamren Kinchens, Jaylen McCollough, Nick Andersen (8) I’m going to stay with Andersen (8) making the 53. He appears to be from the Rams toughness/effort/IQ mold and played generally well. Nate Valcarcel (42) doesn’t justify a opening roster bid, but is a good prospect for the PS. Alex Cook (49) could challenge for the PS, but doesn’t have as much growth potential. Coaches love Tanner Ingle (29) for his hustle and work ethic, but he still struggles to take good angles. Cornerback (4) Trent McDuffie, Jaylen Watson, Emmanuel Forbes, Josh Wallace The Rams got Cam Lampkin (36) plenty of work both outside and in the slot, but I’m not sure his preseason play was enough to crack the billet. AZ Hamilton (44) had some flashes and will get development work on the practice squad. Didn’t see enough consistency from Alex Johnson (17) over three games, but he could sneak onto the PS. Nyzier Fourqurean (39) is in the same boat. Steven Gilmore (10) mopped up. Practice squad (17) RB Dean Conners WR Brennan Presley WR CJ Daniels TE Mark Redman TE Dan Villari OL Austin Blaske OL Bill Murray OL AJ Arcuri DL Tim Keenan DL Bill Norton E Darryl Peterson LB Nikhai Hill-Green LB Elias Neal S Nate Valcarcel CB Cam Lampkin CB AZ Hamilton P Jack Bouwmeester (Exchange) The AD effect and final roster thoughts If the Rams do come to terms and activate Aaron Donald by Monday, I would guess that edge Wesley Bailey becomes the odd man out. Bailey does strike me as the likely most sought after of the Rams final cuts and could therefore be snapped up, but 9 of 10 Rams fans would prefer Donald back in horns over a youngster who still needs a lot of development work. The opening roster may be in line for a couple of tweaks before the opener with the…
