title: NFL Waivers, Where the Vikings Sit, and Other Roster Construction Rules
summary: With the Minnesota Vikings now going through the process of putting together their roster, there will likely be some questions as to how they go about doing that. We are going to attempt to answer those questions in this post. As we’ve previously mentioned, teams have until 5:00 PM Central on Sunday, 30 August to […]
full_text: EAGAN, MN. - JULY 2026: Vikings GM Nolan Teasley left, and head coach Kevin O'Connell speaks to members of the Media at TCO Performance Center in Eagan, Minn., on Tuesday, July 28, 2026. (Photo by Jerry Holt/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images) With the Minnesota Vikings now going through the process of putting together their roster, there will likely be some questions as to how they go about doing that. We are going to attempt to answer those questions in this post. As we’ve previously mentioned, teams have until 5:00 PM Central on Sunday, 30 August to trim their rosters to 53 players. They can do those by letting players go, making trades, and other means that we will detail. Released vs Waived Over the next couple of days, you will hear about players being both released and waived by their teams, including the Vikings. There is a significant difference between those two in terms of what sort of freedom a player has over where he goes after his previous team lets him go. Players with more than four accrued seasons of NFL experience will be released. A player that is released becomes a free agent and is free to sign with another NFL team immediately. Any player with less than four accrued NFL seasons will be waived by their teams. That means they are subject to the league’s waiver process. Waiver Process After teams finalize their 53-man rosters, teams will have until noon Central time on Monday, 31 August to place claims on any players that were let go and are subject to the waiver process. There is a waiver priority list, and that list is the same as the first-round draft order from the 2026 NFL Draft. To refresh your memory, that means it looks like this: Las Vegas Raiders New York Jets Arizona Cardinals Tennessee Titans New York Giants Cleveland Browns Washington Commanders New Orleans Saints Kansas City Chiefs Cincinnati Bengals Miami Dolphins Dallas Cowboys Atlanta Falcons Baltimore Ravens Tampa Bay Buccaneers Indianapolis Colts Detroit Lions Minnesota Vikings Carolina Panthers Green Bay Packers Pittsburgh Steelers Los Angeles Chargers Philadelphia Eagles Jacksonville Jaguars Chicago Bears Buffalo Bills San Francisco 49ers Houston Texans Los Angeles Rams Denver Broncos New England Patriots Seattle Seahawks As you can see, the Vikings sit at #18 on the waiver priority list. That means if they put in a waiver claim on a player, they need to hope that none of the 17 teams above them put in a claim on the same player. If even one of those teams claims the same player, they have priority over the Vikings and the Vikings won’t get that player. Any team can claim as many players as they want during the waiver process. If they are awarded a player, they have to make a corresponding move to add that player to the 53-man roster. Suspended Players A suspended player will not count against the team’s 53-man roster. Jeshaun Jones, who was recently suspended for three games for violating the league’s substance policy, could stay with the team for the first three weeks of the season and not count against the 53-man roster, although he wouldn’t be allowed in the facility or be able to participate in any team activities. Or, if the team were to release him and he signed somewhere else, he would not be available to his new team for the first three weeks of the season, either. Injured Reserve Should the Vikings have any players that they feel need to spend time on injured reserve, they can place two on IR with a designation to return during the season. Those returnees would count against their allotment of players who are allowed to return during the season, but would not count against the 53-man roster for cutdown purposes. International Player Partnership Program Players Right now, the Vikings have a roster exemption for punter Brett Thorson as a part of the league’s International Player Partnership Program. If they determine that he has won the punting battle over Johnny Hekker and makes the active roster, they no longer get an exemption for him. He would be a regular member of the 53-man roster. If they waive him, nobody else claims him, and they bring him back to the practice squad, they could then get an exemption for him to be a 17th member of the practice squad. Practice Squad Once all of the waiver claims have been processed by the league, teams are free to sign players who remain unclaimed to the practice squad. We will have a separate practice squad tracker when the time comes and go over all the practice squad rules in that post. That should be everything you need to know as the Vikings set about building a roster that will, hopefully, improve on their current +3500 odds to win this year’s Super Bowl (thank you, FanDuel Sportsbook ). We’ll be tracking all of the moves the Vikings make on their road to the 53-man roster in our roster tracker, so be sure to keep checking back there for the latest! Do FanDuel link when you can get some odds .

title: Denver Broncos 34, Minnesota Vikings 6: Vikings End Preseason With Ugly Showing
summary: In the final preseason game of the season, the hope is, generally, that you can put together a performance that you can feel good about heading into the games that count, even though a lot of the starters don’t play. The final preseason game of 2026 for the Minnesota Vikings was. . .pretty much the […]
full_text: DENVER, COLORADO - AUGUST 28: Jonathon Cooper #0 of the Denver Broncos tackles Demond Claiborne #21 of the Minnesota Vikings in the first half of a preseason game at Empower Field At Mile High on August 28, 2026 in Denver, Colorado. (Photo by Tyler Schank/Clarkson Creative/Getty Images) | Getty Images In the final preseason game of the season, the hope is, generally, that you can put together a performance that you can feel good about heading into the games that count, even though a lot of the starters don’t play. The final preseason game of 2026 for the Minnesota Vikings was. . .pretty much the exact opposite of that. The Vikings’ defense got scorched by Sam Ehlinger for most of the evening, and the offense failed to find the end zone for the second consecutive game as they fell to the Denver Broncos by a final score of 34-6 in the 2026 preseason finale at Mile High on Friday night. The Broncos got the football first, and immediately went down and put up points on their first possession courtesy of a 43-yard field goal from Will Lutz to make it 3-0. There was some bad news on the drive for the Vikings as undrafted free agent safety Jacob Thomas, who has made quite an impression so far this preseason, hurt his ankle on a third-down play and needed to be helped off the field. The Vikings’ offense, led by Carson Wentz due to J.J. McCarthy being out of this game with an ankle injury, took the field and immediately went three-and-out. Brett Thorson got the first punt of the night, and he blasted a nice 54-yarder that went out of bounds at the 12-yard line. The Broncos’ offense went back out on the field and, once again, pushed the ball down the field in convincing fashion. Jarrett Stidham marched the home team on an 88-yard drive, culminating in a 1-yard touchdown plunge by Adam Prentice, and the Broncos had a 10-0 lead with three and a half minutes left in the first quarter of play. Minnesota’s offense did manage to pick up a first down on the ensuing possession and got the ball out to midfield, but Wentz’s pass to Gavin Bartholomew was stopped short on third down, and the Vikings punted it away again to start the second quarter. Denver turned to Sam Ehlinger at quarterback on the next drive, and the Vikings got themselves a turnover courtesy of safety Khalef Hailassie. Hailassie had a couple of picks last offseason, and he stepped in front of a pass intended for Dane Key to get one in this game, setting the Vikings up in Denver territory. . @YoungLeaf24 GO CRAZY!! 📺: #MINvsDEN @FOX9 pic.twitter.com/hHNamktcjb — Minnesota Vikings (@Vikings) August 29, 2026 With Max Brosmer taking over at quarterback for Wentz, the Vikings turned the interception into three points, as Will Reichard connected on a 46-yard field goal to cut the Denver lead to 10-3. The Vikings appeared to have a third-down conversion to extend the drive prior to that, but an illegal formation penalty took it away and forced the Vikings to settle for the field goal attempt a couple of plays later. Denver returned the ensuing kickoff into Minnesota territory, which I’m sure Matt Daniels wasn’t necessarily thrilled with. The drive didn’t do much with the field position, however, and Lutz came on again for another field goal attempt. This one was a 37-yarder, and the veteran connected to push the lead back to ten once more at 13-3 with five and a half minutes remaining before halftime. A touchback on the ensuing kickoff gave the Vikings good starting field position, and Brosmer led what might have been the best overall drive of the preseason, moving the offense down the field with some solid throws. Minnesota eventually got into a goal-to-go situation. . .and then Brosmer threw it away on three consecutive plays, leading to a 28-yard field goal from Reichard to make it 13-6 with a minute and a half left in the second quarter. Ehlinger and the Broncos got the ball back and marched down the field in short order, connecting on a pair of big passes to get near the Vikings’ red zone with thirty seconds remaining. Ehlinger then found Jaleel McLaughlin out of the backfield for a 20-yard catch-and-run for the Broncos’ second touchdown of the night to make it 20-6 heading into the locker room. The Vikings got the ball to start the second half, and promptly went three-and-out as a third-down conversion was wiped out by yet another penalty. The Broncos responded with a three-and-out of their own on their first possession of the half. Minnesota took over and managed to push the ball to midfield, but ultimately ended up punting the football away once again. A third-down stop by the Vikings on Denver’s next possession was negated by a hands to the face penalty on 3rd-and-13, which we’re sure Brian Flores was absolutely thrilled with. That allowed the drive to push into the fourth quarter, and Ehlinger put the capper on a 17-play, 85-yard drive. . .yes, seventeen plays, eighty-five yards. . .with a 14-yard touchdown pass on a 4th-and-2 play to Cody Schrader to extend Denver’s lead to 27-6 early in the final stanza. To the Vikings’ credit, they responded with another long drive that pushed into the Denver red zone. Ultimately, they found themselves looking at a fourth-and-goal from the Denver 6-yard line and elected to go for it. Brosmer threw a quick pass to Jermar Jefferson out of the backfield, and he was taken down immediately for a turnover on downs. The Vikings’ defense then put the capper on a really awful night by allowing an 88-yard touchdown pass from Ehlinger to tight end Justin Joly, who didn’t have a purple jersey within 20 yards of him when he caught the football. He ran untouched for around the final 40 yards to the end zone, and the extra point extended Denver’s lead to 34-6 with just over eight minutes remaining in regulation. There really wasn’t anything to report after that. Nobody in purple really covered themselves in glory in the preseason finale, and now the focus will shift to the flurry of roster moves that the Vikings will make in order to get their roster down to 53 players. The next time they take the field, it will be for the regular season opener on 13 September when they host the Green Bay Packers at U.S. Bank Stadium. The preseason is over, and not a moment too soon for the Minnesota Vikings, as they fall to the Denver Broncos 34-6 in the 2026 preseason finale. Thank you to everyone who got their coverage of this week’s game right here at The Daily Norseman!

title: SB Nation Reacts Results: Most Believe McCarthy Stays
summary: Just before we get things kicked off in Denver this evening, we’ve got the results of our SB Nation Reacts survey for this week, so let’s get them out there before the festivities get started. This week, we asked you what role you think J.J. McCarthy will have on the quarterback depth chart for this […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings passes the ball against the Baltimore Ravens during the first quarter of the preseason game at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images Just before we get things kicked off in Denver this evening, we’ve got the results of our SB Nation Reacts survey for this week, so let’s get them out there before the festivities get started. This week, we asked you what role you think J.J. McCarthy will have on the quarterback depth chart for this year’s Minnesota Vikings team. The overwhelming majority of you believe that McCarthy will still be a part of the team, but there’s a relatively even split on what, exactly, his role will be. Of those who responded to our survey, 45% believe that McCarthy will end up being the third-string quarterback for the Vikings this season, while 41% believe that he will serve as the primary backup. That means 86% of you think that he’s at least going to be on the roster, which indicates that there’s some sort of sanity around here. . .at least, I think there is, anyway. Of the remainder, 12% believe that the Vikings will end up trading McCarthy away, while 2% of our respondents appear to be in the throes of full-blown McCarthy Derangement Syndrome and believe that the Vikings will just outright cut their 2024 first-round pick before his third season starts while getting nothing in return. That would be pants-on-head levels of crazy, but hey. . .I suppose it could happen. McCarthy is under contract for the 2027 NFL season, whereas Kyler Murray and Carson Wentz are not. If the team is ever going to take any actual, serious interest in attempting to develop him, they’re going to have to get him reps somehow. I don’t know if that’s from running the scout team or running the 2s in practice or what it is. Given that McCarthy, Murray, and Wentz all have fairly prolific injury histories, there’s a decent chance that all three of them see the field at some point this season, too. It just doesn’t make any sense to me to let McCarthy go, but at this point I honestly have no idea what the thought process is with him where the Vikings’ brass is concerned. I guess we’ll find out sooner rather than later, with the roster deadline coming on Sunday and the season opener coming in just over two weeks. As always, I’d like to thank everyone who took the time to vote in our survey for this week and to comment both on the post and in the Feed. We’ll have another one for you next week! title: Vikings Preseason Finale: McCarthy’s Future, Roster Battles, and What to Watch
summary: J.J. McCarthy’s ankle, Max Brosmer’s tape, and Friday’s roster auditions in Denver dominate The Real Forno Show as Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano preview Minnesota’s last exhibition. Tyler opened with the only question that still moves the building: will McCarthy play Friday at 8 p.m. CT against the Broncos? He missed Wednesday so the deltoid […]
full_text: MINNEAPOLIS, MINNESOTA - AUGUST 22: J.J. McCarthy #9 of the Minnesota Vikings walks off the field after the preseason game against the Baltimore Ravens at U.S. Bank Stadium on August 22, 2026 in Minneapolis, Minnesota. (Photo by Stephen Maturen/Getty Images) | Getty Images J.J. McCarthy’s ankle, Max Brosmer’s tape, and Friday’s roster auditions in Denver dominate The Real Forno Show as Tyler Forness and Dave Stefano preview Minnesota’s last exhibition. Tyler opened with the only question that still moves the building: will McCarthy play Friday at 8 p.m. CT against the Broncos? He missed Wednesday so the deltoid ankle sprain could settle. Forness’s read is blunt. “If he does play, and especially coming off of an injury like this, I think it’s another stronger signal that he’s done in Minnesota.” He still expects McCarthy gone by Sunday’s 3 p.m. cut deadline — trade or waiver — and listed Jets, Dolphins, Chargers (Jim Harbaugh), Cowboys, and Cardinals as the shops worth watching, while parking rumor-mill “he wants out” items until Rapoport, Schefter, or Pelissero confirm them. The blame pie is split on purpose. “I think you’re going to have to put blame on both the coaching staff, Kevin O’Connell included, and J.J. McCarthy.” Forness will not settle that argument until McCarthy’s next stop plays out: Darnold renaissance or flameout. Dave asked who Friday is supposed to impress. Tyler’s answer: not the fans first. “I think McCarthy really needs to prove to himself that he can be that guy again… he’s lost that confidence.” The Raiders tape from two years ago is the standard. The meniscus, the slump, and too many voices in his ear (O’Connell, the QB coach, Wes Phillips) are the wreckage. Grant Udinski’s exit is “worth considering at a high level,” Forness said — “I am also not willing to sit here confidently and say that it’s everything.” Brosmer is the other face on the thumbnail. Last year’s UDFA earned QB3 over Brett Rypien, then got thrown into real games he “shouldn’t have had to play.” Friday he may see almost the whole night. Tyler wants last year’s preseason version: anticipation, middle-of-the-field answers, no telegraphed picks. “The only way he’s on the roster is if J.J. McCarthy’s gone.” If McCarthy stays, Brosmer is fighting for a practice-squad tape dump. What they’re watching Friday: J.J. McCarthy’s future : Rumblings from insiders suggest McCarthy wants out and teams have called about a trade. Forness expects resolution by Sunday. Max Brosmer’s opportunity : The undrafted QB may play nearly the entire game. “I wanna see the Max Brosmer of last preseason and I wanna see it take a little bit of a step forward,” Forness said. RB3 battle — Demond Claiborne vs. Zavier Scott : Claiborne needs to prove his speed translates: “Speed only matters if you can use it in a football context.” Scott must show he can block and contribute on special teams. WR6 — Dillon Bell vs. Dontae Fleming : With Jeshaun Jones suspended three games (DUI arrest, per Ben Goessling’s reporting), the sixth receiver spot is open. “Bell had a lot of hype coming into training camp and he’s kinda fallen flat,” while Fleming has been “inconsistent, but solid.” Tight end — Gavin Bartholomew vs. Ben Yurosek : The long-term TE1 conversation is live. “Who do they think can maybe develop into your tight end one next year?” Offensive line depth concerns : Beyond the top six, Forness was blunt: “After that, Dave, it’s kind of stinky.” EDGE/DL: Edge 3 is the hole. Chaz Chambliss (now No. 40 so he can play fullback without reporting) has ST value. Elijah Williams is ahead of Isaiahh Loudermilk. Tyrion Ingram-Dawkins profiles as a 5-tech Linebacker shakeup : Ivan Pace Jr. could be expendable. “If you get enough from both [Jacob] Roberts and Bangally Kamara to where, hey, Ivan Pace expendable, you’re gonna save almost $2.7 million.” Jakobe Thomas (drafted safety) vs. Jacob Thomas (UDFA safety) : “Jacob Thomas has outshined everybody in that secondary, but it’s also UDFA in the preseason. I wanna see the third-round pick play.” CBs: Charles Demmings and Da’Veawn Armstead for CB4/5; Zemaiah Vaughn is the sneak. Jake Golday’s role : Forness envisions a Dallas Turner-like development path — sub-packages only, not a full snap load yet. Punter battle : Johnny Hekker vs. Brett Thorson — watch hang time, direction, and ball placement. Listen: Or on your favorite podcast aggregator. Watch: “Everybody is expendable. Everybody,” Forness said. That is the whole finale. Live Two-Minute Warning lands around 10:45 p.m. CT Friday; Two Old Bloggers takes the 3 p.m. Sunday cutdown. Fan with Us!!! What do you think? Watch the full Real Forno Show from Vikings 1st & SKOL and Bleav, then tell us: if McCarthy takes the first snap in Denver, is that development — or a goodbye tape? Does J.J. McCarthy playing Friday mean the Vikings are already done with him? Do you think McCarthy has played his last snap in purple?

title: 3-Point Stance: Why Jaylen Reed fills a foundational role in the Patriots defense
summary: In the deal that brought Jaylen Reed to the New England Patriots on Monday, it wasn’t the young safety who drew outside attention to the transaction. Instead, the focus centered on the player New England sent to the Houston Texans. Wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. As a homegrown talent selected in the sixth round of the […]
full_text: Foxborough, MA - August 25: New England Patriots cornerback Carlton Davis III and safety Jaylen Reed walk onto the field for practice at Gillette Stadium on August 25, 2026. (Photo by Danielle Parhizkaran/The Boston Globe via Getty Images) | Boston Globe via Getty Images In the deal that brought Jaylen Reed to the New England Patriots on Monday , it wasn’t the young safety who drew outside attention to the transaction. Instead, the focus centered on the player New England sent to the Houston Texans. Wide receiver Kayshon Boutte. As a homegrown talent selected in the sixth round of the 2023 NFL Draft, Boutte, through a redshirt rookie year under Bill Belichick and legal troubles stemming from illegal sports gambling in college , blossomed into a crucial offensive piece that brought the Patriots back to the Super Bowl last season. The “Jaylen Reed trade,” as Executive Vice President of Player Personnel Eliot Wolf called the deal when speaking with the media on Tuesday, featured a mildly underwhelming return for a target that quarterback Drake Maye had significant success targeting downfield in 2025. New England received Reed, who was a backup in Houston, and a 2028 seventh-round pick. Last week, after the Patriots’ preseason victory against the Philadelphia Eagles on Aug. 22, head coach Mike Vrabel, focusing on the development of the team’s young players, said he doesn’t think the team has a very deep roster when asked about personnel usage heading into the Cleveland Browns matchup on Thursday. Much of that thin depth resides on the defense. Adding Reed fills a role behind starters Craig Woodson and Kevin Byard that can play a significant part in the unit’s identity in 2026 and beyond. Unlocks consistent big nickel packages New England covets versatile defenders. It’s been a staple of the franchise for decades, partly because it allows the defense to excel in various personnel packages. At Penn State, the 23-year-old was utilized in several roles across the formation, primarily as a free safety and in the box. Reed, as a senior in 2024, logged 426 snaps in the deep portion of the field and 289 underneath as a physical defensive back. The Patriots’ defense has spent extensive time in training camp practicing in a three-safety package and cycling through rotational players, including Dell Pettus, John Saunders Jr. and Mike Brown. Still, it hasn’t produced the desired results. Standing at six feet and 212 pounds, Reed best fits that mold, possessing the necessary physical attributes to contribute in run defense and by blitzing, lining up next to the linebackers. The safety posted an 80.5 run defense grade on Pro Football Focus for the 2024 collegiate season . He and Pettus are willing defenders when crashing towards the line of scrimmage, which aids a linebacking core that, similar to the safety room, lacked proper depth before the Reed trade. And while the former Texan needs to improve as an open-field tackler, he has the short-area quickness to help in underneath coverage or even in an area New England struggled in last season: following tight ends in man coverage. History at slot corner back In the Super Bowl, the Patriots struggled to maintain coverage on Seattle Seahawks tight end AJ Barner, who secured the Seahawks’ lone offensive touchdown and caught four passes for 54 yards. NFL offenses are emphasizing deploying tall, athletic tight ends who can serve as in-line blockers for the running backs and as receiving threats. And while starting nickel cornerback Marcus Jones, standing at 5-foot-8 and 188 pounds, is a quality tackler for his size, his smaller frame remains a disadvantage when covering tight ends nearly a foot taller than him. During his senior year with the Nittany Lions, Reed also took 153 snaps as a slot cornerback. As good as Jones is in coverage, Reed’s larger frame and physicality better suit him for those matchups at the catch point. Provides immediate depth relief Furthermore, Vrabel spoke about the defense’s lack of effort against Cleveland ahead of the roster cutdown deadline on Sunday. “Not good enough,” Vrabel said Thursday night . “They felt like we got a couple of sudden-change stops and forced them to kick field goals, which I think is always positive. But just not enough. [They] couldn’t match up to the speed of the quarterback on the zone read and some of those things. But we’ll get back to work and figure out who we’re going to get back to work with.” As the starters rested, New England’s cornerbacks faltered, consistently getting beat in coverage and failing to finish tackles at an alarming rate. While Reed was only a sixth-round draft choice in 2025 and appeared in just seven regular-season contests for the Texans last season, his former team displayed trust in him as a rookie by giving him the starting nod in both playoff matchups. Reed allows the Patriots to line up in the nickel packages they’ve tried to establish all offseason and can make a name for himself as a reliable rotational defensive back this season.
author: Andrew Guindon

title: Fans grade Patriots’ trade of Kayshon Boutte
summary: The New England Patriots officially traded wide receiver Kayshon Boutte to the Houston Texans this week, receiving safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028th seventh-round draft pick in return. Boutte’s departure comes after a long offseason full of speculation over his future. The 24-year old requested a trade this past spring as he enters a contract […]
full_text: Feb 8, 2026; Santa Clara, CA, USA; New England Patriots wide receiver Kayshon Boutte (9) against the Seattle Seahawks during Super Bowl LX at Levi's Stadium. Mandatory Credit: Mark J. Rebilas-Imagn Images | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New England Patriots officially traded wide receiver Kayshon Boutte to the Houston Texans this week, receiving safety Jaylen Reed and a 2028th seventh-round draft pick in return. Boutte’s departure comes after a long offseason full of speculation over his future. The 24-year old requested a trade this past spring as he enters a contract year and was set to see both his playing time and production dip after the Patriots upgraded their wide receiver depth chart with A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs. Mike Vrabel even revealed Boutte would have been inactive during the season, barring injuries. As New England’s wide receiver room remained deep even beyond Brown and Doubs, the decision was made to move off of Boutte, who never eclipsed the 600-yard mark, to add depth elsewhere on the roster and open up more opportunities for players like Kyle Williams. But for a Patriots team that remains Super Bowl hopeful — where they currently are tied with the fifth-highest odds on FanDuel Sportsbook to hoist the Lombardi Trophy this season — many believed the team should have kept the pass catcher, who has strong chemistry with quarterback Drake Maye. That is why in the results of the latest SB Nation Reacts survey, 30% of participants voted the trade as a neutral C. Much of comment section agreed, largely do to what was viewed as a minimal return: SlotMachinePlayer The grade for this draft depends on two things: Brown staying healthy, since Boutte was the guy most likely to fill that role if he’s hurt. Reed turning into a useful depth player; something Boutte was. The draft pick was meh. Could have likely gotten a higher comp pick if Boutte went elsewhere at the end of the year. Looking like a D right now, since safety wasn’t a position of need, and Reed didn’t play much. PatriotPapa C. Should have gotten a much higher draft pick beyond the 1-for-1 player trade. Patriots had Houston needing to make the trade having just lost Jayden Higgins with torn ACL. Getting much needed help in run defense was a solid move, but a higher draft pick IN 2027 should have been demanded. For Pats Sake F- Patriots got fleeced. Should have been for safety Jaylen Reed and a 2027 3rd or 4th Round Pick. Instead we got a freaking 2028 7th and a player that has not been as productive as Boutte. Sportsbozo52 I think they got what they wanted. A viable player and a 28 draft choice. Boutte will do well in Texas. May he continue to grow! I am a fan of his and will remain a fan of his, just not when he plays the Patriots. I don’t know much about Jaylin Reed, let’s hope he sticks with the Patriots and can be a contributor for the upcoming season. new_phal3123 I think C+ in the sense that it’s just right down the middle. It’s the reality of the market for that type of WR. I think Boutte is a valuable player but in his role with 1 year left, there’s just not a huge market. The plus comes from getting an immediate contributor rather than just a future day 3 pick. Todger Thirty two teams could be looking for a replacement WR, due to a season ending injury, within one week of the season start All in all, this week’s survey results look as follows: Some were in favor of the trade, as 5% of voters graded the move as an A with 24% giving the deal a B. That may have to do with the potential of Jaylen Reed taking on a larger defensive role in New England and becoming the third safety the team was looking for to pair with Kevin Byard and Craig Woodson. Most fans were on the opposite end of the spectrum, however, as 16% of voters grading the trade as a F with another 25% awarding it a D. Following the move, the Houston Texans are now tied with the Patriots in Super Bowl odds on FanDuel Sportsbook . According to executive vice president of player personal Eliot Wolf, the Patriots were not worried about sending Boutte to a fellow AFC contender . “No, there was no concern about that, and I don’t think there was any concern for them to send us a safety that we think can play,” Wolf said.

title: Patriots final 53-man roster projection ahead of NFL cuts
summary: Training camp is over, the preseason is a wrap, and the New England Patriots are officially on to building their first 53-man roster for the upcoming season. What the reigning AFC champions will do is anybody’s guess, but here is our final projection with the NFL cutdown deadline looming. By Sunday, Aug. 30, at 6 […]
full_text: FOXBOROUGH, MA - AUGUST 22: Kindle Vildor #28 of the New England Patriots reacts to a near interception during a preseason game between the New England Patriots and the Philadelphia Eagles on August 22, 2026, at Gillette Stadium in Foxborough, Massachusetts. (Photo by Fred Kfoury III/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images) | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images Training camp is over, the preseason is a wrap, and the New England Patriots are officially on to building their first 53-man roster for the upcoming season. What the reigning AFC champions will do is anybody’s guess, but here is our final projection with the NFL cutdown deadline looming. By Sunday, Aug. 30, at 6 p.m. ET we will know what they will have done. For now, here is what we think Mike Vrabel and company will do. Quarterback In (2): Drake Maye, Tommy DeVito Out (1): Behren Morton Drake Maye and Tommy DeVito have been the clear 1-2 at the quarterback position throughout the summer. The former is an MVP-caliber quarterback with clear franchise player qualities, while the latter is an experienced player who had some really good moments leading the second-string offense through training camp and preseason. The biggest question is the status of rookie Behren Morton. The seventh-round draft pick showed some promise, but ultimately would be too much of a luxury to have on the 53-man team. He is a prime practice squad candidate, though, even if waiving him comes with some risk. Running back In (4): Rhamondre Stevenson, TreVeyon Henderson, Hassan Haskins , Lan Larison Out (2): Jam Miller , JaMycal Hasty IR (1): Myles Montgomery The running back competition might not have been of the highest quality, but it has nonetheless been entertaining. Under normal circumstances, Terrell Jennings probably would be RB3 behind Rhamondre Stevenson and TreVeyon Henderson. With him being sent to injured reserve and subsequently waived, however, the race reopened. Based on the full body of work after Jennings’ departure from the active team, we project two players to make the cut: Hassan Haskins and Lan Larison, the former as pure running back depth and the latter adding a receiving and kickoff return element to the mix. Of course, there is a chance the Patriots go below 53 players in order to create space for potential waiver claims. In that case, either could be a cut candidate. Fullback In (1): Reggie Gilliam Out: N/A When Reggie Gilliam joined the Patriots as a free agent in March, the Patriots had three fullbacks listed on their roster. Five months later, he is the last man standing: Brock Lampe was released early in training camp while Jack Westover converted back to tight end. Gilliam will make the team to serve as the lead blocker out of I-formation and serve as a potential H-back as well. Wide receiver In (6): A.J. Brown, Romeo Doubs, DeMario Douglas, Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams, Efton Chism III Out (4): Cameron Dorner, Kyle Dixon, Nick DeGennaro, Tejhaun Palmer IR (2): Jimmy Kibble, Jeremiah Webb The Kayshon Boutte trade to the Texans creates a clearer picture at wide receiver. Whereas the team was looking at potentially carrying seven wideouts — even though Boutte’s role on the game day roster would apparently have been non-existent to begin with — it now has six players as relatively safe bets to make the cut: A.J. Brown and Romeo Doubs will be the top duo, with DeMario Douglas the starting slot; Mack Hollins, Kyle Williams and Efton Chism provide depth behind them. The other wideouts are all candidates for the practice squad, with Cameron Dorner and Kyle Dixon in particular worth keeping an eye on. Dorner was the most consistent depth receiver over the course of the summer, while Dixon has looked good during the last two preseason games. Tight end In (3): Hunter Henry, Eli Raridon , Tanner Arkin Out (2): Jack Westover , C.J. Dippre IR (1): Julian Hill As mentioned above, the Patriots might cut their roster below the 53-man deadline in order to create extra space for waiver-wire pickups. In that case Arkin might find himself one of the odd men out. For the time being, we do see him make the team as the top blocking tight end behind the projected top two of Hunter Henry and Eli Raridon. Among those, Henry is likely to hoard reps while Raridon will be more of a package and part-time piece despite showing some flashes over the last month. Offensive tackle In (6): Will Campbell, Morgan Moses, Caleb Lomu, Marcus Bryant, James Hudson III, Dametrious Crownover Out (2): Jack Conley, Lorenz Metz (exempt) Six offensive tackles might seem excessive given the questions about depth elsewhere on the team, but hear us out. Will Campbell and Morgan Moses are the top two, with Caleb Lomu and Marcus Bryant the next men down the depth chart. Both are facing questions, though: the former about his regular season readiness, the latter about the ankle injury he sustained in the second preseason game against the Eagles. Unless Bryant starts the year on injured reserve with a return designation in place of other projected candidates to be mentioned later, we do see the Patriots carry both on their 53-man team. In addition, James Hudson’s tackle-guard flexibility is a plus (and something Lomu could theoretically also provide), while Dametrious Crownover making it through waivers is not a given and releasing him therefore a plan too risky for our liking. Interior offensive line In (4): Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson, Mike Onwenu, Greg Van Roten IR-DFR (1): Ben Brown Out (5): Mehki Butler, Jacob Rizy, JonDarius Morgan, Darrian Dalcourt, Joseph Michalski While we see the Patriots keep a relatively high number of tackles, we see them start the year thin along their interior offensive line. Behind starters Alijah Vera-Tucker, Jared Wilson and Mike Onwenu, we only see one other player make the cut: recent free agent signing Greg Van Roten, whose mix of versatility and experience — let alone his contract — points toward him beating out the competition. We do think the Patriots have another interior lineman in their plans for 2026, though. Ben Brown, who was banged up in the preseason opener, could start the year on injured reserve with the return designation. A reminder: teams can move up to two players to IR with the intention of bringing them back if they are properly designated on cutdown day. Interior defensive line In (6): Milton Williams, Christian Barmore, Cory Durden, Joshua Farmer, Leonard Taylor III, Eric Gregory Out (3): Isaiah Iton , Jeremiah Pharms Jr, Casey Rogers Milton Williams and Christian Barmore are as disruptive an interior duo as there is in the NFL today, but the depth behind them is a question mark. Cory Durden projects as the third option, while the trio of Joshua Farmer and Eric Gregory as well as Leonard Taylor III offer depth against the run (Farmer, Gregory) and pass (Taylor). The numbers are solid and every one of the backups has had his moments in training camp. Overall, however, Williams and Barmore are the only truly-proven commodities in their projected roles. Defensive edge In (3): Dre’Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder , Gabe Jacas PUP (1): Harold Landry III Out (5): Bradyn Swinson , Quintayvious Hutchins, Xavier Holmes, Jesse Luketa , Amari Gainer Harold Landry is not guaranteed to miss the start of the season, per his head coach, but we still see the team keep him on the physically unable to perform list for the first few games. This, in turn, means that the Patriots will start the year quite thin on the edge: with none of the depth pieces truly rising to the occasion, only Dre’Mont Jones, Elijah Ponder and Gabe Jacas have earned spots on the team — for a variety of reason. Fact is, after all, that Jacas in particular has had his issues; the preseason game against the Browns made it painfully clear that he has a long way to go before he can be trusted in an extensive role. As a consequence, this is a position where we can see definitive reinforcements coming through the waiver wire or free agency. As…

title: Patriots vs. Browns: The good, the bad, the s—t that gets you beat
summary: Ahead of his first training camp as New England Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories. The Patriots’ 37-13 loss to the Cleveland Browns on Thursday night saw mostly the second of those categories: there was little of the good, but a lot […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 27: Drew Biber #43 of the Cleveland Browns runs the ball during the third quarter of a preseason game against the New England Patriots at Huntington Bank Field on August 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images Ahead of his first training camp as New England Patriots head coach in 2025, Mike Vrabel explained that he was judging his team’s performances by three distinct categories. The Patriots’ 37-13 loss to the Cleveland Browns on Thursday night saw mostly the second of those categories: there was little of the good, but a lot of the bad and the s—t that gets you beat. If Vrabel looks at his team through those specific categorizations, let’s follow his lead and break down Patriots-Browns accordingly. The good: No major injuries As noted above, the Patriots’ loss to the Browns was mostly bad. There were still a few positives such as wide receiver Kyle Williams scoring his third touchdown in three preseason games, linebacker Namdi Obiazor being active on defense and special teams, or the kicking operation looking good. The biggest positive from our perspective, however, was the lack of any significant injuries. The only scary moment came midway through the second quarter, when left tackle James Hudson — the Patriots’ starter at that spot in lieu of usual backup LT Marcus Bryant — got banged up. However, Hudson eventually reentered the contest and finished with 37 of 59 snaps. It remains to be seen whether or not Hudson actually factors into the 53-man roster mix come Sunday evening. However, the fact that his was the only issue and still seemingly minor in nature is good news for a New England team that lost three valuable players over the first two weeks of preseason: backup interior offensive linemen Ben Brown and Andrew Rupcich against the Colts, followed by Bryant versus the Eagles. The bad: Money downs The Patriots were unable to deliver in most areas on Thursday, but one that stands out in particular were key situations on offense and defense. Offensively, the team went only 4-for-12 on third down, followed by a 1-for-2 fourth down performance (with one of those failed fourth downs a Behren Morton interception that was returned 36 yards to the New England 12-yard line). The unit also finished an uninspiring 0-for-2 in the red zone. The defense, meanwhile, allowed Cleveland to move the chains on eight of 13 third downs. The Browns also went 4-for-6 in the red area, and a perfect 3-for-3 in goal-to-go situations. It wasn’t great. The s—t that gets you beat: Lack of juice Mike Vrabel was hired by the Patriots in January 2025 in large parts because of his reputation as a culture-builder, and he has indeed done a commendable job turning the team around after back-to-back 4-13 seasons. Thursday night, however, saw little of that. Instead, Vrabel’s team showed little juice and was simply outclassed by its opponent from start to finish. The positive is that the team that took on the Browns will not be the one that will face the reigning world champion Seahawks in just under two weeks. None of the true core Patriots were on the field Thursday, and even roster-worthy depth options that struggled — think: Charles Woods and Kindle Vildor — should benefit from the “rising tide lifting all boats” effect. But if we look at the Browns game in a vacuum, none of that matters. For those 60 minutes, the performance and demeanor simply were not good enough.

title: 10 things we learned from Patriots vs. Browns preseason game
summary: The New England Patriots played a horribly boring and just downright horrible game on Thursday in Cleveland to close out their preseason. Even though their 37-13 loss to the Browns was disappointing very much from start to finish, there are always lessons to be learned. Let’s get into what the Patriots’ final preseason contest of 2026 […]
full_text: CLEVELAND, OHIO - AUGUST 27: CJ Dippre #81 of the New England Patriots catches a pass during the fourth quarter of a preseason game against the Cleveland Browns at Huntington Bank Field on August 27, 2026 in Cleveland, Ohio. (Photo by Lauren Leigh Bacho/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New England Patriots played a horribly boring and just downright horrible game on Thursday in Cleveland to close out their preseason. Even though their 37-13 loss to the Browns was disappointing very much from start to finish, there are always lessons to be learned. Let’s get into what the Patriots’ final preseason contest of 2026 taught us about the team. Depth concerns The Patriots didn’t play any starters on Thursday night, and, truthfully, they probably didn’t play many backups either. The lack of depth was still startling. They were outmatched at pretty much every position on the field, and blown out by a team that could be one of the worst in football this year. The Browns also didn’t start anyone of consequence, so it’s not like they were facing tougher competition. It just illustrates the point that head coach Mike Vrabel had made last week about New England’s depth . When looking at the starter level, the Patriots have gotten significantly better as a team. If you start to look down the depth chart, that falls apart pretty quickly. It is like that for a lot of teams, but the Patriots need to continue to string good drafts together and find competent UDFAs to help fill out that depth. The hope is that they can do that moving forward, because it was tough to watch some of the guys out there on Thursday. RB3 competition heating up Hassan Haskins isn’t going to be returning kicks any time soon, but he did look good running the ball. He ran tough and picked up yards even while getting hit behind the line of scrimmage. Conversely, Lan Larison had two straight drops when he was on the field, and, while JaMichael Hasty had a few nice runs, I don’t think he’s the guy who the Patriots want as their third back either. This all might be moot, because Jam Miller didn’t even have a carry, which could signal that the Patriots already know that he’s the RB3, and they didn’t really need to see anything else from him on Thursday night. If I had to put money on it, I’d put my money on Miller, but I guess we’ll find out this weekend. Gabe Jacas, error repeater The Patriots knew that they might not be getting the best out of Gabe Jacas early on with him missing time in the spring and at the beginning of camp, but I can’t imagine they thought he would look quite this bad in actual game action. What worries me is not the lack of production when it comes to rushing the quarterback, or even stopping the run, but the fact that he keeps making the same mistakes. He is continually burned on bootleg, RPO, and option plays, and instead of holding the outside integrity, he comes flying in and gives up the edge. It’s happened in every game that he’s played in. At a certain point, you need to ask whether or not he’s ever going to figure it out. I know we’re not even into the regular season of his rookie year, but I would love to see more from him particularly against replacement-level opponents. Until he figures it out, the Patriots simply cannot put him out on the field on a regular basis — which is not good news considering that he currently projects as the team’s third edge. For the love of god, please sign Christian Gonzalez The depth shouldn’t even matter when we’re talking about Christian Gonzalez, but my goodness, it was even worse than anyone could have expected. Kindle Vildor looked awful, Karon Prunty played okay, but had trouble finishing his tackles. Meanwhile, Kobee Minor and Marcellas Dial Jr. both had horrendously bad plays that led to touchdowns. Again, this should have next to no impact on the Patriots signing one of the best cornerbacks in the NFL, but it certainly can’t hurt. Not sure what exactly the hold up has been for the Patriots, or why they wouldn’t be willing to extend one of not only their best players, but one of the best players in the league, but there is no excuse to them not getting something done. Dominated at the line of scrimmage The Patriots obviously didn’t play any starters, or even a lot of second-stringers, but they were completely dominated on both sides of the line. I thought that Caleb Lomu was able to hold his own when he was in there, but I didn’t see much from anyone else on the offensive line. On defense, they got almost no pass rush and couldn’t stop the run either. It was as bad of a night as you could imagine, with no one showing much of anything. I really like the starters that they have on both sides of the ball, but, as soon as guys start going down, there isn’t a lot of depth behind them. Do we have a punter competition? New England brought in a new punter, Matt Haack, because Bryce Baringer got banged up in the game against the Eagles last weekend. Haack had four punts in his Patriots debut, with thrree of them pinning the Browns inside the 20, including a 63-yarder that was downed at the 2. Baringer looked pretty solid in camp, and it’s clear that kicker Andy Borregales is comfortable with him as his holder. That said, Borregales went 2-for-2 on field goal attempts on Thursday night, and the punts looked great from Haack as well. I think there’s going to be a conversation about which punter to keep starting the season, especially with Baringer a little banged up. Kyle Williams might be a one-trick pony, but it’s a heck of a trick There was a whole lot of concern at the beginning of camp about Kyle Williams. He wasn’t getting enough time with the starters, and people were worried that he was on a worrisome trajectory. Well, he might not be a WR1 at this point in his career (or maybe ever), but he had consistently shown that he does one thing extremely well: he is untouchable on a go-route, especially with no safety help. This single skill should be enough to earn him a few looks a game from Drake Maye, one of the best deep ball throwers in the NFL. I am hoping that he will eventually add more tools to his bag, but having the ability to quickly win off the line and consistently beat coverage deep is a valuable skill, and one which I believe is going to be an important part of the Patriots offense this year. Namdi Obiazor makes a few plays On a night where most guys looked terrible, sixth-round draft pick Namdi Obiazor looked at least pretty good. Starting linebackers Robert Spillane and Christian Elliss weren’t dressed, and neither was the injured Khalil Jacobs, leaving Obiazor to look like the best linebacker on the team on Thursday. Granted, that might not be a high bar, but the youngster nonetheless was one of the few defenders to show up on Thursday. It also helps that he plays a bunch of special teams. This, plus his potential to develop into a player on defense, would be a big boost for a team who doesn’t have any noteworthy long-term depth behind Spillane and Elliss. Behren Morton is unimpressive I have mostly liked what I’ve seen from Behren Morton in training camp, and when he has been given reps, he has made pretty good decisions. He looked pretty poised for a rookie, and looked to be a good candidate to eventually become a backup to Drake Maye. All of that went out the window on Thursday. Morton looked frazzled, made some really bad decisions, and missed on a few throws that could have been big plays — all while going against players who mostly will be out of a job come Sunday night. Ultimately, I think he’s a good guy to keep on the practice squad to see if you can develop him into a usable backup, but, after seeing what I saw Thursday, I’m not going to be super upset if someone claims him off of waivers if the Patriots cut him this weekend. Cutdown day is looming The Patriots have to trim their roster from 91 all the way down to 53 by Sunday afternoon, and they have some tough decisions to make. The first few they are…

title: NFL 2026 Waiver Wire Rules and Order
summary: All NFL teams are now in the process of reducing their rosters to 53 players and while those rosters are never final, the number stands pat at 53. Teams will now play musical chairs with players signing some to their practice squad and claiming some off of waivers. For those unfamiliar with the process, the […]
full_text: METAIRIE, LOUISIANA - JULY 30: A detailed view of a New Orleans Saints Helmet during training camp at Ochsner Sports Performance Center on July 30, 2026 in Metairie, Louisiana. (Photo by Tyler Kaufman/Getty Images) | Getty Images All NFL teams are now in the process of reducing their rosters to 53 players and while those rosters are never final, the number stands pat at 53. Teams will now play musical chairs with players signing some to their practice squad and claiming some off of waivers. For those unfamiliar with the process, the NFL waiver wire is a 24‑hour process for teams to claim players waived from their teams, with priority set by a fixed priority order that decides which team gets a waived player if more than one team submits a claim. In that scenario, the team highest in the waiver order is awarded the player. Waiver order from now through Week 3 is based on that year’s original NFL Draft order. (Any trades that are made in the draft are not taken into account) What are the waiver wire rules? The 53-man cutdown deadline is 5 p.m. CT on Sunday, August 30 after which time every NFL team must be at 53 players. Rosters will be reduced from 90 players to 53 players, which means each team makes 37 cuts. Waiver claims clear at 12 p.m. CT on Monday, August 31. Vested veterans (played four or more accrued seasons) are not subject to waivers and become free agents immediately; players with fewer seasons must clear waivers first. Teams can start signing player to their practice squads, which can hold up to 16 players, or 17 with the International Player designation. What is the waiver wire order? title: Interview with the Enemy: Dallas Cowboys
summary: The New Orleans Saints will head to Arlington to face the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium in Week 3 of the 2026 NFL preseason. To break it down, David Halprin of Blogging The Boys joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: At this point, everyone knows the joint practice between New Orleans and Dallas was chippy as […]
full_text: OXNARD, CALIFORNIA - AUGUST 18: Donovan Ezeiruaku #6 of the Dallas Cowboys pulls off Taliese Fuaga #75 of the New Orleans Saints helmet during joint practice at River Ridge Playing Fields on August 18, 2026 in Oxnard, California. (Photo by Ric Tapia/Getty Images) | Getty Images The New Orleans Saints will head to Arlington to face the Dallas Cowboys at AT&T Stadium in Week 3 of the 2026 NFL preseason. To break it down, David Halprin of Blogging The Boys joins us to preview this weekend’s matchup. NJ: At this point, everyone knows the joint practice between New Orleans and Dallas was chippy as all get out. Before that joint practice and since then, the Saints haven’t really had any issues with scuffles. Has that kind of intensity and physicality been a consistent theme throughout the Cowboys’ offseason? DH: I would say the intensity has been there through training camp, a certain amount of energy, but we haven’t had the scuffles we saw in that joint practice. Christian Parker is our new defensive coordinator and he has brought a swagger back to the defensive side of the ball, and that has led to some trash-talking during practices as a very poor Cowboys defense from 2025 gets a complete makeover. Brian Schottenheimer is also a high-energy coach so there has been some friendly banter and interplay between the offense and defense, but only OLB Donovan Ezeiruaku, who was thrown out of the Saints practice, was also told to leave a practice earlier in training camp for a similar fighting problem. That appeared to be a very isolated incident because we never saw much else like that until the joint practice. I don’t know what happened during the joint practice, but the fighting seemed out of the ordinary for how the Cowboys had conducted most of their practices. NJ: Which Dallas position battle or group of players has the most to gain from the additional preseason reps against New Orleans? DH: The Cowboys are sorting out quite a few position battles. One of the ones that has been watched a lot is who will be RB2 behind Javonte Williams. Jaydon Blue, Malik Davis, Phil Mafah and Israel Abanikanda are all fighting for reps, with Davis in the driver’s seat right now. The Cowboys are also closely looking at their depth at cornerback as they have a cluster of players all trying to get attention. This one may end up needing some outside help once cutdown day happens. There was a good battle at QB2 going on, but many feel like Joe Milton III has locked that up with a couple of excellent performances in preseason. There is also some competition going on along the backup offensive line. NJ: What are you hoping to learn about the Cowboys from Friday’s matchup against the Saints, and what did you learn from training camp and the first two preseason games that you’d like to see the team build on? DH: For most of the offseason, training camp and preseason, Cowboys fans have been eyeing the changes on defense and hoping they make the team better. Last year, the defense was horrible and totally scuttled the season. First-time defensive coordinator Christian Parker has changed the scheme and has overhauled much of the personnel on that side of the ball. So far, it looks like it is working as the defense has played much better. The continuation of that is what Cowboys fans need to see. We know our offense is powerful and can score points, last year they were great. It is all down to the defense if we are going to have success in 2026. NJ: Who is one Cowboys player you think Saints fans should keep an eye on Friday—someone who may not be receiving much national attention but could make a strong impression? DH: Wide receiver Camden Brown went undrafted as a rookie. He only had one strong college season in his senior year after he transferred, and wasn’t really on our radar after the Cowboys signed him. In training camp, he exploded. He just kept making plays and catching the attention of everybody. Then in the first preseason game he had two spectacular touchdown catches, and in the last game he added a 69-yard catch-and-run pass completion. He has come out of nowhere to the brink of making the roster. If he shines again on Friday, the Cowboys will have to keep him on the roster, it would be criminal negligence not to. NJ: According to FanDuel Sportsbook , the Cowboys (-126) are currently 2.5-point favorites over the Saints (+108) in Sunday’s matchup; what is your final score prediction? DH: Predicting scores for preseason games feels like a losing proposition all around because you never know who will play for how long, and what the coaches want to look at that might not be the best strategy for winning the game. But since you asked, I’ll go with Cowboys 24 Saints 13. Thank you again to David Halprin for joining us to preview this week’s matchup! You can check out the rest of his work here .

summary: The New Orleans Saints are 0-2 in the preseason so far and didn’t look pretty in a 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. With New Orleans entering their final preseason match, it feels vital to go into the regular season on a high note. Head coach Kellen Moore has already announced very few starters […]
full_text: Dec 23, 2012; Arlington, TX, USA; Dallas Cowboys tight end Jason Witten (82) catches a pass during overtime of the game against the New Orleans Saints at Cowboys Stadium. The catch breaks the single season receptions record for a tight end in the NFL. The Saints beat the Cowboys 34-31 in overtime. Mandatory Credit: Matthew Emmons-USA TODAY Sports | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New Orleans Saints are 0-2 in the preseason so far and didn’t look pretty in a 34-0 loss to the Los Angeles Rams. With New Orleans entering their final preseason match, it feels vital to go into the regular season on a high note. Head coach Kellen Moore has already announced very few starters will see playtime against the Dallas Cowboys. Despite the reserves seeing the bulk of the playing time, there’s still plenty of matchups to pay attention to on Friday night. Saints secondary vs. QB Joe Milton III Cowboys quarterback Joe Milton III has been lighting it up in the preseason. Through two games, Milton has thrown for 286 yards and 3 touchdowns with just seven incompletions. For short, the Saints defense that just allowed 254 passing yards is in for a challenge. Milton’s talent is exceptional, and he may be one of the league’s best raw talents. While he hasn’t been able to put it all together as a starter in the league, his name often comes up as a trade target for teams looking for a young passer. The Saints secondary had a strong showing against the Jacksonville Jaguars in their first preseason outing, despite the loss, but followed it up quickly with a poor performance against the Rams. With questions entering the season centered around the secondary, they’ll need a strong performance on Friday to increase confidence in the depth. Saints pass rush vs. Cowboys pass protection Part of Milton’s success has been the Dallas pass protection. Through two games, the Cowboys have only allowed one sack, with Milton himself not suffering a sack. In preseason week one, the Saints pass rush logged four sacks, with Michael Heldman recording two. But like every other facet of the game, the Saints’ pass rush was terrible against the Rams, failing to record a quarterback hit. If New Orleans wants to slow down the powerful Cowboys offense, it will come with slowing down the Dallas quarterbacks. If the Saints can replicate their success from their first outing, they will severely increase their chances of coming out on top and winning their first game of preseason. RB Kendre Miller vs. Cowboys run defense Running back Devin Neal and Ty Chandler each suffered significant injuries against the Rams. These injuries only emphasized the depletion of available backs the Saints have in the running back room. With the injuries, the Saints traded for Zamir White. Despite the trade, running back Kendre Miller is still the player with the best chance to take over for Alvin Kamara while he’s away with an injury. Through two games, the Cowboys have allowed 242 rushing yards. While facing a defense that has been vulnerable to the run, the Saints’ run game has been inconsistent. In his preseason debut against the Rams, Miller only rushed for 22 yards on six carries. While underwhelming, the fourth-year running back had plenty of plays negated by penalties and still showed the ability to create explosive plays. Friday’s matchup is a great opportunity for the young running back, who has a big opportunity to see playtime this season.

title: NY Giants trade for Baltimore Ravens’ DT to bolster run defense
summary: The New York Giants are trading for Baltimore Ravens defensive tackle C.J. Okoye, per a report from Mike Garafolo of the NFL Network. The Giants are sending the 2028 seventh-round pick they got for Joshua Ezeudu to the Ravens in exchange for Okoye. It was widely expected that the Giants would make moves to reinforce […]
full_text: Baltimore Ravens defensive tackle C.J. Okoye | IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect The New York Giants are trading for Baltimore Ravens defensive tackle C.J. Okoye , per a report from Mike Garafolo of the NFL Network. The Giants are sending the 2028 seventh-round pick they got for Joshua Ezeudu to the Ravens in exchange for Okoye. It was widely expected that the Giants would make moves to reinforce an interior defensive line that has been a weakness throughout the summer and preseason. It makes sense that their first move would be to acquire a player that not only has rare traits but is also familiar to John Harbaugh. Okoye played for John Harbaugh in 2025 with the Ravens after playing for Jim Harbaugh as an international pathway player (originally from Nigeria) for the Los Angeles Chargers in 2023 and 2024. His experience with John Harbaugh isn’t Okoye’s only link to the Giants, and Okoye came into the International Pathway Program at the insistence of Giants’ great Osi Umenyiora . Okoye, 24, is a massive defensive tackle, listed at 6-foot-6, 365 pounds. That said, he also has impressive physical traits, with surprising movement skills for such an enormous young man. Okoye played in 13 games for the Ravens last season, making 15 tackles in 214 defensive snaps. He’s still learning the game of football, as well as how to use his formidable tools. Okoye’s first organized game of football was his first preseason game for the Chargers in 2023, a game in which he also got his first sack . Former teammate Morgan Fox (Chargers’ defensive tackle) said in 2024 that Okoye was only just “starting to figure out football, which is terrifying.” Okoye had been listed as a second-string defensive tackle for the Ravens, which is significant considering the Ravens have ESPN’s second-ranked defensive tackle group . He’s also been a part of one of the NFL’s best preseason run defenses, and is coming off of a strong game against the Washington Commanders with a tackle, QB hit, and a fumble recovery.

title: New York Giants mailbag: Deonte Banks, roster size, more questions
summary: Adam Jacobs asks: Like all Giants fans, I am very excited about the coming season. I have a question about Banks. Everyone knows about his struggles the past two seasons, as well as the encouraging signs since the start of training camp. Is his (perceived) improvement more about a change back to a press, man-to-man defense, […]
full_text: Adam Jacobs asks: Like all Giants fans, I am very excited about the coming season. I have a question about Banks. Everyone knows about his struggles the past two seasons, as well as the encouraging signs since the start of training camp. Is his (perceived) improvement more about a change back to a press, man-to-man defense, a change in the coaching staff, or something else? I am more than happy if they could get good production out of him beyond returning kickoffs. Do you think this is just trying to impress the coaches, or is this a turning the corner thing? Ed says: Adam, I don’t know what you are getting by asking if “this is just trying to impress the coaches.” Every player who isn’t an established star is always hoping to impress his coaches. In reference to Deonte Banks, the change in both his play and his demeanor have been real. Banks has been playing like the guy the Giants hoped he would be when they used a first-round pick on him in 2023. The change in coaching staffs and schemes has a lot to do with it. Maybe there were things going on in the young man’s life that affected him. We don’t know. Banks doesn’t like to talk to the media. When he does talk, his answers are very short. He isn’t going to tell us much. I don’t know if he will be a starter, but Banks looks like a player who can certainly contribute at cornerback. Joseph Evans asks: I know it’s most likely in the Collective Bargaining Agreement, but why is it you can only dress 45 on game day? With the amount of injuries, that doesn’t make sense to me. Ed says: Joseph, teams can dress 46. If they elevate two players from the practice squad, that number rises to 48. But, your question, of course, regards why there is any type of limit. It really has to do with competitive balance. Say one team has five injured players who cannot dress for a game. The opposing team has only two. The NFL wants each team to dress the same number of players in each game, theoretically so that one team is not at a numerical disadvantage. For me, there is a better way to accomplish this. Let teams dress 53 players for each game. If you have three players who are injured and cannot dress on your 53-man roster, teams should be allowed to activate three players from the practice squad — without needing to pass players through waivers to get them back on the practice squad. To me, full rosters would improve the quality of play. Join the conversation! Sign up for a user account and get: Fewer ads Create community posts Comment on articles, community posts Rec comments, community posts New, improved notifications system! Bob Donnelly asks: The kickoff (not kickoff coverage) is perhaps the only aspect of a preseason game that is not impacted by the other 21 players on the field. Through two preseason games how do you view this aspect of the kicker competition? Ed says: Bob, it is something we rarely see during practices. Honestly, it isn’t nearly as important as it was prior to the change in the rules that discourages touchbacks. There just isn’t enough to go on for me to say one guy is better at kickoffs than another. Spencer Gross asks: I just read your piece about JC Davis and I found it interesting about him watching and learning from Thomas. My question to you is do you know if Neal ever tried to learn from Thomas? Did Thomas ever mentor him? I’ve read you say Thomas is a stand up guy during interviews but I wonder about that dynamic between the two. Thomas is a captain so it’s evident he has leadership qualities but I’m curious about that relationship. Ed says: Spencer, I don’t really know the nature of the relationship between Neal and Thomas. Neal is in his fifth year in the league now, so he’s pretty much beyond the “mentoring” stage. I would have to believe that over the course of 4+ years that Thomas has tried to help him. Derick Gross asks: Is Nagy allowed to be on the sideline, but watch the offensive plays on a screen with a view from the booth? That way he could get the bird’s eye view of the play unfolding, but still communicate directly with players on the sideline. Ed says: No, Derick. There are tablets on the sideline, but I am not sure how quickly they show photos or replays of plays. Certainly not quickly enough to call the next play. Nagy will end up wherever he and John Harbaugh deem to be the best spot. Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, Normally, when I hear “noncontact” injury, I think if the cleats gripping too well but Austin’s foot apparently slipped. In Germany, I have to change to winter tires come the snow season. In the grass v turf debate, I never hear people talk about the cleat configuration. Since the cleat is half of the equation, I just wonder if the NFL or NFLPA have looked into it. Is this question ever asked? Ed says: Kölner, you are looking for a problem where one doesn’t exist. It is my understanding that NFL players have about 75 varieties of cleats to choose from. Read this from nearly 10 years ago about how much goes into player footwear. Anthony Viola asks: A friend of mine saw a recent interview with the LBs (Burns, Carter, Reese, and Thibs I believe) and he came away with the impression that they were not a tight knit group of players. I was very surprised to hear this. In your opinion, based on what you see and hear, is there any truth to what my friend said? I did not see the interview so admittedly I am getting this opinion/comment second hand. Ed says: Anthony, I think that’s nonsense. The interview they did was mostly a light-hearted interview with a national media member more or less asking silly questions to get a reaction. The other thing about that interview was that the three edge players insisted that Arvell Reese be included. That’s just looking for an issue where one doesn’t exist. title: NY Giants coach John Harbaugh explains not playing Jaxson Dart vs. Jets
summary: When the New York Giants meet the Dallas Cowboys in their Sept. 13 season-opener, quarterback Jaxson Dart will not have faced live competition in 29 days. Dart played briefly in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings, but has not played since. Head coach John Harbaugh considered having Dart play Friday against the New York […]
full_text: Jaxson Dart watches Friday’s game. | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images When the New York Giants meet the Dallas Cowboys in their Sept. 13 season-opener, quarterback Jaxson Dart will not have faced live competition in 29 days. Dart played briefly in the preseason opener against the Minnesota Vikings, but has not played since. Head coach John Harbaugh considered having Dart play Friday against the New York Jets, but decided that playing the second-year quarterback was “not worth the risk.” As he had in the days prior to the game, Harbaugh acknowledged the concern about the layoff for Dart. “I think there is a concern, and the concern is that they won’t have played in a game for a long time,” Harbaugh said. “So, will there be a rust factor, those kinds of things. We’re just going to have to make sure we do everything we can in practice to make sure our guys are sharp and ready to go. But we just decided to go that route and probably take the more conservative route. “We just decided not to take the chance.” Harbaugh pointed out that if Dart had played, other frontline players would also have had to play. “If Jaxson plays, a lot of other guys are going to play too, and then is it worth the risk?,” Harbaugh said. “We got out of the game with no serious injuries, so that’s good, and it probably would have gone that way too, and we’d be happy and they would have gotten some reps. But we chose not to go that way, so I understand. Any criticism of it, I do understand.” Injury updates: Tyrone Tracy has a stinger Running back Tyrone Tracy passed a concussion test, but Harbaugh said he does have a stinger. Cornerback Korie Black suffered a groin injury. Harbaugh said cornerback Art Green suffered an undisclosed “minor injury.” Odell Beckham has ‘done enough’ Harbaugh stopped short of saying that Odell Beckham Jr. would make the Giants’ 53-man roster, but admitted he has “done enough” to be on an NFL team. “I don’t want to like say exactly who’s making it right now and not, what the considerations are. And things can happen,” Harbaugh said. “But I think I would answer the question yes. I mean, I think he has done enough to make an NFL roster for sure. He’s played well, and he’s gotten better as his camp’s gone along. He deserves credit for that. He’s done a really good job with it.” A new play-caller … for one night only Quarterbacks coach Brian Callahan called offensive plays vs. the Jets. No, he is not taking over that job from offensive coordinator Matt Nagy . Harbaugh said this was “standard” preseason preparation. “You never know if something happens. If Nags can’t make it to the game, gets caught in North Jersey traffic or something like that, we might need Cally to do it,” Harbaugh said. “But that was just something different. Last week we had (defensive pass coordinator/secondary coach) Donald D’Alesio call the defenses a little bit, so I think it’s a pretty standard thing to do in preseason.”

summary: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to name their 53 man roster. full_text: Good morning, New York Giants fans! Here are the stories you need to know as the Giants get ready to name their 53 man roster. Giants by the numbers: Just how grueling was John Harbaugh’s training camp? | The Athletic The Giants have held 21 practices from the start of training camp to this point. They held 15 practices over the same stretch last year. Harbaugh’s practices have been longer, with 12 sessions lasting more than two hours. Just four of Daboll’s practices ran over two hours last year. Every coach drills situational football, but Harbaugh dedicates more time to game management — leading late, trailing late, end of half, etc. — than any of the previous four Giants coaches I’ve covered in the post-Tom Coughlin era. No stone has gone unturned by Harbaugh. The Giants have rehearsed everything from their pregame stretching routine to the victory formation. It will be shocking if the Giants aren’t effective at converting on fourth-and-1 because they’ve seemingly drilled that situation as much as any other this summer. Matt Simms impressed by Giants OC NFC East Preview: Is This the Cowboys’ Year? | The Ringer If you are a Giants fan and want to believe that this team can be frisky and compete for a wild-card spot this season, go for it. There’s a scenario in which Harbaugh shows he’s still got it, Dart is an exciting playmaker (and stays healthy), and Carter emerges as a Defensive Player of the Year candidate. But I can’t get there. Harbaugh did not look like a great coach with the Ravens last year. I need to see a lot more from Dart before believing that he can be a real difference maker. This roster still has a lot of holes and lacks depth. And I’m not sure that the offensive coaching staff will be able to do more with less. This feels more like a transition year in which Harbaugh figures out which guys he wants to build with going forward. Projected record: 6-11 How every 2026 NFL draft pick has looked in the preseason | ESPN.com Round 1 (No. 10): Francis Mauigoa, G. Mauigoa fits in nicely on the Giants offensive line. He has been the starter at right guard since Day 1 of camp, where he has proven to be a big help with his nasty style of play, specifically in the run game. New York seems to have big plans for Mauigoa. The only downside is he missed some time this summer with a stinger, which comes after he was diagnosed with a herniated disc in his back earlier this year. It’s something to keep an eye on moving forward. Round 2 (No. 37): Colton Hood, CB. It has been an up-and-down summer for Hood, but he is still competing with Deonte Banks, Greg Newsome II and Paulson Adebo for playing time at one of the two outside spots. It’s likely that Hood starts the season as a backup, but he’ll get a chance at some point. His competitiveness has flashed, which has made life difficult for receivers but also led to some penalties. 10 First-Round NFL Rookies Blowing Away Expectations at Training Camp | SI.com Arvell Reese, LB, New York Giants. When Arvell Reese was drafted No. 5 overall by the New York Giants, the premier question became whether he’d be staying at off-ball linebacker, or making the rumored transition to edge rusher. With the Giants loaded at defensive end, they decided to keep him at his college position. Reese has looked very comfortable at linebacker throughout camp. The former Ohio State standout has been displaying his athleticism and sideline-to-sideline ability.
