title: Washington Commanders 53-man roster projection after preseason finale
summary: The Commanders have employed a large roster over the spring and summer. It’s now time to trim this 91-man group to 53 active players.   We’re at that point now, with Washington’s preseason formally ending with Friday night’s 41-3 loss to the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium.   The roster limit drops by a […]
full_text: The Commanders have employed a large roster over the spring and summer. It’s now time to trim this 91-man group to 53 active players. We’re at that point now, with Washington’s preseason formally ending with Friday night’s 41-3 loss to the Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium. The roster limit drops by a bunch on Sunday at 6 p.m. ET. This is never an easy stretch in the NFL, for players who don’t make the initial cutdown or the subsequently practice squad formed. It is part of the league’s structure, with competition and fit ultimately deciding which players make the 53-man roster. After taking Washington’s training camp and full preseason slate into consideration, here’s how the roster could shape up, with some notes on folks who could be on the move right after. OFFENSE Q uarterback (3) Jayden Daniels Marcus Mariota Athan Kaliakmanis Analysis: Athan Kaliakmanis wasn’t given a spot on this roster. The seventh-round pick earned it, and Friday night’s mess didn’t take that away. He has proven a daring playmaker unafraid of pushing the ball down field. He deserves a role as the No. 3 quarterback and while developing as a signal caller. Running back (4) Bill Croskey-Merritt Rachaad White Kaytron Allen Jeremy McNichols Analysis: Jeremy McNichols has been out for some time now with a quadriceps injury , and his return timetable remains unknown. His track record as an all-around back, especially as a pass protector, is worth a spot. If he needs an IR stint, the Commanders can elevate Robert Henry Jr. from his likely destination, the practice squad. Receiver (6) Terry McLaurin Stefon Diggs Antonio Williams Jaylin Lane Treylon Burks Dyami Brown Analysis: It’s very possible that I got swayed too much by Friday night’s preseason game. Seeing Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown sit while Luke McCaffrey played changed my mind about this position group. Appropriately or not, I moved McCaffrey off the list at the last minute. Dan Quinn said some of the reasoning of who played Friday was about snaps coming off the joint practice. That didn’t change my mind. If that was all for show or to generate trade leverage for another receiver or McCaffrey simply was asked to play over others, then I’ll own it. The signs just seemed so clear on Friday night. I also originally had Jaden Bradley making it over a vet — you’ve gotta make a bold prediction somewhere — but I pulled that back and followed the breadcrumbs in this position group. Tight end (4) John Bates Chig Oknokwo Ben Sinnott Colson Yankoff Analysis: The first three on the list are givens. Colson Yankoff has proven an adept receiver and a core special teams player. With how much tight ends are featured in coordinator David Blough’s scheme, they need a fourth tight end with Yankoff’s versatility. Offensive line (9) Brandon Coleman Chris Paul Nick Allegretti Sam Cosmi Josh Conerly Jr. D.J. Humphries Trent Scott Andrew Wylie Matt Gulbin Analysis: I’ll be honest. I don’t love this position group’s construction. There are too many career tackles and not enough interior guys. Trent Scott has some experience at guard and that’ll help in reserve, with Matt Gulbin as the primary backup center. You don’t see Julian Good-Jones listed here. Maybe that’s a surprise, maybe not. He just hasn’t played well. I’d bet Washington exercises patience with recent signing D.J. Humphries and lets him acclimate over the next few weeks. I also think Washington isn’t finished with this position group, and we’ll see some adds either before or shortly after roster cuts. Oh, and Laremy Tunsil will be designated to return off IR on cut day if there’s even a shred of possibility he can come back this season. DEFENSE Defensive line (5) Daron Payne Charles Omenihu Tim Settle Shy Tuttle Javon Kinlaw Analysis: Leaving Ricky Barber – and a sixth defensive lineman overall – off the roster was a tough choice considering the rotational nature of the position group. The Commanders can make do with five and keep Barber and maybe Byron Cowart on the practice squad for use as elevations should depth be required in the early going. Edge rushers (4) Odafe Oweh K’Lavon Chaisson Joshua Josephs Jovantae Jean-Baptiste Analysis: Dorance Armstrong’s one-game suspension starts on Sunday, so he’ll be added to the group once he’s eligible to return. Jovantae Jean-Baptiste could be moved to make up for him. We’re going with four edge rushers here, especially with linebacker Leo Chenal capable of setting into a role rushing the passer, if required in a pinch. Inside linebackers (5) Sonny Styles Frankie Luvu Leo Chenal Jordan Magee Kain Medrano Analysis: Overall, this is a deep and talented group with tons of speed. Sonny Styles, Frankie Luvu and Leo Chenal are a really good frontline group. The Commanders have a quality reserve and special teams player with Jordan Magee I’m not going to be swayed by Friday’s mess, where Kain Medrano and Ale Kaho struggled. Medrano stays as an important special teams player. Cornerbacks (5) Mike Sainristil Amik Robertson Trey Amos (to IR) Rasul Douglas Fabian Moreau Analysis: Trey Amos has hardly practiced. Not in the offseason program, barely in training camp. Even if he’s not an immediate IR candidate, he’ll need time to get in shape and acclimate. That’s why five cornerbacks are necessary here, safety Tyler Owens capable of playing in the slot. Antonio Hamilton was considered, but Fabian Moreau sitting out Friday night (and Quinn’s recent compliments) suggests he’ll make the team. Safeties (5) Quan Martin Nick Cross Jeremy Reaves Tyler Owens Percy Butler Analysis: The (relatively) early Will Harris release took some drama from this position group, with Nick Cross, Quan Martin and Jeremy Reaves as the steady defensive options. Tyler Owens can play nickel back as well, providing the versatility required of coordinator Daronte Jones’ defense. Butler’s another key special teams asset. Specialists (3) Drew Stevens Tress Way Tyler Ott Analysis: No notes on this one. Stevens won the kicking job fair and square. Way and Ott are real pros.

title: Ravens 41, Commanders 3: Four takeaways from Washington preseason loss
summary: BOX SCORE  The Commanders preseason is over.   All three exhibition games are in the books, capped by Washington’s 41-3 loss on Friday night against the neighboring Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium.   This was Washington’s last official act with a 91-man offseason roster, with the NFL mandating it be trimmed to 53 players […]
full_text: BOX SCORE The Commanders preseason is over. All three exhibition games are in the books, capped by Washington’s 41-3 loss on Friday night against the neighboring Baltimore Ravens at M&T Bank Stadium. This was Washington’s last official act with a 91-man offseason roster, with the NFL mandating it be trimmed to 53 players by Sunday at 6 p.m. ET . It’s hard to say how much the preseason finale weighs in overall player evaluation as part of a far larger body of work. This contest was waged between those lower on the depth chart, with few earmarked for the 53-man roster available in this one. That still doesn’t excuse how bad the Commanders were in this contest. They couldn’t do anything right in this one and got dominated in all phases that didn’t involved Tress Way punting. I mean, it was awful. We still mined this contest for insight. Let’s examine (with a microscope) four takeaways relevant to the 2026 Commanders : Luke McCaffrey in trouble? We knew the Commanders would hold most major contributors out of the preseason finale. They ended up deeming 41 players inactive. Yeah, you read that right. This was a situation where Commanders season-ticket holders should be happy this one was played in Baltimore. That miles-long inactives list included most of the names you’d expect, featuring plenty of star power and folks you’ll see in the box score this fall. There might be some clues in those selected to play versus not and their odds of making the 53-man roster. Did it influence my 53-man roster projection, coming out late Friday night? It certainly did. Especially at receiver. Luke McCaffrey played — so did Van Jefferson – while Treylon Burks and Dyami Brown sat. Let’s read some tea leaves, shall we? Did McCaffrey draw the short straw to ensure enough targets with six receivers sitting? Is Washington shopping McCaffrey and wanting to give teams another look? Or is he firmly on the roster bubble? That last thing might be the case, as surprising as that might’ve sounded a few months back. This receiver corps is deeper than it was in 2025, especially with Stefon Diggs on board, Antonio Williams looking really good, and Jaylin Lane secure as a punt return man who can handle kickoffs. Playing doesn’t mean you’re cut, not by any stretch, but it raises an eyebrow in McCaffrey’s case. Tyler Owens brings an edge Defensive back Tyler Owens is a thumper. We saw that against the Lions, when he demolished a running back while rushing the passer, but we’ve known that for a while. Owens reminded the forgetful on Friday night, with two huge hits early in the contest. That includes one right at the goal line: GREAT hit right at the goal line by Tyler Owens who denies the ball carrier💪🏻 pic.twitter.com/Te4rMbsVHx — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 28, 2026 Owens brings a unique energy to the safety position and aggressiveness to his slot play. And let’s not forget his work on special teams play. This is a guy Washington needs deeper on the depth chart. With how he has played, Daronte Jones should be prompted to carve out a role for this physical presence. Bubble players don’t show well Commanders will form their 53-man roster based on a summer’s worth of work, not one preseason game right at the finish line. Friday’s contest won’t negate an otherwise solid preseason, but several fighting for a final roster spot seemed to falter at the finish. Linebackers Ale Kaho and Kain Medrano fit into that group, with struggles tackling and in coverage. Receiver Jaden Bradley, who has made some nice catches this preseason, fumbled returning a kick in the first half. Running back Robert Henry, who fumbled last week, had a misstep in pass protection. Interior linemen Julian Good-Jones was the third center to play, and wasn’t particularly good in that showing. Usually this third preseason game is an opportunity for a guy to go out and demand a spot on the 53. That's not happening tonight with the Commanders — Mitchell Tischler (@Mitch_Tischler) August 28, 2026 Running back Kaytron Allen isn’t on the roster bubble, but he lost a fumble on Washington’s opening drive. Trash this tape The phrasing above is definitely old-fashioned. No one uses actual tape/film anymore. And no one’s throwing a tablet in the trash. You simply select the game file, push the delete button and then hit confirm. I mean, the Commanders won’t really do it. There’s always something to teach from, but most of the Commanders players who were active for this final preseason contest won’t be making the team. Those who do will largely want to forget what happened on Friday night in Baltimore, which capped a rough week of Ravens dominance in a joint practice and then this game. If we are going to spin this segment forward, it only reinforces the fact the offensive line needs help from a depth perspective. There aren’t many reserves who look ready to play a regular-season game at this point. GM Adam Peters is gonna have to make a move a center, and maybe pick up another guard. Bottom line: Those who continue on to the regular season can’t make the types of mistakes frequently on display in this contest, where little went right. The best part? It’s over. Now on to the regular season.

title: Commanders preseason: Ricky Barber among players to watch vs. Ravens
summary: Most Commanders you’ll see featured during the 2026 campaign won’t play Friday night’s preseason finale against Baltimore.   Head coach Dan Quinn made that crystal clear this week, saying frontline players would get heavy reps in Wednesday’s joint practice against the Ravens to cap their training camp.   That means the cast you see Friday […]
full_text: Most Commanders you’ll see featured during the 2026 campaign won’t play Friday night’s preseason finale against Baltimore. Head coach Dan Quinn made that crystal clear this week, saying frontline players would get heavy reps in Wednesday’s joint practice against the Ravens to cap their training camp. That means the cast you see Friday at M&T Bank Stadium will feature those battling for spots near the bottom of the 53-man depth chart and the practice squad. That doesn’t mean this upcoming game is without merit, though you must look a little harder to find it. Most of the hay’s in the barn evaluation-wise, but finishing with a flourish may help some roster hopefuls secure a spot. Notice how you don’t see quarterback Athan Kaliakmanis or defensive back Tyler Owens listed. I think those guys are already in. There are a few players worth highlighting here that could improve their stock and standing by punctuating the preseason with a strong performance. DL Ricky Barber A first-year pro after spending most of last season on the practice squad, Ricky Barber has shown well during training camp. That’s also true of his preseason performances. While the Commanders vastly upgraded their defensive front, Johnny Newton’s torn pectoral muscle has created an opening for a young player like Barber. He leads the team with 10 tackles and a sack over the first two preseason games, and was solid when elevated from the practice squad in 2025, especially on this play. Ricky Barber's first career NFL sack. The UDFA rookie from UCF has been waiting for his opportunity to play all season. pic.twitter.com/dasUXczJ35 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) December 25, 2025 Barber surely has a practice-squad spot locked up, unless someone snags him off waivers, where he could provide insurance at the position. Barber could earn a spot should the Commanders keep six defensive linemen, though Byron Cowart’s angling for the same gig. A strong finish could help Barber in this instance, to highlight a strong body of preseason work. DB Darius Rush Credit where credit’s due: This one’s inspired by John Portis’ excellent roster case for Darius Rush, a supreme athlete and special teams maven who clearly cares about the kicking game. A team needs players like that, to champion the often thankless work done on the coverage and return units. Darius Rush with a great special teams tackle pic.twitter.com/nVkl7lSg4J — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 15, 2026 Two red zone opportunities for rookie Ja'Kobi Lane. Two incompletions. pic.twitter.com/avY8MY5zLc — Sam Cohn (@samdcohn) August 26, 2026 Showing a little something on defensive coverage in the preseason, even if it’s the tools to develop into a solid player in that area, will strengthen his case to be kept around in Washington. He might not make the 53-man roster, but he could well help this season as a practice squad elevation and continue to earn reps with hard work. LB Ale Kaho Ale Kaho has had a strong preseason, showing off the athleticism and special-teams prowess worthy of a reserve linebacker spot. Ale Kaho with the INT! Nice drop by Ale, but the pressure up front caused this. pic.twitter.com/hEeikyD29A — Tiller56 (Hogs Haven) (@Tiller56) August 15, 2026 It seems like the Commanders like Kaho and have him under strong consideration should they keep a fifth linebacker as I think they will. Fellow UCLA product Kain Medrano ’s direct competition for that spot and he’s an Adam Peters draft pick with somewhat similar traits. It’s tough to say who has the upper hand at this point – probably Medrano – and this is the type of competition that could go to the bitter end even with most decisions already made. A final evaluation could further prove his worth, though it’s nearly impossible he won’t earn a practice squad spot at minimum. WR Jaden Bradley The undrafted rookie out of UNLV has been talked about a ton over the course of this Commanders preseason, with mostly positive sentiments from players, coaches and observers alike. I mean, what’s not to love about a hard worker who makes plays like this? Jaden Bradley getting arm-barred and still making the one-handed catch! pic.twitter.com/iUCFJd66v3 — COMMANDERS FOOTBALL (@HogsHaven) August 22, 2026 His play would put him in line for a roster spot on this team, but that’s hard to imagine in an impacted position group. There are times, however, when teams take a flier on a young player with upside who plays special teams over a veteran with a defined ceiling. Could more wow plays against the Ravens sway general manager Adam Peters to keep Bradley on the 53-man roster. Could Washington get him through waivers and onto the practice squad? Probably, but it’s a risk. Maybe he’s on the initial 53-man and gets moved a week or so later. There’s so much worthy competition for the sixth receiver spot, but Bradley has a case he can keep on making Friday night. OT D.J. Humphries This player doesn’t fit the theme we’ve created for this post. Humphries is an established veteran, albeit towards the end of a standout career. He made it clear to on-site reporters following Wednesday’s joint practice that he’s not a savior at the left tackle spot. He’s here to provide depth behind Brandon Coleman. This game will offer a sneak peek of what Humphries can do at this stage, with but a small amount of scheme knowledge under his belt. Keep an eye on his game reps – there might not be many – for an indication of where he’s at after spending most of camp away from an NFL team.

title: Commanders News: Can Ale Kaho & Antonio Hamilton earn roster spots tonight?
summary: The Daily Slop – 28 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. full_text: LANDOVER, MD - AUGUST 14: Ale Kaho #51 of the Washington Commanders celebrates with teammates after intercepting a pass during the second half of a preseason game against the Miami Dolphins at Northwest Stadium on August 14, 2026 in Landover, Maryland. (Photo by Scott Taetsch/Getty Images) | Getty Images The Daily Slop – 28 August 2026 Editor’s note: Each day, Hogs Haven compiles a collection of articles, podcasts & tweets from around the web to keep you in touch with the Commanders, the NFC East, the NFL and sports in general, with a sprinkling of other stuff. Enjoy! Commanders links all squared away @CarterMachinery | #RaiseHail pic.twitter.com/rADCbxW6TB — Washington Commanders (@Commanders) August 28, 2026 Articles Sports Illustrated 5 Questions Commanders Still Must Answer Before Final Roster Cuts 3. How Many Running Backs Can Washington Keep? The running back room became a lot more interesting once the preseason started. Jacory Croskey-Merritt showed up to camp with more muscle and ready to compete, but he has what Dan Quinn has described as a lower-body issue that he’s working through. Kaytron Allen has continued strengthening his case , while Robert Henry Jr. went from being an afterthought in most roster projections to somebody Washington has to seriously consider after his performance against Miami. Jeremy McNichols looked fairly secure as the veteran fourth back entering camp before a quadriceps injury removed him from several important late-preseason opportunities. Washington then signed veteran Craig Reynolds , initially because the team simply needed another healthy running back to get through practices and games. Still, every additional body adds another option. The decision here can’t be made strictly by looking at rushing totals either. Pass protection, special teams, third-down reliability, and which backs can actually be active on game day will matter. Allen and Henry have made this a much harder decision than it seemed a month ago, and Washington now has to decide whether the young backs have done enough to change the original roster math. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders Roundtable Why Athan Kaliakmanis should replace Sam Hartman on the Commanders roster Kaliakmanis has completed 17 of 24 passes for 249 yards, averaging 10.38 yards per attempt with zero interceptions and an aggregate passer rating that reflects a quarterback playing with confidence rather than just managing the game. His 10.38 yards per attempt is elite by any standard — in the regular season, that number would rank among the best in the NFL. It’s preseason, yes. But the traits it reflects — arm talent, intermediate accuracy, downfield aggressiveness, comfort in the pocket — don’t disappear when the games start counting. The scheme fit matters too. David Blough’s offense is built on play-action, RPOs, and rollouts that require a quarterback who can plant and drive the ball downfield from unconventional platforms. Kaliakmanis looks more comfortable after two preseason games than Hartman has in three years of being in the building. To read more of this article, CLICK HERE Commanders.com Mailbag: Bill and a roster long shot (or two) Do you feel Jacory Croskey-Merritt has improved his pass blocking enough this offseason to warrant more snaps on third downs? I would say so, and it’s arguably what has stood out the most about Croskey-Merritt, who had a good camp. His struggles in that area were one of the reasons he received fewer carries in the middle of last season, despite his abilities with the ball in his hands. There’s more to being an NFL running back than carrying the ball; it’s something that every rookie player at the position must learn. I don’t think he was ever unwilling to pass block, but learning the proper techniques and physical requirements can take time. Croskey-Merritt has put his full effort into improving that area of his skill set, and it has shown up on the field. That’s going to get him more snaps on the field, and if fans have shown anything over the past year, it’s that they love when they see Bill in the lineup. Who’s your long shots for making the season-opening 53? The one that comes to my mind is Antonio Hamilton Sr. He has such a good story being an 11-year veteran who has bounced around the league. He was with the Commanders last year and performed well in spot duty. He does have some length to his frame, but what really makes him stand out is his energy and enthusiasm. He gives his all on every play, and that kind of effort matters to coaches. If he does make the team, it would likely be mostly for special teams purposes, but players like Hamilton are welcome in that unit. I have no idea how many cornerbacks they plan to keep, but if they do keep five, it wouldn’t surprise me if he was one of them. I think you could make the same case for Ale Kaho . A longer installation process should keep defenses off balance over the full 17-game slate. Washington needs variance to avoid the Miami trap The biggest risk for Blough’s offense is falling into a predictable pattern. Anderson pointed to the Miami Dolphins’ timing-based attack under coach Mike McDaniel as a cautionary tale. That system was easily dissolved once defenses realized it ran the same concepts out of the same three formations, requiring defenders only to fill three predetermined spots to shut it down. Washington cannot afford to be one-dimensional. title: How every 2026 NFL draft pick has looked in the preseason
summary: When will Fernando Mendoza start? Should we expect big things for Sonny Styles, Ja'Kobi Lane and Cashius Howell? We checked in on all 32 NFL teams' rookie classes.
full_text:
The NFL's cut-down deadline is Sunday, and the 2026 NFL season  is less than two weeks away. But before 32 NFL rosters get pared down to 53 players  each, we're doing our annual inventory of the most recent draft class through training camp.

 We asked our NFL Nation writers to size up how all 257 draftees have fared since being selected. They have updates on every player who went off the board, from No. 1 pick Fernando Mendoza to Broncos linebacker Red Murdock , this year's " Mr. Irrelevant ." Who is in line to start for their team? Who is outplaying their draft position in the preseason and could make an early impact? And which high picks are falling behind?

 Rookies are grouped by team below, and each team is listed in the order by which it made its first selection in April. That means we begin with the Raiders' class, before hitting the Jets and Cardinals and so on.

 

 
 Jump to a team: 
 ARI | ATL | BAL | BUF | CAR | CHI | CIN 
 CLE | DAL | DEN | DET | GB | HOU | IND 
 JAX | KC | LAC | LAR | LV | MIA | MIN 
 NE | NO | NYG | NYJ | PHI | PIT | SF 
 SEA | TB | TEN | WSH 

 

 
 

 Las Vegas Raiders 
 Round 1 (No. 1): Fernando Mendoza , QB.  Mendoza might not be the Week 1 starter, but signs of him being a franchise quarterback are there. Throughout training camp, players and coaches have praised the Heisman Trophy winner's improved confidence. He's unafraid of targeting tight windows. On top of that, he has a firmer grasp of the system, resulting in better command of the offense. "That's hard to do as a young guy," center Tyler Linderbaum said. "You're dealing with a lot of new things, a whole new offense. So seeing the growth in his command and operation, it's a good starting point."

 Round 2 (No. 38): Treydan Stukes , S. Stukes has picked up momentum lately. He performed well against the Texans in the second preseason game and played mostly with the first-team defense during the final week of training camp.

 Round 3 (No. 67): Keyron Crawford , edge rusher. Crawford has flashed at times during training camp while working mostly with the second-team defense. He's currently behind Maxx Crosby , Kwity Paye and Malcolm Koonce , but the Raiders like to rotate their edge rushers in games. So Crawford should get some playing time this season.

 Round 3 (No. 91): Trey Zuhn III , G/OT. The Raiders view Zuhn as an interior offensive lineman, but he has played right tackle in preseason games. It seems like Las Vegas is prepping Zuhn to be a swing tackle this season.

 

 Round 4 (No. 101): Jermod McCoy , CB. McCoy's first preseason game was rough, allowing two touchdowns. But he has looked much better since, especially in man coverage against the Texans. The Raiders will continue to be patient since McCoy hasn't played football in more than a year due to a knee injur y, but there's confidence that he'll eventually be a reliable outside corner.

 Round 4 (No. 122): Mike Washington Jr ., RB. The Raiders are expected to rely on Washington quite a bit, especially with Ashton Jeanty 's recent ankle injury . Washington's performance this preseason shows he could handle the extended workload.

 Round 5 (No. 150): Dalton Johnson , S. Johnson will be a depth piece in the secondary, with Las Vegas using him as a nickel in practice lately.

 Round 5, (No. 175): Hezekiah Masses , CB. Masses has received a fair number of first-team reps throughout training camp. There is not a ton of veteran experience among the Raiders' cornerbacks, so Masses has an opportunity to make a difference.

 Round 6 (No. 195): Malik Benson , WR. Benson has been a reliable pass catcher for both Kirk Cousins and Mendoza. Will that translate into the regular season? Only time will tell, but Benson has set himself up to get playing time.

 

 Round 7 (No. 229): Brandon Cleveland , DT.  Cleveland might have a tough climb to make the initial 53-man roster and could start the season on the practice squad. -- Ryan McFadden 

 
 

 New York Jets 
 Round 1 (No. 2): David Bailey , Edge. Bailey looks like the real deal . His first-step quickness is exceptional, and he flashes surprising power on his bull rushes. If there's a knock, it's that he needs to show more awareness in run defense. Bailey will start in the base defense and play in several sub packages. "He's everything that we expect him to be," coach Aaron Glenn said.

 Round 1 (No. 16): Kenyon Sadiq , TE. He missed virtually the entire training camp due to a setback from offseason hernia surgery . Sadiq is expected to be ready for Week 1, but the lost time will hurt his ability to make an early impact. When healthy, he's a versatile and explosive player who can line up anywhere, including the backfield. Offensive coordinator Frank Reich will have fun utilizing Sadiq, describing him as "a high-horsepower guy," but it will take a while.

 Round 1 (No. 30): Omar Cooper Jr ., WR. Many assumed Cooper would be the No. 3 receiver behind Garrett Wilson and Adonai Mitchell , but that's not a lock. Cooper lost ground in camp and is now engaged in a battle with Isaiah Williams for that job. Cooper's explosiveness isn't dazzling, and his route running needs refinement. He has lined up mostly on the outside, but he's capable of playing the slot.

 Round 2 (No. 50): D'Angelo Ponds , CB. Ponds was expected to compete for the nickel job, maybe even an outside corner position, but he missed the entire camp with a calf strain. It's fair to wonder if he will be active in Week 1, considering the lost time. It has been a frustrating summer for Ponds.

 Round 4 (No. 103): Darrell Jackson Jr ., DT. Jackson has been a pleasant surprise who has played his way into the defensive line rotation.

 Round 4 (No. 110): Cade Klubnik , QB. He doesn't have the biggest arm, but the organization loves his intangibles, which is a big reason he's the odds-on favorite to be the No. 2 quarterback.

 Round 6 (No. 188): Anez Cooper , G. He went from third team to second team after the first preseason game. Cooper will make the 53 but could be inactive on game day.

 

 Round 7 (No. 228): VJ Payne , S. Payne is expected to return soon from an early-camp injury but will be at the bottom of the 53-man roster if he's not put on the practice squad. -- Rich Cimini 

 
 

 Arizona Cardinals 
 Round 1 (No. 3): Jeremiyah Love , RB. When he was healthy, Love was everything the Cardinals imagined -- fast, quick, strong, a great route runner, great hands. His teammates raved about him and all the facets of his game. When he finally made his debut against the Raiders in the second preseason game, he ended up with a high ankle sprain and hasn't practiced or played since. He won't play again this preseason and might not practice until Week 1.

 

 Round 2 (No. 34): Chase Bisontis , G. Bisontis was put on injured reserve with a torn left MCL that he suffered during the preseason game against the Raiders. Before that, Bisontis was progressing each week, according to coach Mike LaFleur. He was likely going to be a backup but could've been inserted into the starting lineup if needed.

 Round 3 (No. 65): Carson Beck , QB. Beck is dealing with sore ribs after taking a hit during the Hall of Fame Game on Aug. 6 and hasn't practiced or played since. He was making steady growth before then, showing flashes of his arm and touch during training camp. He might be back soon, but his injury stunted his training camp progress.

 Round 4 (No. 104): Kaleb Proctor , DT. Proctor was put on season-ending IR with a torn meniscus that he suffered during OTAs.

 Round 5 (No. 143): Reggie Virgil , WR. Virgil has impressed during training camp and has put in enough good tape to likely make the team as a bottom-of-the-depth-chart receiver.

 Round 6 (No. 183): Karson Sharar , LB. Sharar dealt with injuries during OTAs and minicamp but has recovered and is starting to find his footing.

 

 Round 7 (No. 217): Jayden Williams , OT. Williams worked his way up to the second-team offensive line throughout camp, impressing…

title: 2026 NFL projected sack leaders: Top 50 pass rushers
summary: Will Aidan Hutchinson topple Myles Garrett as the sack champion? What about Micah Parsons? Seth Walder projects this season's top sack-getters.
full_text:
Myles Garrett broke the single-season sack record last season, but a different edge rusher leads our 2026 sack projections.

 That player? The Detroit Lions ' Aidan Hutchinson , who our statistical model forecasts to rack up 12.5 sacks this season.

 This is the sixth consecutive year we've run our sack forecast for veteran pass rushers based on a statistical model that uses information about a player's past performance and current circumstances to project how many sacks he will record in the upcoming season. The model's inputs include:

 
 Sack totals and rates for each of the past two seasons 
 Projected snaps, via ESPN's Mike Clay 
 Pass rush win rate, which uses data from NFL Next Gen Stats 
 Past sack rates for the quarterbacks on each player's schedule 
 Team win totals from the betting market 
 Where a player aligns 
 Age 
 
Only defensive linemen and edge rushers are included, and rookies are excluded. Also, though we recently upgraded our pass rush win rate metrics , this analysis features the legacy version of that metric. Future years will incorporate the upgrades. These projections often appear low. However, they are a projection of a player's mean outcome in 2026 -- including injuries. If we could guarantee health for every player, everyone's forecast would be much higher.
 Now, let's dive into the 2026 projections, looking at the top 10 forecasts, plus a few other notables (including one outside the top 50). There's also a top-50 list below. 

 

 
 Jump to: 
 Projected top 10 | Full top-50 list 
 More notable projections to watch 

 
 

 

 1. Aidan Hutchinson , Detroit Lions 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 12.5 
 2025 sack total: 14.5

 This is the second straight year that Hutchinson leads our sack projections, despite having never actually led the league in sacks. But everything lines up for him to have a huge season.

 Two years ago, he had a prolific first five games (7.5 sacks, 35% pass rush win rate) before suffering a season-ending leg injury . Last season, Hutchinson stayed healthy and delivered 14.5 sacks in 17 games. If anything, this projection might be underrating Hutchinson, because while his legacy pass rush win rate was above average, he moved up to fourth among edge rushers in the updated version.

 The other big reason Hutchinson's forecast is so strong is playing time. Unlike many pass rushers, Hutchinson rarely comes off the field. He played 91% of his possible defensive snaps last season, a much higher rate than players such as Will Anderson Jr . (66%) or Nik Bonitto (62%).

 Hutchinson has two other perks working in his favor, the quality of the Lions' overall team (eighth in ESPN's Football Power Index ) and the ease of their schedule (second easiest, according to FPI). That means Detroit should be ahead often, which is when sacks most frequently occur.

 
 

 

 2. Micah Parsons , Green Bay Packers 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 11.1 
 2025 sack total: 12.5

 The X factor is how much Parsons will play. Clay has Parsons projected to play 619 snaps this season, slightly down from the 669 he played in 14 games in 2025 -- which indicates a slight increase in snaps per game if Parsons were to come back from his knee injury in Week 6 and play the rest of the season. Still, it's incredible that Parsons is projected to miss a third of the season yet still manages to have the second-best forecast.

 How?

 If we compare him to Myles Garrett , Parsons had a better pass rush win rate in each of the past two seasons, more sacks per game two years ago, is more than three years younger and is on a team that blitzes more. But if there's one overriding reason Parsons is ranked here, it's the combination of win rates alongside his previous double-digit sack seasons.

 Parsons is a master of winning on a down-to-down basis but has never had more than 14 sacks in a season. But that could happen at any moment.

 

 

 3. Will Anderson Jr ., Houston Texans 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.5 
 2025 sack total: 12

 Anderson emerged as truly elite in 2025, finishing second in Defensive Player of the Year voting to go along with his 12 sacks. There's no reason to expect a drop-off this season.

 Anderson has proved himself the past two seasons in terms of sacks and pass rush win rate, is young and on a relatively good team (the Texans' win total at DraftKings is 9.5 , shaded to the over) with a particularly good defense. He and Danielle Hunter (8.7 projected sacks, 12th most) make up arguably the NFL's most fearsome pass rushing duo.

 Plus, the Texans get the additional bonus of facing a sack-friendly schedule of quarterbacks that includes games against Lamar Jackson (9.8% sack rate), Justin Herbert (8.8%), Jaxson Dart (8.5%) and Cam Ward (9.4%) twice.

 

 

 4. Nik Bonitto , Denver Broncos 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.3 
 2025 sack total: 14

 Bonitto backed up his breakout 13.5-sack campaign in 2024 with 14 sacks in 2025. This season, he gets the benefit of being part of a Broncos defense that is not only strong overall (with great cornerbacks) but also blitzes at an above-average rate.

 If there's one thing holding Bonitto back, it's playing time. Last season, he only played 62% of Denver's defensive snaps and was in only 60% of the time in clear pass-rushing situations. That puts a ceiling on his forecast. In addition, Bonitto is a player we might be overrating based on the use of the legacy win rates, which were higher on him than the updated version released a week ago. Still, this is a mighty strong projection.

 

 

 5. Myles Garrett , Los Angeles Rams 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 10.1 
 2025 sack total: 23

 Yes, I'm as surprised as you are that Garrett is not No. 1 on this list. Even though I know how the model works, I still thought the NFL-record 23 sacks from last season would be enough to put him over the top. Not quite, it turns out!

 There are three primary factors working against Garrett:

 
 1. He is 30 years old 
 2. The Rams blitzed only 19% of the time last season, the second-lowest rate in the NFL 
 3. Los Angeles faces a quarterback slate that takes sacks less frequently than average 
 
 That's enough to hold back Garrett's projection, even coming off a record season in which he was the NFL's Defensive Player of the Year . And his age is a definite factor. While it's possible Garrett will be the same type of elite player well into his 30s, this model considers the drop-off of some previous edge rushers at this point in their careers.

 Do I think having Garrett fifth is underselling him a bit? I do, especially since the model is not considering the possibility of Aaron Donald unretiring and taking some heat off him. But there are real variables that are holding back Garrett's 2026 sack projection.

 

 

 

 6. Brian Burns , New York Giants 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.7 
 2025 sack total: 16.5

 Burns has always been a very good pass rusher -- and something of a pass rush win rate darling -- and exploded for 16.5 sacks in his second season in New York. And the Giants' pass rush has gotten even deeper.

 Those 16.5 sacks are enough to launch Burns, 28, into the top 10. But he has a few things working against him. His forecast is negatively affected by only having 8.5 sacks in 17 games in 2024. And while the Giants have a great pass rush, they aren't expected to be a great team. Middling teams don't play with a lead as often, which means fewer desperate opponents frequently passing to catch up.

 

 

 7. Nick Bosa , San Francisco 49ers 
 Projected mean 2026 sack total: 9.4 
 2025 sack total: 2

 This assumes that Bosa is healthy enough to play Week 1, which isn't a guarantee right now. The star edge rusher has been out for most of training camp with soreness and tendinitis as he works his way back from a torn ACL suffered last September.

 Despite the injury, Bosa's previous history is enough to include him in the top 10. In 2024, Bosa recorded nine sacks and also ranked fifth…

title: Why more NFL teams than ever are using GoPros on their QBs
summary: Six NFL teams are using GoPro cameras on their quarterbacks, but not always for the reasons you might think.
full_text:
ASHBURN, Va. -- Washington Commanders quarterbacks coach D.J. Williams heard something that resonated with him after listening to quarterback Jayden Daniels call a play in the huddle.

 It wasn't the third-year quarterback giving additional instructions to his offensive line, running backs or receivers. It wasn't words of encouragement to the unit, either.

 It was ... singing.

 As Daniels surveyed the defense at the line of scrimmage, he was crooning along to the song "Here We Go Now" blasting over the practice facility's loudspeaker.

 

 Then, he called out the cadence, took the snap and delivered a strike to third-year receiver Luke McCaffrey for a touchdown. Williams saw the completion live, but he heard the rest later while rewatching practice thanks to what was attached to Daniels' helmet: a GoPro camera.

 "He was bobbing his head, singing the song and then he said 'hut' and made the play," Williams said.

 The Commanders are one of six teams -- along with the  Miami Dolphins , Cleveland Browns , Dallas Cowboys , Philadelphia Eagles and New England Patriots  -- that have equipped the tiny, mountable devices on their quarterbacks' helmets this summer. The reasons vary: In some cases, it's for the vision the camera provides, which helps coaches and players see each play from the quarterback's vantage point. In others, the value is in giving coaches a peek into the communication taking place on the field, helping them get deeper insight into how QBs and other players -- such as the center making protection calls -- are communicating at the line and in the huddle. The cameras have even been experimented with on defense.

 Washington, particularly, has found the camera useful to gauge Daniels' comfort level and progress in new offensive coordinator David Blough's system, but others haven't seen the need for the technology. The Kansas City Chiefs , for example, have never used a GoPro on their quarterbacks. Instead, coach Andy Reid stands roughly 10 yards behind the offense during 7-on-7 and full-team sessions.

 "I'm a versatile GoPro," Reid said, laughing.

 For those teams that do use them, the GoPro can provide help, particularly if there's a young quarterback or a new offense -- such as in Cleveland, where the Browns have a new scheme and three quarterbacks who are either rookies or in their second season.

 "It's a valuable tool," said first-year Browns coach Todd Monken.

 

 

 THIS ISN'T THE first time football teams have used the technology. GoPros have been used in college for a while. Former NFL quarterback Nathan Peterman said he used one while he played at Pitt in 2015 and 2016. The Arena League used an in-helmet camera in 2014 that was designed to give viewers, not so much the coaches and quarterback, a different perspective. The Miami Dolphins and Pittsburgh Steelers experimented with helmet cameras in 2023 , and the Eagles had used one as far back as 2016.

 This summer and offseason, NFL teams have adopted the cameras more than ever. Perhaps the most obvious reason is the view a camera provides for evaluation purposes.

 Browns starting quarterback Deshaun Watson said he likes the vision it highlights. He can be taken back into the huddle to see how the offensive players are responding to him through their body language and eye contact. Then, he can review his post-snap progression -- where he's looking on each pass play.

 "It's a good point of view, a different point of view for us to learn and study," Watson said.

 Miami quarterback Malik Willis , who signed with the Dolphins as a free agent following two seasons in Green Bay, is using a GoPro for the first time this year. He, like Watson, said he uses it to check his eye progression and likes being able to see the different landmarks on the field where they want plays to attack.

 Willis said the ability to review reps from his own perspective provides him with lessons and information he wouldn't have received otherwise.

 "Spatial awareness and understanding some of the coverage recognition stuff," Willis said. "It gives you the same view you had when you were on the field and then you can see what coverage it went to and it's like -- you can take that with you, because you will be in that same position again. It's different from looking at it from the sky view, but it's awesome. I love it."

 

 The other reason NFL teams have gone to GoPros this summer is perhaps more surprising: the audio.

 "... Unless you want to be standing in the huddle to hear what's actually being relayed from myself, to them, to the players," Monken said. "And then it allows you to pre-snap and then, post-snap, get an idea where their eyes are. Are they in the right place?"

 The sound capture allows coaches to hear how a quarterback manages the huddle and the line of scrimmage.

 "So much is done pre-snap, and that's what the GoPro gives you," said Browns quarterbacks coach Mike Bajakian. "It gives you the quarterback's thought process and his communication."

 That's why Minnesota mounted one on veteran QB Sam Darnold in 2024. The Vikings wanted to help then-rookie quarterback J.J. McCarthy catch up on the offense while he was sidelined with a torn ACL. They wanted him to see Darnold's vision and how he spoke in the huddle -- how clear and concise McCarthy would need to be when relaying information, calling out each play with conviction.

 They presented him the information by rewatching practices from the GoPro's perspective on a large wall in their draft room.

 "It's pretty cool," offensive coordinator Wes Phillips said at the time.

 

 

 GOPROS ARE NOT for everyone, however. Reid has been a head coach three years longer than the GoPro, created in 2002, has existed. Some other teams and coaches find similar benefits using different means.

 Chicago Bears offensive coordinator Press Taylor said he remembers seeing quarterback Chase Daniel use one in 2016, when Taylor was an assistant quarterbacks coach with the Philadelphia Eagles . But it's not something the Bears use now. Instead, he said they get the same information by using pole cameras, which he estimates are around 8 or 9 feet tall and positioned about 7 yards behind the quarterback. They're also miked up.

 "It's probably very similar," Taylor said.

 The New York Jets used a GoPro last year, but new offensive coordinator Frank Reich and quarterbacks coach Bill Musgrave opted against the technology this season. Instead, the Jets are using a camera for a down-the-line view, aiding the defensive line so they can tell if they're aligned onside. Coach Aaron Glenn said players would often ask if they lined up offside. Now they can tell.

 "The film doesn't lie, so we get a chance to watch it that way," Glenn said. "Every coach is different, and I want those guys to be able to coach the way they feel like they can get those guys to improve, so that'd be the reason why [they stopped using GoPro]."

 There are other ways quarterbacks try to enhance their game. Washington's Daniels has used a virtual reality headset since his final year at LSU, when he won the Heisman Trophy. He prefers those visuals over the GoPro.

 "I don't go back and watch it," Daniels said of the GoPro footage, before adding that he does value the audio component, "because it's on top of the helmet and my eyes might be somewhere else, but my helmet's that way."

 Commanders backup quarterback Marcus Mariota is entering his 12th NFL season. He said he has been open to using a GoPro for the first time. He cited his background playing at the University of Oregon, where they were "always pushing the envelope."

 Mariota agrees on the audio benefits, but, like Daniels, also sees limitations with the visual element. He said it shows a wider range of vision than he sees on the field. Sometimes he'll be asked if he saw how a linebacker or corner was situated because the GoPro picked it up.

 "You're like, not really because I'm kind of facing a different way," Mariota said.…

title: Biggest decisions facing the Raiders ahead of roster cutdown deadline
summary: We answer the five biggest questions the Raiders are facing ahead of cutdown day.
full_text:
HENDERSON, Nev. -- Tough decisions are ahead for Las Vegas Raiders coach Klint Kubiak.

 Kubiak, general manager John Spytek and the rest of the staff will come together to cut the Raiders' roster down to 53 players ahead of Sunday's 6 p.m. ET deadline. The time leading up will feature countless hours watching film and evaluating the players on the roster. With Las Vegas first in line on the waiver wire, the team will also look at the moves around the league to see if there's an opportunity to add help.

 "You develop relationships with these guys since April, and they give you their heart and soul and all their time, and eventually, it comes down to this," Kubiak said. "But there's also so many examples of guys that have been cut and make practice squads and make a team, or guys that get claimed by other teams, or guys that get cut five times and make 12-year careers."

 Here is a look at some of the biggest decisions facing the Raiders:

 

 Should the Raiders keep three quarterbacks? 

 Kubiak said the team has been discussing possibly having three quarterbacks ( Kirk Cousins , Fernando Mendoza and Aidan O'Connell ) on the 53-man roster. If the Raiders keep O'Connell, he would be another strong voice in the quarterbacks room, as his experience could benefit Mendoza. Each quarterback has said that they have learned from one another throughout the offseason and training camp.

 

 "It's going to be some hard decisions on who's [QB1], who's [QB2], and that's not a decision that we have to make today," Kubiak said. "But those are discussions that are ongoing."

 O'Connell believes he can still be a starting quarterback in the NFL, and the opportunity to do so is no longer present in Las Vegas. Cousins is expected to be the Week 1 starter, while rookie Mendoza waits until it's time for him to be the next face of the franchise.

 If the Raiders cut O'Connell, who is an unrestricted free agent in 2027, they would save $3.64 million in cap space, according to Over The Cap data. Las Vegas, however, could try to find a trade partner. He would be an intriguing trade candidate for any team looking for an experienced backup with starter experience.

 In 17 career starts, O'Connell has thrown for 3,579 yards, 18 touchdowns, nine interceptions and a completion percentage of 62.5%. On top of that, O'Connell has played well during training camp, and he orchestrated an impressive go-ahead touchdown drive in the preseason win over the Houston Texans last week.

 

 What to do with the depth at wide receiver? 

 Kubiak called out the wide receivers last week, demanding improvement. The position group entered training camp as one of the weak spots on the roster. Ahead of the roster cutdown deadline, there are still a ton of questions regarding the wideouts. The Raiders do not have a true WR1. The door is open for Tre Tucker and Jalen Nailor to emerge. Either way, both should be quality complementary players in the passing game, which revolves around tight end Brock Bowers .

 The real question is how the Raiders will fill out the rest of the WR room. Jack Bech can be a big-body receiver -- 6-1, 214 pounds -- in the slot and adds run-blocking support. But he has had an underwhelming camp, for the most part, whereas rookie Malik Benson has flashed multiple times in practice and games. But will his strong play translate in the regular season against stronger competition? As for second-year wide receiver Dont'e Thornton Jr. , he hasn't practiced since Aug. 7 because of an undisclosed injury. It wouldn't be out of the realm of possibility that he begins the season on injured reserve.

 When factoring those elements, the Raiders' depth at wide receiver is not in a good spot. And Las Vegas might have to wait until the offseason to find a long-term solution at the position. For now, it might be best for Las Vegas to improve its wide receiver depth through free agency or trade. Recently, the Texans acquired Kayshon Boutte from the New England Patriots via trade. The Raiders could do something similar. Or Las Vegas could wait on how roster cuts play out across the league and see if there is a veteran pass catcher available who could make an impact.

 

 

 Will Ashton Jeanty's injury force the team to add RB help? 

 Second-year running back Jeanty is recovering from a likely ankle sprain. Even though the Raiders are optimistic that Jeanty's injury is not long term, it's still uncertain if he will miss time during the regular season.

 If Jeanty doesn't miss time, the Raiders should be comfortable with the current depth at running back. That means the team will ask a lot from rookie Mike Washington Jr ., but he has shown that he's capable of handling the workload. In three preseason games, Washington had 23 carries for 168 yards. Meanwhile, Dylan Laube played well during camp, showing he could be a nice backup option.

 But things would get tricky if Jeanty misses more time than anticipated, as they might have to seek outside help. The current list of free agent running backs is pretty thin. But that will change in a few days after teams trim their rosters. Still, it seems like the Raiders should be fine at running back.

 

 The case for Cian Slone or Patrick Johnson to make the 53-man roster 

 One of the hardest decisions that faces the Raiders will be to figure out who gets the final spot at edge rusher. It will come down to undrafted rookie Slone and sixth-year veteran Johnson. Both players have made plays on defense and special teams in the preseason.

 Slone, 23, is younger and has impressed teammates and coaches with his high motor. Johnson, 28, has been the most productive defensive player in three preseason games. In 81 defensive snaps, Johnson racked up 11 tackles, two sacks, six pressures and four run stuffs. It's also worth noting that Johnson played mostly with the second-team defense in the preseason finale against the San Francisco 49ers . He remained on the sideline, watching the third-team finish the game.

 Slone has the upside, but Johnson might have the best chance to make a bigger impact early, which should weigh into the decision after  Keyron Crawford was carted off the field because of an ankle injury.

 

 Is there room to keep Jordan Meredith ? 
 

 Among the players from last year's roster on the bubble is interior offensive lineman Meredith. The fifth-year player has started in 19 games over the past two seasons, splitting time between guard and center. Meredith is best suited at guard, even though the past two coaching staffs have used him at center.

 Based on the Raiders' interior lineman situation, it might be tough for Meredith to make the initial 53-man roster. Right guard Jackson Powers-Johnson and Caleb Rogers have been alternating starting reps. It seems like Powers-Johnson will end up being the starter, meaning Rogers will be a strong backup to play either guard spot.

 Rookie Trey Zuhn III played at every position on the offensive line this summer. Against the 49ers, Zuhn lined up at center with other members of the starting offensive line, and he also played at right tackle with the second-team. Kubiak has been impressed with Zuhn's ability to play multiple positions.

 But Meredith could be on the outside looking in.

title: Is Vikings rookie Caleb Banks healthy and ready to perform?
summary: It appears Banks is over his foot surgeries, but questions linger about the first-rounder's conditioning.
full_text:
EAGAN, Minn. -- The biggest question facing the Minnesota Vikings ' top draft pick this summer was clear: Is defensive lineman Caleb Banks healthy after undergoing three surgeries to repair a broken left foot?

 The answer has been a clear affirmative. Banks has missed only one practice, and that was a planned rest day, while playing 47 defensive snaps in the first two preseason games. 

 Which brings us to the second-biggest question: Can he play at the level the Vikings projected when they made him the No. 18 selection of the 2026 draft?

 That answer is less obvious.

 The consensus after watching Banks move through his first training camp is that he is not yet ready to dominate NFL offensive lines. Opponents have found ways to get lower position on his 6-foot-6 frame and push him backwards, and Banks himself acknowledged last weekend that "I'm definitely not in shape" after missing most of his final college season and all of the Vikings' spring practices because of the foot injury. 

 At the very least, however, Banks appears to have joined nose tackle Domonique Orange -- a third-round draft pick -- in earning a regular spot in the Vikings' initial defensive line rotation. 

 "The one thing about [Banks] is he works and it's important to him," defensive coordinator Brian Flores said. "And in my experience, guys who work at it and continually try to improve, they improve and develop."

 

 Banks was one of the more intriguing draft decisions in the NFL this spring. Under the leadership of interim general manager Rob Brzezinski, the Vikings had Banks ranked among the top 10 prospects in the draft. Some people in the organization mentioned him in the context of a long line of Hall of Fame-level defensive linemen in franchise history, from the Purple People Eaters to John Randle to Kevin Williams . But after the foot injury limited him to four games in his final season at Florida and then resurfaced at the NFL combine with another fracture, Banks' draft value grew less certain .

 The Vikings' medical staff examined his foot during a predraft visit and emerged confident that it would fully heal in time for the season. That projection has proved accurate, but the residual loss of conditioning has been obvious to all. Banks joked after Saturday's  13-3 preseason loss to the Baltimore Ravens that he needed to start running more post-practice gassers.

 Flores concurred with that assessment, but believes it puts Banks in a category with many other players.

 

 "He's right that he may not feel like he's in the best of condition," Flores said, "but I'm not sure he really even knows what that looks like, just like any other rookie. And I don't blame him for that. It's something he's going to have to learn on the fly. He's gotten a little bit of a feel for it in these preseason games, what the first half looks like, what starting the third quarter looks like.

 "With these rookies, there's no way for them to step in and think that they're going to have the experience to really know what NFL football's like. But I would say our group's doing a good job. Our coaches are doing a really good job of trying to get them prepared and as ready to go as we possibly can, knowing that we can't mimic what an NFL game is like. And so I think he's right to feel like, 'Hey, I'm not where I need to be.' And I don't think he'll really know until we're really in it."

 Judging Banks' play as the season begins will require the recent context of Flores' scheme, which has often asked defensive linemen to focus on assignments that don't result in splash plays .

 

 Banks did some gentle freelancing in the 13-10 preseason win against the New York Giants  on Aug. 15. After recognizing that he was not going to be double teamed, he used a swim move to get past guard Francis Mauigoa and into the backfield as the Giants handed the ball to running back Cam Skattebo . But Banks missed the tackle, later saying that Skattebo was "faster than I expected," and the play went for 7 yards on first down. 

 Asked about that decision this week, Flores smiled. He made clear that he wants players to have an "element of freedom" and to experiment in training camp and the preseason, in part to learn the value of carrying out the original assignments.

 "That's part of the learning process though," Flores said. "And I ask those guys to try to jump inside. See if you can get there or take the edge. But if you're [past] the quarterback, now you've learned that you probably shouldn't do that. Or you jump inside and they get outside of you, now you've learned. It's like a little kid with a hot stove. He doesn't know it burns until it burns. But that's what training camp is for. That's what preseason's for."

title: Titans still high on Carnell Tate despite lack of preseason production
summary: Tennessee still believes Carnell Tate will be the playmaker it envisioned after making him the No. 4 pick in April.
full_text:
NASHVILLE, Tenn. -- After making a big splash when he first stepped onto the field in OTAs, things have been relatively quiet during the last couple of weeks for Tennessee Titans rookie receiver Carnell Tate . 

 He had carried that initial momentum into minicamp and the start of training camp, but he didn't record a catch in two preseason games on five targets after playing a total of 35 snaps with the starting offense.

 That's hardly the statistical start anyone wanted, but Tate still remains highly regarded by the coaching staff. And they still feel he will be a top playmaker in their offense.

 "I have a great amount of confidence in Tate and how he goes about his business, what he does on the practice field," offensive coordinator Brian Daboll said Tuesday. "Look, I think everybody would love to have 15 catches. But he's doing the right stuff. He's in a good headspace. He's where he's supposed to be."

 

 Tate said he understands the ball isn't always going to find everybody and isn't letting the lack of production over a few preseason games frustrate him.

 "Not every day is going to be your best day and not every game is going to be your best game," Tate said. "I'm just staying levelheaded, going out to compete each and every day. You just got to know how to play with emotion, not let emotion play with you. That's the biggest thing. I just stay calm. Don't get too high. Don't get too low."

 Titans receivers coach Greg Lewis challenges his receivers to know all the pass catching spots in the offense. This way they're interchangeable and get a better understanding of the full passing concept on each play. Despite being a rookie, Tate has been able to pick up the concepts and execute accordingly.

 Lewis called Tate one of the best rookies he's worked with coming from college to the NFL. He praised Tate for the mature way he carries himself, specifically the study habits and how well he's able to implement what he learns on the field.

 Moving across the formation is nothing new for Tate, who noted how as a freshman at Ohio State he had to move to the slot when Emeka Egbuka suffered an ankle injury. Tate also played multiple spots as a sophomore to create mismatches for himself and teammate Jeremiah Smith. This also helped him post 51 receptions for 875 yards and nine touchdowns in his final season.

 Now Tate will be moving around to help create favorable matchups for himself and veteran wideouts  Wan'Dale Robinson  and Calvin Ridley . Having them in the room has also helped Tate digest the playbook. Both Robinson and Ridley have played for Daboll in the past. Robinson with the New York Giants and Ridley at Alabama.

 "I'm leaning on guys that have been around guys that have been around [Daboll]," Tate said. "I pick up and learn as much as possible from Wan'Dale because he's played every position in the offense and has been with [Daboll] for the past four years. And [Ridley] is familiar with the offense as well."

 One of Tate's best plays this summer came from the slot, when he made a leaping catch down the field during a team period as the Titans prepared for joint practice with the  Seattle Seahawks . Tate collided with safety Kevin Winston Jr . but managed to hold onto the pass from Cam Ward despite the contact. He didn't return to practice that day but was on the field when the Titans returned to practice two days later.

 That explosive play is exactly what the Titans were thirsty for when they made him the No. 4 overall pick in April after seeing him catch five touchdowns of 40 yards or more during his career at Ohio State. Various draft analysts lauded Tate for his polished route-running, natural hands-catching ability and fantastic body control while calling him an immediate impact player.

 

 Lewis said he feels Tate has all the skills to be an impactful player. But he challenged Tate to play with more violence as a receiver "every single day, on every single rep, in every single opportunity, whether it's a drill, meeting or any game situation."

 Tate showed some of that in a joint practice against the  Chicago Bears  on Thursday, hauling in two touchdowns from Ward, who targeted him12 times with seven of them resulting in completions. Tate said he's continuing to build on his connection with Ward and he has stayed ready for the ball to come his way.

 "He wants the ball," Ward said. "So when it comes his way, he's urgent to it. He goes up and high points it. He's been great and may not have the splash plays as of late, but he's going to be a key reason why we have success on offense. No. 14 is going to be a playmaker for sure."

 Tennessee now heads into its preseason finale Saturday ( 6 p.m. ET, NFL Network ) against the Bears with Ward giving praise to the way Tate aggressively attacks the football, and despite things not clicking yet on game days, it's that aggression in other moments (like Thursday) that have made Ward still go to Tate. 

 "He's got a dog mentality," Lewis said of Tate. "You ain't going to see it. You just see him go out there and dice you up, not say anything and then come back and do it again."
